polymarket-5238401.text:
A third U.S.
aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East over the weekend as President Donald Trump continued to ratchet up economic pressure on Iran and threaten renewed military strikes.
USS Theodore Roosevelt pulled into the U.S.
Central Command area of responsibility Sunday, according to The Wall Street Journal and Axios, citing unidentified U.S.
officials.
CENTCOM did not directly answer an email query about Roosevelt, instead referring Stars and Stripes to an X post late Monday announcing that the carrier was in the command’s area of responsibility.
Also on Sunday, Iran launched six drones targeting the Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain, the first such attack on the island nation since early September, according to news reports.
Bahrain said it had intercepted and destroyed several projectiles in Iranian air attacks while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed “successful impact.”
Manama, the country’s capital, is home to Naval Support Activity Bahrain, which includes U.S.
Naval Forces Central Command/U.S.
Fifth Fleet.
Riffa is about 11 miles from NSA Bahrain.
Iranian missile and drone attacks have repeatedly struck the Navy installation since the war began in February.
The attacks came as Trump has appeared to pivot away from diplomatic efforts to end the war with Iran, instead leaning on a U.S.
maritime blockade, other economic pressure and threats of renewed strikes to pressure Tehran into making concessions.
Iran has intensified its attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters in recent weeks, with attacks reaching levels not seen since the U.S.
and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran.
Those days have long since passed,” Trump said Thursday on Truth Social.
“We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
In enforcing the blockade, U.S.
forces have turned away 150 commercial ships and disabled five others, blocking Tehran from exporting more than $30 billion in crude oil, CENTCOM said earlier this month.
Some analysts have warned that intensifying economic pressure could provoke further Iranian aggression.
“If history is any guide, Iran will at some point resort to violence to try to force Washington to reconsider,” Bilal Saab, a Chatham House associate fellow wrote in an analysis published last week.
He added Iranian efforts to escalate would be unlikely to sway Washington, which is convinced the blockade is working.
There have been at least 14 attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters so far this month, following 35 attacks in October, according to data from the U.K.
Maritime Operations Center and the International Maritime Organization.
By comparison, there were 19 confirmed attacks on ships in the region in March.
Roosevelt’s arrival marks the second time this year the U.S.
has had three aircraft carriers in the Middle East.
It’s unclear, though, whether the U.S.
will keep three carriers in the region or whether Roosevelt will relieve Japan-based USS George Washington or USS George H.W.
Bush.
Those carriers have been in the Middle East since August and April, respectively.
Bush relieved USS Gerald R.
Ford, which ended a record-setting 326-day deployment in May.
Last week, families of service members aboard Bush were reportedly told during a meeting in Norfolk, Va.
with acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao that the carrier would not be home for the holidays, according to reports from Military Times and MS Now as well as the local newspaper, The Virginian-Pilot.
The carrier departed Norfolk on March 31 for a scheduled deployment.
Citing operational security, the Navy declined to answer Stars and Stripes’ questions about whether Bush’s deployment had been extended.
Operational demands on forward-deployed sailors and Marines are “always unpredictable,” the service said.
polymarket-5238401.title: Stars and Stripes, Navy carrier coverage (Roosevelt, Middle East, Iran attacks, Bahrain)

polymarket-5238401.text:
A U.S.
aircraft carrier has departed the Middle East, leaving two others in the region as Iranian attacks on neighboring countries threaten to widen the war.
The departure comes as President Donald Trump reportedly considers a major expansion of U.S.
airstrikes against Iran in an effort to break a prolonged military stalemate.
USS George Washington left the region earlier this week following the arrival of the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt.
That leaves Roosevelt and USS George H.W.
Bush as the two remaining carriers in the Middle East.
Washington is now conducting routine operations in the U.S.
7th Fleet area of operations, the Navy said.
It wasn’t clear whether Washington’s escorts, including the destroyer USS Shoup, also left the Middle East.
The carrier’s departure leaves at least 15 Navy warships in the Arabian Sea.
All told, there are some 50,000 U.S.
military personnel in the Middle East.
Washington, the Navy’s only forward-deployed aircraft carrier, entered the Middle East in August to relieve USS Abraham Lincoln amid concerns about the well-being and mental health of its service members.
Bush departed Norfolk, Va., in late March and arrived in the Middle East in April.
Families of sailors aboard Bush reportedly learned during a recent meeting with acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao that the carrier would not be home for the holidays.
Earlier this month, Trump signaled a shift away from diplomacy seemingly to rely on a U.S.
maritime blockade against Iranian ports, other economic pressure and the threat of renewed large-scale military strikes against Iran.
Trump is weighing a joint four- to seven-day airstrike campaign with Israel that would focus on Iran’s missile and drone stockpiles along with energy facilities, The New York Times reported Wednesday, citing unidentified U.S.
and Israeli officials.
The White House did not directly answer questions about options Trump was said to be reviewing, instead referring to comments the president recently made on Fox News.
During a Wednesday interview about Iran potentially using biological weapons, Trump did not say if he was considering renewed, large-scale strikes against Iran.
But he did seem to indicate that any potential U.S.
action could be weeks away.
“We’re going to have a new year coming up and will see what happens after January 1st,” Trump said.
“But they’ve been nasty, these are nasty people.”
During a Sunday interview with Fox News, Vice President JD Vance said Trump was considering several alternatives including declaring U.S.
operations complete and exerting additional diplomatic or military pressure.
Trump would not let the conflict become a “forever war,” Vance said.
Iran launched drone strikes this week against Bahrain and Kuwait, targeting U.S.
military equipment.
Bahrain’s capital, Manama, hosts a major hub of the U.S.
Navy, while Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait is an important installation for the U.S.
Air Force.
In response, the U.S.
launched precision airstrikes on an Iranian military site on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf.
Meanwhile, the U.K.
Maritime Trade Operations Center on Wednesday reported separate attacks on two vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, including one that resulted in a shipboard fire and a missing mariner.
So far this month, Iran has attacked at least 18 vessels transiting in or near the strait, according to reports from the UKMTO, a British military organization that monitors threats to commercial shipping in the region.
polymarket-5238401.title: Stars and Stripes, George Washington leaves Middle East

polymarket-5238401.text:
NAVAL STATION NORFOLK, Va.
— The sun peeked over the horizon tinting the haze gray hull of carrier USS George H.W.
Bush (CVN-77) orange while sailors on Pier 14 busied themselves preparing for the carrier to shove off across the Atlantic.
The mood of families at the pier Tuesday was subdued without the pomp and cheer of last summer’s deployment of USS Gerald R.
Ford (CVN-78) – the last carrier to leave the East Coast.
With the early morning departure and a brisk wind, most families had said goodbye to their sailors the night before to meet the rolling curfew that had the crew aboard by 10 p.m.
Monday.
For the last 25 days, ship’s company of Bush and Naval Sea Systems Command rushed to make the last repairs in the month after certifying to deploy while the crew spent time with their families ahead of Tuesday’s morning departure.
East Coast carrier deployments for the last several years have been prone to extensions beyond the standard six months with families preparing for sailors to be gone for eight months or more.
Deputy Fleet Forces commander Vice Adm.
John Gumbleton gave the sailors a pep talk over the carrier’s intercom, the sound carrying down to the families on the pier.
“Believe in your shipmates.
Believe in the officers and chiefs that will lead you,” he said over the 1MC.
“We’re aware the uncertainty of these deployment dates has caused anxiety and frustration.
Our goal was to preserve as much time to make the ship ready, and for you to have time with your loved ones… In the months ahead, be honest with yourself and look out for one another.”
Just before 9 a.m., Bush sailors marched to the edge of the flight deck of the carrier gripping their covers tight to keep them from blowing off their heads in the 30-mile-per-hour gusts as they manned the rails.
At least two “Dixie Cups” were lost to the wind by the time the sailors were in place.
Speaking to reporters at the pier, Carrier Strike Group 10 commander Rear Adm.
Alexis Walker gave no hints to reporters on the pier ahead of Bush’s departure on where the strike group was headed.
“There is a published length of deployment, but who knows how long it’s going to take, and when our job is done around the world, then we’ll come home,” he said responding to reports that Bush was joining naval forces amassed in the Middle East in support of the U.S.
and Israel’s war with Iran.
Bush’s commander Capt.
Robert Bibeau said, “I use the firefighter analogy.
If you call the fire station and ask the firefighters where the fire is going to be tomorrow, they don’t know.
But they do know that they’re ready, they want to be there, and they’re going to solve the problem.”
Carrier Air Wing 7 will be embarked on the carrier.
Bush and the air wing will join with its guided-missile destroyer escorts USS Mason (DDG-87), USS Donald Cook (DDG-75) and USS Ross (DDG-71) with the staff of Norfolk-based Destroyer Squadron 22 embarked.
The deployment will also be the first East Coast use of the Navy’s CMV-22B Osprey as a carrier onboard delivery aircraft with a detachment from the “Mighty Bisons” of Fleet Logistics Multi-Mission Squadron (VRM) 40 embarked.
Carrier Air Wing 7 Includes:
- The “Jolly Rogers” of Strike Fighter Squadron (VFA) 103 – F/A-18F – from Naval Air Station Oceana, Va.
- The “Rampagers” of VFA 83 – F/A-18E – from Naval Air Station Oceana.
- The “Gunslingers” of VFA 105 – F/A-18E – from Naval Air Station Oceana.
- The “Wildcats” of VFA 131 – F/A-18E – Naval Air Station Oceana.
- The “Patriots” of Electronic Attack Squadron (VAQ) 140 – EA-18G – from Naval Air Station Whidbey Island, Wash.
- The “Sun Kings” of Airborne Command and Control Squadron (VAW) 116 – E-2D – from Naval Air Station Point Mugu, Calif.
- The “Mighty Bison” of Fleet Logistics Multi-Mission Squadron (VRM) 40 — CMV-22B — from Naval Air Station Norfolk.
- The “Grandmasters” of Helicopter Maritime Strike Squadron (HSM) 46 – MH-60R – from Naval Air Station Jacksonville, Fla.
- The “Nightdippers” of Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 5 – MH 60S – from Naval Air Station Norfolk, Va.
The strike group will finish assembling later this week, USNI News understands.
“We do know where we’re going, but as with always, we will go where the nation needs us,” Walker said.
“Depending on what pops up in the world, we’ll be responsive and flexible and ready to go wherever we’re needed.”
While the Bush Carrier Strike Group‘s leadership emphasized the unpredictability of carrier deployments, the Navy’s focus has been supporting the ongoing strikes in Iran as part of the month-long Operation Epic Fury.
The Gerald R.
Ford Carrier Strike Group is set to push their deployment to 11 months, Chief of Naval Operations Adm.
Daryl Caudle said Tuesday.
“We’re going to see a record-breaking deployment by Ford.
We will probably go into the 11th month of deployment operations.
For those who are not in the Navy, that’s an extraordinary thing to even think about… My hat’s off to the Ford,” Caudle said during a U.S.
Naval Institute and CSIS event on Tuesday.
If Ford’s deployment extends past April 15, the carrier will have been deployed for 294 days, breaking the post-Vietnam War carrier deployment record.
As of Tuesday, Ford has been deployed for 280 days.
The carrier anchored off the coast of Split, Croatia, following a brief stop for repairs at Naval Station Souda Bay, Greece, after the ship suffered a fire that started in the carrier’s laundry.
The fire displaced hundreds of sailors aboard the ship and required the Navy to dispatch mattresses to Europe pulled from John F.
Kennedy (CVN-79) and clothes from across the fleet.
In a statement, U.S.
6th Fleet said the crew and other engineers had rehabilitated seven berthing compartments and that military and civilian law enforcement were continuing to investigate the fire that started in the ship’s laundry facilities.
“She’s going to be back on station again here soon and [then] on some much-deserved leave,” Caudle said.

polymarket-5238401.text:
NORFOLK, Va.
— Military families across Hampton Roads are facing more uncertainty after learning that the USS George H.W.
Bush Carrier Strike Group's deployment is being extended for a second time, potentially keeping thousands of sailors away from home for an entire year.
The strike group departed Naval Station Norfolk on March 31 for what was originally expected to be a standard six- to seven-month deployment.
More than seven months later, families are now being told to prepare for the possibility that their loved ones could remain deployed for as long as 12 months.
According to reporting from MS NOW, Navy leaders delivered that news during a Nov.
9 town hall at Naval Station Norfolk, telling families their loved ones would miss the upcoming holidays and that a yearlong deployment was a worst-case scenario.
For military spouses and families who have already spent months waiting for a homecoming, the possibility of another extension brings new challenges.
"These are families who are now facing the potential of a full calendar year without their their person," said Sarah Streyder, a military spouse and the executive director and co-founder of Secure Families Initiative, an organization that advocates for military families.
Streyder spoke with News 3 about the emotional toll extended deployments can have on military households, particularly when families have already begun preparing for their loved ones to return.
"That is a whole calendar year of missed birthdays, holidays, t-ball games, homecoming dances, you name it, right?
A whole year," Streyder said.
While deployments are a familiar part of military life in Hampton Roads, Streyder said there is a significant difference between preparing for a lengthy separation and learning that an expected homecoming is being pushed back.
"Long deployments suck.
Extended deployments are even worse in some cases because you have this light at the end of the tunnel that you start to make plans around, and you start to allow yourself that glimmer of hope that the light at the end of the tunnel is coming, and for all of a sudden that to be yanked further or to be indeterminate," she said.
That uncertainty can affect everything from family celebrations and childcare arrangements to the emotional well-being of spouses and children.
For parents managing a household while their spouse is deployed, an extension can mean additional months of handling daily responsibilities alone.
For children, it can mean more missed milestones and continued uncertainty about when a parent will return.
Streyder said those challenges are especially difficult when families do not have a clear timeline for a reunion.
The USS George H.W.
Bush Carrier Strike Group has already been deployed for more than 200 days.
The latest reported extension would be the second since the strike group departed Norfolk in March.
Although families have reportedly been told to prepare for the possibility of a 12-month deployment, that does not necessarily mean the Navy has formally ordered the strike group to remain at sea for an entire year.
The distinction matters for families trying to plan their lives around a homecoming date that remains uncertain.
The challenges associated with extended deployments have also been acknowledged by senior Navy leadership.
Adm.
Daryl Caudle, the chief of naval operations, previously discussed the importance of providing sailors and their families with more predictable deployment schedules during remarks in Norfolk.
Caudle said seven months should be the goal for deployments and emphasized the need for better communication about how long sailors can expect to remain away from home.
The impact of an extended deployment is not limited to families.
Retired Navy Vice Adm.
Herm Shelanski previously told News 3 that longer deployments can place additional strain on both sailors and the ships on which they serve.
"It gets pretty rough.
It gets rough on the ship because of maintenance, it gets rough on the crew morale," Shelanski said.
Shelanski also raised concerns about how repeated lengthy deployments could affect the Navy's ability to retain experienced sailors.
"You know if they're extended for these extended periods then the consequence of that is that many of these experienced sailors may be disheartened and say I don't want to go through that again and get out," he said.
The reported extension is also drawing attention from Virginia lawmakers.
U.S.
Sen.
Mark Warner told News 3 that he is pressing the Navy for answers about the deployment and the strain it is placing on military families.
"The men and women of our military serving as part of the USS George H.W.
Bush Carrier Strike Group have already spent more than 200 days away from home and are facing extensions to that deployment that add to the challenges they and their families have navigated now for months," Warner said in a statement.
Warner linked the prolonged deployments to the ongoing war with Iran, criticizing the Trump administration's handling of the conflict.
"These prolonged deployments, driven by President Trump's war of choice in Iran, are taking an enormous toll on our servicemembers and their families in Virginia and across the country," Warner said.
The senator said military families deserve greater certainty about when their loved ones will return.
"Our sailors and their loved ones deserve more than uncertainty and indefinite extensions.
They deserve clear answers and a concrete plan to end this war and bring them home," Warner said.
"I am pressing the Navy for answers about its plans to bring these sailors home and how it intends to address the serious strain these decisions are placing on our military families."
For Streyder, the situation highlights the challenges families face when deployment schedules change with little certainty about what comes next.
Military spouses may be accustomed to adjusting plans and managing unexpected challenges, but that does not make prolonged separations any easier.
"It's so hard.
It's so hard," Streyder said.
News 3 has reached out to the Navy seeking additional information about the reported extension, the expected deployment timeline and what resources are available to support affected families.
As families await those answers, many are left preparing for another holiday season apart — without knowing exactly when their loved ones will finally return home.

polymarket-5238401.text:
The Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS George H.W.
Bush and its strike group departed Naval Station Norfolk on Tuesday for a regularly scheduled deployment, the Navy announced.
The Navy did not provide details on the destination of the carrier, but with the USS Gerald R.
Ford currently sidelined with maintenance issues outside the U.S.
Central Command area of responsibility, there is a warship vacancy in the Middle East that it could potentially fill.
“Our sailors are ready and able to do the nation’s bidding,” said Rear Adm.
Alexis T.
Walker, commander of Carrier Strike Group Ten, which is embarked with Bush.
The carrier strike group — which encompasses more than 5,000 personnel — includes the flagship carrier, along with the Arleigh Burke-class destroyers USS Ross, USS Donald Cook and USS Mason.
Carrier Air Wing 7, which is embarked on George H.W.
Bush, includes nine aircraft squadrons.
In preparation for its deployment, Carrier Air Wing 7 flew 1,586 sorties and logged 693 arrested landings during the day and 682 at night as part of its Composite Training Unit Exercise, which it completed on March 5.
The strike group most recently deployed to the U.S.
Naval Forces Europe–U.S.
Naval Forces Africa area of operations from Aug.
2022 to April 2023.
The USS Gerald R.
Ford is currently undergoing repairs in Croatia after a non-combat fire broke out in the main laundry room on March 12.
The blaze injured three sailors, one of whom had to be flown off the ship to receive medical care.
All three were in stable condition after the incident, which affected roughly 100 sleeping berths and forced 200 other sailors to receive treatment for smoke-related injuries.
The Ford was previously operating in the Red Sea in support of Operation Epic Fury and was on pace to set the record for the longest-at-sea U.S.
Navy deployment ever, as it approached an 11-month extended deployment mark.
The current record is held by the USS Midway, which was deployed at sea for 332 days during the Vietnam War.

polymarket-5238401.text:
The deployment of the USS George H.W.
Bush aircraft carrier to the Middle East has been extended, according to a new report, following the record-breaking deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which raised serious concerns about the welfare of U.S.
personnel serving at sea for prolonged periods.
U.S.
Navy officials told families of service members aboard the Bush that their relatives would not return home for the holidays and that the deployment could last as long as a year, according to a meeting recording obtained by MSNOW.
A Pentagon official told Newsweek the Department of Defense does not discuss "future or hypothetical movements" to protect operational security.
The U.S.
Navy has been contacted for comment.
Read More on World
Most carrier deployments last between six and seven months, although they can be extended.
They typically include port calls to replenish supplies and allow crew members to rest.
Aircraft carriers operate alongside other warships, including destroyers, and carry an embarked air wing, together forming a carrier strike group.
The Bush carrier strike group is currently deployed in the Arabian Sea along with the USS George Washington and its accompanying ships.
The Bush left Norfolk, Virginia, on March 31.
The Lincoln returned to its home port in San Diego, California, on October 8, after departing the West Coast in November 2025.
The Lincoln made brief stops in Guam in December 2025 and September 2026, and in Oman in July 2026.
According to the Navy, its crew spent 208 uninterrupted days at sea between the December Guam stop and the July Oman stop, setting a record for modern aircraft carriers.
In the weeks leading up to the Lincoln's arrival in Thailand, family members and U.S.
lawmakers raised concerns that the roughly 5,000 personnel aboard the carrier were overworked, and lacked access to basic hygiene supplies and adequate nutrition.
A 2025 study by researchers including those at the U.S.
Naval Health Research Center found that sailors experienced significant stressors while at sea, including inadequate rest and limited access to mental-health care.
Nearly half of the 441 sailors surveyed said services to help them manage stress were inadequate.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said there had been eight suicide attempts across the Lincoln carrier strike group during its deployment, according to a September 22 letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand.
“I’m sorry, I’ve been there.
I know what it feels like; I know how hard it is when your kids are asking, ‘When’s daddy coming home?
When’s mommy coming home?’” Cao told roughly 500 family members of Bush personnel during a meeting in Norfolk on Monday, according to MS NOW.
The Bush's crew went 187 days without a port call before stopping in Thailand for four days in early October, MSNOW reported.
Admiral Karl Thomas, commander of U.S.
Fleet Forces Command, told family members on Monday that Iran had "peppered" U.S.
ships in the Middle East, including with drones, according to MSNOW.
"It’s hard to defend and that’s what those sailors are doing," Thomas reportedly said.
More than eight months after the U.S.
and Israel launched strikes against Iran, there is little sign of an imminent peace agreement, although the intensity of the conflict has eased since its opening weeks.
How Do The Bush and Lincoln Compare?
Both the Bush and Lincoln are Nimitz-class nuclear-powered aircraft carriers.
The U.S.
Navy operates two classes of nuclear-powered aircraft carriers: the Nimitz class and the Ford class.
The Navy has 10 Nimitz-class aircraft carriers, while the USS Gerald R.
Ford is the only operational Ford-class carrier.
The newer class is expected to gradually replace the Nimitz-class ships over the coming decades.
The Bush is the newer carrier, commissioned in January 2009.
The Office of Naval Research said it incorporated a "number of improvements" over earlier Nimitz-class carriers, including upgraded data-management systems and redesigned propellers.
It also incorporates larger air-conditioning plants, changes to its communications systems and weapons elevators, and a bulbous bow designed to reduce water resistance, according to the Government Accountability Office.
Although the Lincoln is nearly 20 years older, it completed a Refueling and Complex Overhaul (RCOH) in 2017, a major refurbishment lasting more than four years.
The work included refueling its nuclear reactors, upgrading aircraft-launch systems, replacing thousands of components and repainting the hull.
The Lincoln returned home after a 321-day deployment, while the Bush, which left Norfolk on March 31, could remain deployed for as long as a year, according to the reported warning to families.
If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline for free, confidential support.
U.S.
service members and veterans can call 988 and press 1, or text 838255, to reach the Veterans/Military Crisis Line.
Military OneSource also offers support to service members and their families at 800-342-9647.

Learn more about Martyn here.

The U.S.
military is back to two aircraft carriers supporting Iran war operations after the USS George Washington left the Middle East.
The departure came in the same week the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived, briefly putting an unusually high three carriers in the waters off Iran.
The Roosevelt and the USS George H.W.
Bush now anchor the naval force enforcing the blockade of Iranian ports.
◉ Key Facts
- ►The USS George Washington left the U.S.
Central Command area after roughly three months, with the Navy’s Pacific Fleet confirming the move on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.
- ►The USS Theodore Roosevelt reached the region on Sunday, November 15, 2026, so the three-carrier overlap lasted only a few days.
- ►The USS George H.W.
Bush, which first deployed to the region in the spring, left in early October and has since returned; more than a dozen destroyers, cruisers and a littoral combat ship are also there.
- ►The U.S.
naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in force; it was reimposed on July 14, 2026.
- ►The Iran war began February 28, 2026, and no ceasefire is currently in force.
Cmdr.
Katie Koenig, a spokesperson for the U.S.
Pacific Fleet, said the Japan-based George Washington is now under the fleet’s control and “conducting routine operations” in the Asia-Pacific region.
The carrier left the U.S.
Central Command area of operations, according to the Pacific Fleet and multiple U.S.
officials.
It is expected to return to its homeport of Yokosuka, Japan, though it is unclear whether it will make a port call on its way east.
With the George Washington now in the Indian Ocean, two carrier strike groups remain in the Middle East.
The change is the latest in a series of carrier rotations tied to the war.
The George Washington strike group arrived in the 5th Fleet area on August 19 to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln.
That arrival came the same week the Lincoln began heading home after more than eight months on deployment, which the Navy said was to complete a long-planned maintenance availability.
The George Washington and Lincoln operated together in the region for about a month before the Lincoln departed.
The Roosevelt’s arrival on Sunday, November 15, followed by the George Washington’s exit, created a similar brief overlap, which put three strike groups in the Middle East for a couple of days.
The Washington’s deployment also carried a strategic cost for the Pacific.
Its move to the Middle East left the U.S.
without a carrier in the Indo-Pacific.
Before heading to the Middle East, it made port calls in Vietnam and Guam and conducted patrols in the Philippine Sea.
The Pacific Fleet’s statement that the ship is back under its control indicates the carrier is returning to the region where it is normally based.
The Bush, which has returned to the region, and the Roosevelt are now the two carriers there, along with more than a dozen destroyers, cruisers and a littoral combat ship.
The carriers are among the U.S.
Navy ships enforcing the blockade of Iranian ports.
The U.S.
has also carried out some limited strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which nearly a third of the world’s oil passed before the war began on February 28.
📚 Background & Context
The United States and Israel began the war against Iran on February 28, 2026.
A ceasefire took effect April 8 and collapsed in early July.
The U.S.
naval blockade of Iranian ports began April 13, was lifted in June and was reimposed July 14.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but its implementation stalled over disagreements about guaranteeing freedom and security of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
The strain of long deployments has been part of the story.
The George Washington was pulled from a South China Sea patrol shortly after reports of mental health and supply issues emerged aboard the Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea at more than 240 days.
Rotating carriers in and out lets the Navy keep a continuous presence while limiting how long any single crew stays at sea.
It also means any carrier committed to the Middle East is unavailable elsewhere.
The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though not at the intensity of the war’s early stages.
The U.S.
says it is enforcing a naval blockade of Iran’s Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping there.
There was no deal between Washington and Tehran as of November 17.
The next questions are how long the Roosevelt and Bush stay, when relief carriers might be sent, and whether the Pacific gets a carrier back.
Neither the Navy nor the Pentagon has laid out a schedule for further rotations.
💬 What People Are Saying
Based on public reaction across social media and news platforms, here is the general consensus on this story:
- 🔴Many conservative commentators emphasize that two carriers plus a dozen-plus escorts keep the blockade credible.
Some argue the U.S.
should apply firmer consequences to Iran for attacks on shipping.
- 🔵Many liberal commentators focus on the strain of extended deployments on sailors and ships, and on leaving the Indo-Pacific without a carrier.
They call for a diplomatic path out of the standoff.
- 🟠Across groups, many readers see the move as a routine rotation.
Their larger concerns are the length of the conflict, the Strait of Hormuz and energy prices.
Note: Social reactions represent general public sentiment and do not reflect Political.org’s editorial position.

A U.S.
aircraft carrier has departed the Middle East, leaving two others in the region as Iranian attacks on neighboring countries threaten to widen the war.
The departure comes as President Donald Trump reportedly considers a major expansion of U.S.
airstrikes against Iran in an effort to break a prolonged military stalemate.
USS George Washington left the region earlier this week following the arrival of the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt.
That leaves Roosevelt and USS George H.W.
Bush as the two remaining carriers in the Middle East.
Washington is now conducting routine operations in the U.S.
7th Fleet area of operations, the Navy said.
It wasn’t clear whether Washington’s escorts, including the destroyer USS Shoup, also left the Middle East.
The carrier’s departure leaves at least 15 Navy warships in the Arabian Sea.
All told, there are some 50,000 U.S.
military personnel in the Middle East.
Washington, the Navy’s only forward-deployed aircraft carrier, entered the Middle East in August to relieve USS Abraham Lincoln amid concerns about the well-being and mental health of its service members.
Bush departed Norfolk, Va., in late March and arrived in the Middle East in April.
Families of sailors aboard Bush reportedly learned during a recent meeting with acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao that the carrier would not be home for the holidays.
Earlier this month, Trump signaled a shift away from diplomacy seemingly to rely on a U.S.
maritime blockade against Iranian ports, other economic pressure and the threat of renewed large-scale military strikes against Iran.
Trump is weighing a joint four- to seven-day airstrike campaign with Israel that would focus on Iran’s missile and drone stockpiles along with energy facilities, The New York Times reported Wednesday, citing unidentified U.S.
and Israeli officials.
The White House did not directly answer questions about options Trump was said to be reviewing, instead referring to comments the president recently made on Fox News.
During a Wednesday interview about Iran potentially using biological weapons, Trump did not say if he was considering renewed, large-scale strikes against Iran.
But he did seem to indicate that any potential U.S.
action could be weeks away.
“We’re going to have a new year coming up and will see what happens after January 1st,” Trump said.
“But they’ve been nasty, these are nasty people.”
During a Sunday interview with Fox News, Vice President JD Vance said Trump was considering several alternatives including declaring U.S.
operations complete and exerting additional diplomatic or military pressure.
Trump would not let the conflict become a “forever war,” Vance said.
Iran launched drone strikes this week against Bahrain and Kuwait, targeting U.S.
military equipment.
Bahrain’s capital, Manama, hosts a major hub of the U.S.
Navy, while Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait is an important installation for the U.S.
Air Force.
In response, the U.S.
launched precision airstrikes on an Iranian military site on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf.
Meanwhile, the U.K.
Maritime Trade Operations Center on Wednesday reported separate attacks on two vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, including one that resulted in a shipboard fire and a missing mariner.
So far this month, Iran has attacked at least 18 vessels transiting in or near the strait, according to reports from the UKMTO, a British military organization that monitors threats to commercial shipping in the region.

SEOUL, Nov 4 (Reuters) - North Korea fired multiple missiles on Wednesday toward the sea off its east coast, South Korea's Defence Ministry said, marking Pyongyang's fourth such weapons launch in a month.
The South Korean military detected the missiles that were fired from the Sondok area, an eastern coastal region of North Korea, the ministry said.
Seoul and Washington were closely analysing the launch and remained ready to respond to any potential provocation, it said.
North Korea has carried out a series of weapons tests this year, including the launch of a missile that flew more than 900 km (559 miles) as well as testing hypersonic missiles.
Seoul's announcement came hours after Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, ruled out dialogue with Washington until the US abandoned what she called its hostile policy.
She also repeated Pyongyang's denial that it was behind the hacking at crypto exchange Binance after the FBI accused North Korea of carrying out the heist.
The missile launch followed a North Korean media report that leader Kim Jong Un visited a naval shipyard building a destroyer and stressed the importance of a powerful naval force.
North Korea's frequent missile tests this year also suggest Pyongyang may be nearing completion of preparations for mass production, potentially including weapons for export to Russia, said Lee Choon-geun, a missile expert and board member at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST).
"Before mass production and deployment, you typically need many tests," Lee said.
"Or they may be looking to export missiles in bulk to Russia, in which case they would need to run a lot of tests before shipping."
(Reporting by Heejin KimEditing by Ed Davies)

polymarket-6403111.text:
North Korea says it tested an advanced air-defense missile and rehearsed a fire strike this week, pressing ahead with weapons development as prospects for renewed talks with Washington remain uncertain.
The tests were part of the military’s “obligatory activities,” according to a Thursday report by the state-run Korean Central News Agency.
The air-defense missile test evaluated new materials, guidance technology and the system’s ability to detect, identify and track targets, KCNA said.
A separate “firepower subunit” demonstrated a fire strike the same day, the report said, without identifying the weapons involved or providing exercise details.
South Korea’s military detected several missiles fired Wednesday morning from the Sondok area, about 105 miles northeast of Pyongyang, toward the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan.
The South’s Ministry of National Defense did not specify the number or type of missiles detected.
South Korean navy Capt.
Jang Do-young, a spokesman for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said Thursday that U.S.
and South Korean forces were still analyzing the launches.
Based on initial data, “the missiles North Korea launched yesterday could potentially have belonged to several different missile types,” he said during a briefing in Seoul.
“Rather than making a definitive assessment and announcing the missile types while that analysis was still underway, our military chose to share information about the launches while continuing to fully monitor and assess the situation, without revealing our surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities,” Jang said, according to a briefing transcript.
The Hawaii-based U.S.
Pacific Command said in a statement on its website Tuesday that it is aware of the missile launches and is consulting closely with allies and partners.
The command declined by email Thursday to comment further on North Korea’s claims.
U.S.
Forces Korea did not immediately respond to a Thursday email requesting comment.
The latest tests come amid speculation that President Donald Trump may seek another meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, although no renewed negotiations have been announced.
Leif-Eric Easley, an international studies professor at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, said the North’s continued weapons development and other activities complicate U.S.
efforts to reengage with Pyongyang.
“North Korea’s numerous weapons tests, record crypto heists, aggressive rhetoric against Seoul, and sanctions-violating cooperation with Moscow seriously complicate engagement,” he said by email Thursday.
The FBI, in a Saturday statement on its website, blamed North Korea for stealing more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, an allegation Pyongyang has denied.
The State Department announced last week that the United States, European Union and Australia have imposed sanctions targeting Pyongyang’s use of overseas workers, malicious cyber activities and individuals involved in unlawful cooperation with Russia, according to a joint statement.
Easley said South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s administration supports renewed diplomacy between Trump and Kim to ease tensions and reopen the door to inter-Korean dialogue.
But a summit that “shelves denuclearization would undermine deterrence and create policy friction among Washington, Seoul, and Tokyo,” he said.
Stars and Stripes reporter Yoojin Lee contributed to this report.

Summary
North Korea launched two ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area on Monday, October 12, 2026, prompting consultation among U.S.
Pacific Command and its allies.
PACOM said the launches posed no immediate threat to U.S.
personnel, territory or regional allies.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff detected the launch at about 9:20 a.m., with at least one missile flying more than 900 kilometers.
Key Facts
- U.S.
Pacific Command said it was consulting closely with its allies and partners after the launches.
- PACOM reaffirmed that the United States remains committed to defending the U.S.
homeland and its regional allies.
- South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said at least one missile traveled more than 900 kilometers.
- North Korea previously launched one ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea on October 3.
U.S.
Pacific Command (PACOM) said Monday that North Korea launched two ballistic missiles recently while stressing that the move poses no immediate threat to the United States or its allies.
"The Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched two ballistic missiles on October 12, 2026 (KST)," the command said in a statement, referring to North Korea by its official name.
The command said it was aware of the launches and was consulting closely with its allies and partners.
"Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to U.S.
personnel or territory, or to our allies," it said.
It added that the U.S.
remains "committed to the defense of the U.S.
homeland and our allies in the region."
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said Monday (Korea time) it detected the launch at about 9:20 a.m.
from the Pyongyang area and that at least one of the missiles flew more than 900 kilometers.
The North's latest missile launch came after it fired one ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea on Oct.

polymarket-6403111.title: North Korea Missile Launches 1984-Present (CSIS Missile Defense Project)

polymarket-6403111.text:
Updated January 2026
Origins
Throughout the 1960s and early 1970s as part of military cooperation pacts with the Soviet Union, North Korea was delivered surface-to-air and artillery rockets and trained on how to build and operate multiple-rocket launchers.
Separately, it reached agreements with the People’s Republic of China to provide coastal defense capabilities such as anti-ship cruise missiles and the transfer of China’s missile research and development.
This foundational know-how was the basis on which the North Korean indigenous missile program was established.
The North Korean ballistic missile program began in 1976 when it first acquired the SCUD-B from the Soviets, brokered through Egypt.
After reverse engineering the SCUD technology, it began missile testing in 1984 and has conducted more than 300 launches of numerous missile capabilities since that time, including short-, medium-, intermediate- and intercontinental- range ballistic missiles, as well as submarine-launched ballistic missiles and space-launch vehicles.
The failure rate of its missile launches remains high but has also improved over time.
Through 1994, the failure rate was roughly 50%.
Between 1994 and 2011, that failure rate dropped to approximately 23%, and between 2011 and 2023 the failure rate dropped to roughly 15%.
While many of North Korea’s missile launches are designed to support the development and validation of new systems, not every launch is strictly a “test.” Some serve political or strategic purposes, timed to coincide with military or diplomatic events, demonstrate resolve, or send a message to domestic or foreign audiences.
Others may be operational training exercises or demonstrations of deployed capabilities.
As such, this fact sheet refers broadly to missile launches, recognizing that these events often serve multiple overlapping objectives aside from purely technical validation.
Through the Kim Dynasty
Kim Il Sung (1984-1994)
Under the Kim Il Sung regime, North Korea conducted 17 missile launches, 16 of which were carried out at the Tonghae Satellite Launching Ground near Musudan-ri.
Seven original launches were carried out in 1984 followed by a period of no launches between 1985 and 1989, with 10 follow-on launches taking place between 1990 and 1994.
The first capabilities tested were short- and medium-range SCUD variants, including the Hwasong-5, Hwasong-6, and the No Dong-1.
Additionally, in the Spring of 1994, North Korea tested its first cruise missile capability, the KN-01.
Kim Jong Il (1994-2011)
The North Korean missile program progressed glacially for the first half of Kim Jong Il’s reign.
From 1994 to 2002, North Korea would launch only once, debuting the Taepodong-1 prototype in August 1998 as a space launch vehicle.
Between 2003 and 2009, missile activity spiked.
North Korea conducted 43 launches during this window that included further refinement of its cruise missile platform and short- and medium-range ballistic capabilities.
In 2006, it introduced the Taepodong-2, which would later be used as part of the Unha-3 orbital launch system unveiled in 2009.
Notably, in 2006, North Korea conducted its first nuclear test at the Punggye-ri Nuclear Test Facility, and its second in May 2009 interspersed between launches of its medium-range and space launch capabilities.
The regime would conduct zero missile launches during the final two years of Kim Jong Il’s tenure.
Kim Jong Un (2011-Present)
Upon assuming leadership, Kim Jong Un undertook a concerted effort to expand and develop North Korea’s ballistic missile program.
Between 2012 and 2025, North Korea has conducted more than 272 missile launches and debuted a variety of missiles with increasing ranges.
Missile launch and development infrastructure has also expanded, and in some cases been established in proximity to and in connection with the state’s nuclear facilities.
In 2015, the North debuted its first SLBM, the KN-11, and its first IRBM, the BM-25 Musudan, one year later, testing each several times.
Multiple nuclear tests have also been conducted over this time, with the largest and most recent occurring in September 2017.
Today, North Korea touts several theater cruise missile capabilities; short-, medium- and intermediate-range missile capabilities; at least two SLBM varieties; a long-range cruise missile; and two ICBM platforms, the Hwasong-17 and Hwasong-18.
In 2023, North Korea was confirmed to have launched 36 missiles, mostly of the short- and medium-range variety.
However, North Korea often launches multiple missiles at once, so the actual number is likely higher than 36 missiles.
In 2023, the North attempted on three separate occasions to place a satellite in orbit.
The first two attempts suffered failure during boost phase.
The North was able to successfully place its spy satellite in orbit upon its third launch attempt.
The regime’s space-launch efforts to establish satellite capabilities are significant because the space-launch vehicles use the same ICBM motors to power flight, and satellite capabilities would provide it greater intelligence and targeting abilities.
North Korea began 2024 with a January launch of an intermediate-range ballistic missile fitted with a hypersonic glide vehicle and debuted several new systems, including the Pulhwasal-3-31 cruise missile and the Padasuri-6 anti-ship missile.
Throughout the year, launches highlighted theater-range cruise and ballistic missile capabilities, culminating in October’s launch of the solid-fuel Hwasong-19 ICBM.
By year’s end, North Korea had conducted at least 30 missile launches.
North Korea conducted its first missile launch of 2025 on January 6 when it launched an upgraded version of its Hwasong-16, an intermediate-range ballistic missile fitted with a wedge-shaped payload billed as a “hypersonic glide vehicle.” According to Japanese and South Korean military intelligence, the missile flew approximately 700 miles before landing in the Sea of Japan, and although the North claimed that the hypersonic vehicle successfully conducted evasive maneuvers during flight, both South Korean and Japanese sources dispute this.
On January 14, the DPRK fired several short-range ballistic missiles that traveled for approximately 150 miles before landing in the Sea of Japan, according to South Korean sources.
On January 26, the North launched several sea-to-surface cruise missiles into the Yellow Sea.
It referred to the cruise missiles as “strategic,” likely intended to denote their ability to carry nuclear warheads, though this has not been confirmed by independent sources.
On February 26, Kim Jong Un oversaw the launch of two cruise missiles from the West Sea Barrage area.
The missiles flew approximately four miles before appearing to strike a building on Sangchuira Island near Nampho.
At the onset of the U.S.-ROK’s annual joint exercise, “Freedom Shield,” on March 10, North Korea launched multiple ballistic missiles toward the Yellow Sea.
According to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, the missiles were likely short-range.
On April 28 and 29, North Korea conducted the first weapons launch from its newly launched Choe Hyon-class destroyer, purportedly firing supersonic cruise missiles, strategic cruise missiles, surface-to-air anti-aircraft missiles, as well as non-specified “ship-to-ship tactical guided weapons,” among other non-kinetic defensive systems.
After observing the missile launches, Kim Jong Un suggested that testing of the ship’s short-range ballistic missile system would occur in the near future.
On May 8, North Korea launched multiple short-range ballistic missiles from Wonsan, with the longest traveling approximately 800 kilometers before landing in the Sea of Japan.
South Korean military officials indicated that the launch may have been conducted to assess the performance of missile systems potentially intended for export.
On May 22, North Korea fired multiple cruise missiles into the East Sea.

polymarket-6403111.text:
New Missiles But Fewer Launches, a Missile Sub Reveal, and a Nuclear-Armed Air Force
This article is from the third edition (October-December 2025) of 38 North’s quarterly product, North Korea Briefing, that monitors key internal developments in North Korea.
For the full series, click here.
During the fourth quarter of 2025, North Korea unveiled a new solid-propellant intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), a new version of the KN-23 short-range ballistic missile (SRBM), and a new probably conventional air-launched cruise missile (ALCM).
However, the year 2025 featured fewer total ballistic missile launches than for each year from 2022-2024—and no ICBM launches, deepening North Korea’s prior emphasis on theater missile activities.
Pyongyang revealed for the first time most of the hull of the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN) under construction.
And Kim Jong Un announced the Air Force would be assigned a nuclear deterrent mission, which at least initially appears to entail operating road-mobile launchers for dual-capable land-attack cruise missiles (LACMs).
New and Modified Missiles at Arms Expo and Parade
The North unveiled what it termed the “new” Hwasong-20 (HS-20) solid-propellant road-mobile ICBM and a new version of the KN-23 solid SRBM carrying a hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) at the early October “military hardware exhibition Defense Development-2025” and October 10 military parade in Pyongyang.
These and other revelations at the arms expo and parade were reported extensively on 38 North on November 4.
Context and Implications
The exhibition and parade did not reveal any dramatically new ballistic missiles.
The “new” HS-20 appeared to offer little more than the previous HS-19 ICBM, and the addition of an HGV to the KN-23 SRBM will likely make a marginal improvement to missile defense penetration, assuming it is deployed.
This should not be surprising given prior improvements to the large variety of missile systems the North has unveiled since 2019, providing Pyongyang updated, mature missile systems across the entire spectrum of ranges.
Therefore, aside from multiple warheads if they are successfully developed, future improvements are much more likely to be incremental—although the North probably will continue to increase the overall number of missiles and launchers deployed.
Fewer Missile Launches in 2025, but It’s Not Just the Numbers
The October 23 Wall Street Journal reported that North Korea “sharply reduced” the number of missile launches conducted in 2025 compared to each year between 2022 and 2024.
It attributed the reduction to Pyongyang’s increased confidence (which reduced its need to “seek attention” with launches) and a shift from launches to factory visits and declarations by Kim Jong Un as a means to “convey North Korea’s military strength.”
Context and Implications
North Korea has reportedly conducted some 15 ballistic missile launches in 2025, compared to 41 in 2024, 31 in 2023, and 69 in 2022.
More interesting than the numbers is the fact that all but one of the 2025 launches were SRBMs (an intermediate-range ballistic missile was launched in January), deepening 2024’s emphasis on theater missile activities.
This also means no ICBMs or submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs) were launched in 2025.
Only one ICBM—the first and only HS-19—was launched in 2024, and the North has not launched a purpose-built SLBM (as opposed to a sub-fired KN-23 SRBM) since 2019.
The recent emphasis on theater missiles is underscored by adding in LACM launches: at least 10 or so were reportedly launched in 2024 and 12 in 2025, including two reportedly observed by Kim Jong Un on December 28.
It is highly debatable whether the North really cared about “seeking attention” with missile launches, especially after its apparent rejection of improved relations with the West in the wake of the failed 2019 Hanoi summit.
That said, it would not be surprising if political motivations played an important role in the decision to launch fewer missiles and no strategic systems in 2025, since in Pyongyang political motivations for missile launches are probably more important than technical and operational ones.
However, other factors probably contributed as well, including the completion of several missile development programs, a likely priority on exporting KN-23 and possibly KN-24 SRBMs to Russia for use against Ukraine, a possible desire to supersede the HS-19 ICBM with an announced new version incorporating the same more powerful first stage that is being developed for the HS-20, and the lack of an available missile submarine large enough to deploy the newer SLBMs North Korea has displayed but not yet flight-tested.
More of the New “Nuclear-Powered” Submarine Hull Revealed
North Korean press on December 25 reported on a recent visit by Kim Jong Un to the construction site for a “8,700-tonnage nuclear-powered strategic guided missile submarine.” Associated photos looking up from below showed most of the submarine inside its construction hall.
Context and Implications
The previous images of the sub this March only showed the lower portion of part of the hull.
Although possibly retouched, the new photos appear credible.
In addition to six torpedo tubes in the bow, the new photos reveal an extended-length sail containing 5-10 probable ballistic missile launch tubes akin to the former Soviet Golf-III/Project 601 diesel/electric missile sub.
(As the new sub is not seen from above, the number of missile tubes cannot be confirmed.) Housing the missile tubes in the tall sail instead of a shorter “turtleback” section aft of the sail, like most of the world’s missile subs do, suggests the new sub is intended to accommodate SLBMs that are much longer in size—at least 14 meters and even 18 meters long.
(The longest SLBM displayed by the North to date, in April 2022, was some 13.5 meters long.) A longer missile may be needed to reach intercontinental range, an objective set out by Kim in January 2021.
There is no open-source reporting that North Korea has yet built or tested a submarine nuclear reactor, and the new photos do not reveal whether one is installed in the new sub.
At this point, the idea that the hull is equipped with an operable nuclear reactor should be regarded with great skepticism, although this possibility cannot be ruled out—especially if Russia provided a reactor or extensive technical assistance (of which there is little evidence to date).
Even if the sub is reactor-equipped, a year or two of fitting out probably would be required before it rolled out of the construction hall ready to begin sea trials, with additional time required to reach operational status.
Air Force to Add Nuclear Deterrent Mission
North Korean press reported a November 28 visit by Kim Jong Un to an airbase marking the 80th founding anniversary of the North Korean Air Force.
Kim noted “that the Air Force will be given new strategic military assets and entrusted with a new important duty,” and “will play a role in the exercise of the nuclear war deterrent.” Accompanying photos of a weapons display at the airbase showed a road-mobile LACM launcher, three different Hwasal-class LACMs, and a new-type tactical ALCM on a Su-25 Frogfoot ground attack jet.
Context and Implications
Kim did not specify what the Air Force’s new nuclear role will entail, but the display implies at least some LACM launchers will be subordinated to the Air Force and equipped with all three known Hwasal missile variants.
The Air Force LACMs probably will be in addition to those already under the Strategic Forces.
This is probably the most sensible way to give the Air Force a nuclear role, as road-mobile LACMs are more survivable both pre-launch and in-flight than Pyongyang’s obsolescent combat aircraft, and have enough range (1,500-2,000 km) to cover all of South Korea from anywhere in the North.
The size and square cross-section of the new ALCM resemble the German-Swedish Taurus missil

North Korea Increases Ballistic Missile Launches This Year [Yang Nakgyu's Defence Club]
Diversifying Tactics After Sending Troops to Ukraine
Adopting Mixed-Strike Tactics Including Drones
This year, North Korea is increasing the number of ballistic missile launches.
In the past, North Korea targeted mainly South Korean Air Force bases and launched only ballistic missiles, but it is now expected to further increase the frequency of ballistic missile launches as it shifts to a strategy of mixed salvos, combining new short-range ballistic missiles, multiple rocket launchers, and drones.
According to the number of North Korean ballistic missile launches announced by the military authorities on September 15, there were 38 launches in 2022, 18 in 2023, 12 in 2024, and 6 last year, showing a decrease each year.
Aside from regular training exercises with conventional strike weapons, there were no other notable exercises.
However, North Korea's dispatch of troops to Ukraine has led to greater tactical diversity.
On the 12th, North Korea conducted another joint fire assault drill, mobilizing not only tactical nuclear weapons and conventional strike weapons but also drones.
By employing "simultaneous, mixed salvos" of a wide variety of weapons, North Korea is reflecting lessons learned from the Russia-Ukraine war.
This appears to be an attempt to demonstrate its capability to evade and strike South Korea’s air defense networks during wartime.
Photos released by North Korea on the 14th show what appear to be North Korea’s version of the Iskander (KN-23), super-large multiple rocket launchers (KN-25), Hwasal series strategic cruise missiles, and loitering munitions (suicide drones).
While North Korea has previously conducted combined launches of short-range ballistic missiles (SRBMs), cruise missiles, and multiple rocket launchers, it is unusual to include drones in such launches.
This move appears to signal an intent to penetrate the South Korea-U.S.
air defense network and strike strategically important areas at the outset of a conflict.
One notable aspect of this drill is the use of thermobaric weapons, which Russia has deployed in actual combat during its invasion of Ukraine.
North Korea has also followed this method, loading thermobaric munitions onto the KN-25, a short-term, mass-destruction weapon, and launching them.
Experts believe North Korea will continue to increase the number of ballistic missile launches in order to refine its tactics of launching salvos with a diverse mix of weapons.

North Korea Says Test-Fired New Air Defense Missile System, Long-Range Cruise Missile
- Other Media news
- November, 05, 2026 - 11:07
The North's report came after South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the North firing multiple missiles toward the East Sea from the Sondok area in South Hamgyong Province early Wednesday, Yonhap news agency reported.
The Missile Administration's test of a new air defense missile system was aimed at confirming its technical capabilities, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
"The test-fire proved the technical specifications and reliability of the new material and intelligent multiple guided mode of the projectile, target identification and tracking capability of the air-defense missile system and its detection information processing device," it said.
In addition, a firepower subunit of the long-range strategic cruise missile unit in the eastern area staged a strike drill on the same day, using a long-range strategic cruise missile against a virtual airport target, according to the report.
The JCS earlier said the missiles flew less than 300 kilometers, with authorities leaving open the possibility that they involved a close-range ballistic missile.
Wednesday's launch came as Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, issued back-to-back statements this week rejecting a US investigation that blamed the North for stealing more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
It also coincided with the US midterm elections, widely seen as a referendum on US President Donald Trump halfway into his second term.
North Korea's latest weapons tests appeared to be aimed at responding to Freedom Flag, the ongoing South Korea-US air drills, experts said.
Earlier this week, Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission, criticized Seoul-Washington's combined exercises, including Freedom Flag, accusing the "enemies" of intensifying their "military moves in public or behind closed doors."
Wednesday's test was the North's fourth weapons test in a week, starting with the firing of a 600-millimeter "ultra-precision" multiple rocket launcher Thursday, with leader Kim in attendance.
It tested a cluster bomb that can be mounted on tactical ballistic missiles Saturday and a "dispersal warhead" for a strategic cruise missile Monday.
The Rodong Sinmun, the official newspaper of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea, did not cover the last three events.

polymarket-6403111.text:
North Korea Test Fires Strategic Cruise Missiles: KCNA
- Other Media news
- November, 03, 2026 - 11:54
The Nov 2 launch came a day after North Korea tested cluster bomb warheads, as tensions with Seoul have risen after a landmine blast along their heavily fortified border wounded three South Korean soldiers, AFP reported.
“The middle-sized dispersal warhead tipped on the cruise missile is capable of turning into ashes a target area of 5ha to 6ha with its highest-density power,” the official Korean Central News Agency reported on Nov 3.
The test “perfected the capability to deliver a vertical strike against the target by improving the terminal maneuverability of the cruise missile”, KCNA said, “taking into consideration the natural and geographical characteristics of the targeted area”.
A North Korean official was quoted as saying the test was conducted “because our armed forces should defend the security of the country and deter all sorts of threats”.
“Various combat functions of such strongest weapon system will help defend the DPRK from potential threats from outside and renew the military capabilities of the state,” the general director of the Missile Administration said, using the acronym for North Korea’s official name.
The nuclear-armed North recently trialed a range of weaponry including attack drones, a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
South Korea’s military did not announce the cruise missile launch, as it had also not done with Nov 1’s test.
Unlike ballistic missile launches, North Korean cruise missile tests are not prohibited by the United Nations’ Security Council sanctions.
Asked on Nov 2 about Nov 1’s reported test, Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesperson Jang Do-young said South Korea and the United States were “closely coordinating and conducting a highly detailed analysis of its characteristics and specifications”.
“Our military does not announce all projectiles launched by North Korea,” said Jang.
“Whether to make an announcement is determined through a comprehensive military assessment, taking into account the protection of surveillance and reconnaissance assets and capabilities, operational security and other factors,” he added.

- North Korea launched multiple ballistic missiles from near Pyongyang into the East Sea on Sunday, with South Korea’s military reporting a flight distance of about 900 kilometers.
- The United States said the launches pose no immediate threat to U.S.
forces or allies and confirmed close coordination with South Korea and regional partners.
North Korea launched multiple ballistic missiles into the East Sea on Sunday morning, according to South Korea’s military, marking Pyongyang’s first missile launches of the year.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missiles were fired from an area near Pyongyang at about 7:50 a.m.
local time and traveled approximately 900 kilometers before landing in the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan.
The military said it has maintained an enhanced readiness posture following the launches.
The missile launches were carried out as regional leaders prepared for a summit between South Korea and China scheduled for Monday, where North Korea is expected to be on the agenda.
Seoul has been pressing Beijing to take a more active role in efforts aimed at denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula.
The launches represent Pyongyang’s first missile activity this year.
North Korea’s most recent prior test occurred on November 7, when it fired a short-range ballistic missile into the East Sea, according to South Korean military records.
The United States acknowledged the launches and said it was coordinating with allies.
In a public statement, U.S.
Indo-Pacific Command said: “We are aware of the missile launches and are consulting closely with our allies and partners.
Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to U.S.
personnel or territory, or to our allies.
The United States remains committed to the defense of the U.S.
homeland and our allies in the region.”
South Korea’s Presidential Office convened an emergency security meeting after the launches.
Officials told Reuters that two ballistic missiles were fired into the East Sea, prompting consultations among senior defense and national security officials in Seoul.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff said South Korean and U.S.
intelligence authorities were conducting a detailed analysis of the missiles, including their type and flight characteristics.
No immediate damage or casualties were reported in connection with the launches.
Ballistic missile tests by North Korea are prohibited under multiple United Nations Security Council resolutions, but Pyongyang has continued such activity in recent years as it expands its missile programs.
The regime has argued that the tests are part of its sovereign right to self-defense, a position rejected by the United States and its allies.

polymarket-6403111.text:
North Korea says it tested a cruise missile warhead capable of scattering explosives across an area as large as 15 acres, its second reported test of a cluster-type weapon in three days.
The North’s Missile Administration carried out the test Monday using a strategic cruise missile equipped with a medium-sized dispersal warhead, according to a Tuesday report by the state-run Korean Central News Agency.
The warhead can destroy an area of 12 to 15 acres, KCNA claimed, without providing further details about the system.
The test evaluated the warhead’s destructive power and the cruise missile’s flight characteristics during a vertical strike, according to the report.
A dispersal warhead opens over a target to scatter smaller munitions or other agents across a wide area.
Monday’s reported launch followed Saturday’s test of a cluster-bomb warhead for a tactical ballistic missile that North Korea claimed could turn an area of 30 to 32 acres “into ashes.”
South Korea’s military has declined to confirm the launches, saying cruise missiles can be difficult to detect at long ranges.
Acknowledging each launch would reveal the South’s response capabilities or its own assets, navy Capt.
Jang Do-young, a spokesman for South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, said Tuesday.
The military does not “want to reveal our hand to North Korea,” he said, according to a transcript of a briefing in Seoul.
When North Korea launches cruise missiles from long distances, “detection may be limited under certain circumstances,” Jang said.
Unlike ballistic missiles, cruise missiles fly at relatively low speeds and altitudes and use the Earth’s curvature to bypass terrain, he explained.
Nevertheless, South Korea has sufficient capabilities to detect and respond if the North launches cruise missiles toward the South, Jang said.
Seoul for decades has had fully operational precision-strike systems that exceed what Pyongyang claims to have achieved with its cluster-type weapons, he added.
North Korean Gen.
Kim Jong-sik said in Tuesday’s KCNA report that developing a variety of weapons systems is more urgent than ever.
Monday’s test demonstrated the system’s combat capabilities, which Kim described as essential to defending the North against potential threats and strengthening the country’s military, KCNA reported.
U.S.
Forces Korea referred a request for comment to U.S.
Pacific Command in Hawaii.
“We do not discuss specific intelligence collection capabilities, detection timelines, or operational assessments in detail,” the command said in an unsigned email Monday in Hawaii.
The command said its priority remains defending the United States and its allies while working closely with South Korea to maintain readiness and counter potential threats.

▲ A news report on North Korea's missile launches is displayed on a TV screen in the waiting area of Seoul Station on October 29.
North Korea fired multiple missiles toward the East Sea on the morning of November 4, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) announced.
The JCS stated that it detected several missiles launched into the East Sea from around the Sondok area in South Hamgyong Province.
The military explained that South Korea and the United States closely monitored the launches from the preparation stage and detected and tracked the missiles immediately after liftoff.
The JCS also emphasized that while closely watching various North Korean movements under a steadfast South Korea-U.S.
combined defense posture, it maintains the capabilities and readiness to overwhelmingly respond to any provocation.
While the JCS typically detects North Korea's ballistic missile launches in real time and notifies the press immediately, it stated in today's notice that missiles, rather than ballistic missiles, were fired.
The military is currently conducting a detailed analysis of the projectile's specifications, flight range, and whether it was a ballistic missile.
The missile launches took place on November 3, local time, while voting was underway in the U.S.
midterm elections, which serve as an interim assessment of the second year of Donald Trump's administration.
In particular, the provocation occurred shortly after Kim Yo-jong, director of the General Affairs Department of the Workers' Party of Korea, mentioned dialogue with the United States as an option in a statement protesting North Korea being identified as the culprit behind the Binance hacking incident.
In a statement issued on November 4, Kim stated toward the United States that "the options for safeguarding peace certainly include dialogue, but this does not necessarily equate to our national interests," raising speculation that Pyongyang might be leaving room for U.S.-North Korea dialogue.
However, in the same statement, Kim also signaled a hardline response, warning that "under the current reality where new records are being set in the execution of the U.S.
hostile policy, it is only natural that new records should also be created in our reflexive response."
Earlier, on November 2, Kim Jong-sik, first vice department director of the Munitions Industry Department of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, also criticized combined and joint military drills conducted by South Korea and the U.S., as well as trilateral exercises including Japan.
He signaled an intense military response, stating that "the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's national defense policy to accelerate and strengthen its nuclear war deterrence will remain unwavering."
If the latest launches are confirmed to be ballistic missiles, it would mark the third such launch in a week, following tests on October 29 and 31.
Including cruise missile launches, this marks Pyongyang's fourth show of force against South Korea over the past week.
On October 29, North Korea simultaneously fired about 10 rounds of 600 mm super-large multiple rocket launchers (KN-25), followed by a test fire of tactical ballistic missiles equipped with dispersing warheads on October 31.
On November 3, the North disclosed the results of an assessment test on the destructive power of cluster warheads for strategic cruise missiles and a vertical strike flight characteristics test targeting simulated sites, both conducted on November 2.
In reporting its recent test launches, North Korea has repeatedly showcased scenes of missiles striking targets simulating South Korean military installations—such as frontline guard posts, aircraft hangars, and artillery positions—blatantly revealing its intent to threaten South Korea.

take all possible measures for precaution, including readiness for contingencies.

make every effort to gather and analyze information in close cooperation with the U.S., the ROK, and other countries, and 2.
continue to take all possible measures to conduct surveillance in readiness for the occurrence of contingencies.

President Donald Trump said Tuesday he still likes "Elon a lot," despite their high-profile split earlier this year over the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
At the end of the administration’s monthly Cabinet meeting, FOX Business’ Edward Lawrence asked Trump whether Musk was "back in [his] circle of friends" after their falling-out.
Trump responded: "Well, I really don't know.
I mean, I like Elon a lot." He praised Musk’s endorsement during the 2024 campaign before noting their disagreement over electric-vehicle policy.
Musk was a fixture in the White House in the early days of the second Trump administration as he took on the role as the Department of Government Efficiency's de facto leader.
He served as a special government employee with the Trump administration to help lead DOGE, frequently attending Cabinet meetings and joining Trump during public events.
Musk's tenure with DOGE wrapped up at the end of May.
TRUMP TEASES MUSK AT FORUM AS ONCE-FROSTY DYNAMIC SEEMS TO TAKE A TURN
Musk had also championed Trump during the 2024 election cycle, criss-crossing battleground states that ultimately all voted for the Republican candidate over former Vice President Kamala Harris.
Trump repeatedly celebrated Musk for his efforts at DOGE to remove potential federal overspending, fraud and mismanagement – an effort assailed by government employees and Democrats who protested both the Trump administration and Musk repeatedly earlier this year.
TRUMP RENOMINATES MUSK ALLY JARED ISAACMAN TO LEAD NASA AFTER EARLIER REVERSAL
The cozy friendship fell to pieces in June, however, when Musk began publicly ridiculing the "One Big Beautiful Bill," which was a massive piece of legislation Trump signed into law in July that advances his agenda on taxes, immigration, energy, defense and the national debt.
Musk railed against the legislation, which Trump had been rallying Republican lawmakers to pass since the beginning of his second term, posting on X that it would be the "BIGGEST DEBT ceiling increase in HISTORY" and also claimed in a personal attack on Trump that "@RealDonaldTrump is in the Epstein files."
Trump previously told the media that his relationship with Musk changed when he began discussing plans to eliminate the electric vehicle mandate, which would affect Musk's signature electric company, Tesla.
Trump signed a trio of congressional resolutions in June ending California's restrictive rules for diesel engines and mandates on electric vehicle sales, with Trump celebrating that his signature "will kill the California mandates forever."
WHITE HOUSE TAUNTS LIBERALS WITH PROVOCATIVE MEME-FILLED DEBUT ON BLUESKY
The pair abruptly parted ways in June, with Musk weeks later offering some support to Trump's presidential actions on social media, such as praising a ceasefire deal between Israel and Gaza in July.
Musk was seen physically back in Trump's orbit in September during the memorial service for Charlie Kirk, Turning Point USA's founder who was assassinated on Sept.
10.
The pair was seen sitting next to each other and chatting during the ceremony.

18 at the White House for a dinner with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, as well as dozens of high-profile business leaders.
Trump's latest remarks on Musk unfolded during his Cabinet meeting, which marked his ninth such meeting since the start of his second administration and matched the total number of full Cabinet meetings former President Joe Biden held across his four-year tenure.
