polymarket-6440122.text:
For more than a year, leaders from the country’s largest technology firms have worked to win President Trump’s favor as he returned to the White House.
From meetings at Mar-a-Lago to hefty inauguration donations, their efforts were on full display from the first day of Trump’s, with CEOs like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg sitting in the front rows of the president’s inauguration while some top Republicans watched from overflow rooms.
But the technology industry has since faced several ups and downs under the second Trump administration, testing their relationships with a president known for his unpredictability.
Amid personal feuds and debates over artificial intelligence policy, some of the newer relationships have held, while others faced turbulence.
Elon Musk attends the Annual Meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Thursday, Jan.
22, 2026.
(AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)
Elon Musk
The president’s relationship the CEO and founder of SpaceX and Tesla has been the most volatile of his second term, starting as a swift alliance and ending with a public blowout.
While their relationship publicly devolved last June, tensions have eased since, with Musk joining Trump on his state visit to China earlier this month.
Up until the 2024 election, Musk largely stayed out of politics, and at times, seemed skeptical of Trump, who also publicly criticized the tech billionaire in the past.
But as Musk’s politics shifted right under the Biden administration, he endorsed Trump’s reelection bid, appeared alongside him at campaign rallies and donated hundreds of millions to reelect Trump and other Republicans.
Musk led Trump’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, where the business leader spent large chunks of time at the White House, even appearing at one Cabinet meeting.
He continued his work at the White House for four months until his status as a special government employee expired in late May, seemingly leaving on good terms with Trump.
Musk, however, drew fire from Trump days later after he spoke out against the president’s tax and spending bill.
He also took credit for Trump’s electoral victory in 2024 and later accused Trump of being named in the Jeffrey Epstein files, backing calls for the president to be impeached in an hours-long tirade onsocial media.
Musk quickly tried to walk his claims back to make peace with the president, who wished him well and said they likely wouldn’t be speaking for a while.
The tech billionaire floated creating a third party, but talks of this died down by the end of summer.
By August, Trump softened his tone, stating Musk had a “bad moment,” but is a “good person.”
The two reunited at the September funeral of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, and Trump later told reporters he spoke “on and off” with Musk.
Musk later appeared at a White House state dinner last fall, and at a Mar-a-Lago event earlier this year.
In the largest and latest sign of reconciliation, Musk was one of two executives aboard Air Force One with Trump for the China state visit earlier this month.
Dario Amodei, CEO and co-founder of Anthropic, attends the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Jan.
23, 2025.
Dario Amodei
The Anthropic CEO is another AI executive with a complicated relationship with Trump and his White House.
Unlike Musk, however Amodei’spersonal politics and the company’s safety-first approach to AI made him a likely target of the president.
Prior to the 2024 election, Amodei in a Facebook post likened Trump to a “feudal warload,” urging followers to vote for former Vice President Kamala Harris, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Amodei often breaks with tech competitors, and the administration, over AI safety, endorsing state and federal measures that would add oversight to the design and operation of these models.
Warning of the dangers of unmonitored AI, Amodei wrote in an op-ed last year opposing a proposed 10-year moratorium on state regulation of AI.
Despite Amodei’s personal beliefs, the company continued its government work, including at the Pentagon, where up until recently, it was the only AI system permitted to work in the agency’s classified networks.
Following a public dispute over safeguards for domestic mass surveillance and autonomous lethal weapons, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth labelled the company as a supply chain risk, prohibiting the use of Claude in the Department of Defense.
Amid the clash, a memo from Amodei to staff was leaked, in which he argued the Trump administration opposed the company because it did not donate to the president or showed “dictator-style” praise as company competitors.
Amodei apologized for the internal memo, explaining it was a reaction to Trump’s social media post slamming the firm as “an out of control radical left company.”
While the Pentagon has doubled down on their criticism, Trump and other senior administration officials extended an olive branch less than two months after the fallout.
Trump told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” the AI firm “tends to be on the left,” but “we get along with them.”
“They’re very smart, and I think they can be of great use.
I like smart people, I like high-IQ people and they definitely have high IQs,” he said.
“I think we’ll get along with them just fine.”
Amodei was then invited to the White House to meet with senior administration officials, and the company has been kept in the loop on ongoing AI policy.
Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos speaks at the Amazon re:MARS convention in Las Vegas on June 6, 2019.
Jeff Bezos

Elon Musk appears to have reunited with Donald and Melania Trump, per a post shared on X on Sunday.
“Had a lovely dinner last night with @POTUS and @FLOTUS,” Musk wrote on the platform.
“2026 is going to be amazing!”
The update comes days after Musk seemed to indicate he has started donating to Republican candidates ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
“America is toast if the radical left wins,” Musk wrote on X on January 1.
“They will open the floodgates to illegal immigration and fraud.
Won’t be America anymore.”
Musk also reshared a video from conservative influencer @jackunheard that was captioned, “BREAKING: Elon Musk is reportedly going all-in funding Republicans to help President Trump take back full control in the November midterms.”
The dinner also appears to be an indication Musk and Trump are back in one another’s good graces after their public falling out last year.
In June Musk insisted Trump was among those listed in the Epstein files.
“Time to drop the really big bomb: @realDonaldTrump is in the Epstein files,” Musk said.
“That is the real reason they have not been made public.
Have a nice day, DJT!”
Musk also insisted Trump was “ungrateful” and couldn’t have won the 2024 election without his assistance.
Trump eventually acknowledged Musk’s outbursts and told White House reporters in June, “Elon and I had a great relationship.
I don’t know if we will anymore.
I’m very disappointed in Elon.
I’ve helped Elon a lot.”
Trump also insisted he would have won Pennsylvania (and therefore the election) without Musk’s help.
A week later Musk expressed some regret about his commentary.
“I regret some of my posts about President Donald Trump last week,” Musk wrote on X about his incendiary posts.
“They went too far.”

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump will award Elon Musk and other leading American innovators the nation’s highest honors for scientific and technological achievement Thursday, Fox News Digital has learned, marking Trump’s first time presenting the awards.
"The Trump administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology.
These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation," White House spokesperson Liz Huston told Fox News Digital.
The honorees, who will be recognized at the White House’s Science: A New Golden Age Summit, include some of the most powerful figures in American technology and mark Elon Musk’s latest return to Trump’s orbit after his high-profile departure from the administration and subsequent public rupture with the president.
Trump will award the National Medal of Science to Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su, while Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation during the summit, Fox News Digital learned.
TRUMP UNVEILS AMERICA.GOV AS AI-POWERED HUB FOR PASSPORTS, MEDICARE ENROLLMENT AND MORE
The ceremony will mark the first time Trump has presented the National Medal of Science and the National Medal of Technology and Innovation during either of his administrations.
The summit will bring together leading scientists and tech innovators to discuss how super intelligence and private-sector investment can accelerate scientific breakthroughs and strengthen U.S.
leadership in science and technology.
NEW BOOK ON ELON MUSK EXAMINES THE BILLIONAIRE’S MIND, MOTIVATION AND MAKING LIFE MULTI-PLANETARY
Musk’s expected award marks another step in his return to Trump’s orbit after their relationship ruptured last year.
The split followed Musk’s departure from DOGE, when he blasted Trump’s signature tax-and-spending bill as a "disgusting abomination," setting off a personal feud that included Trump threatening his government contracts.
The two have since renewed ties, with Musk again appearing alongside Trump at a recent technology leader lunch and was present during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit.
The Tesla CEO has also returned to an advisory role in the Trump administration, co-leading the Pentagon’s Project Meridian, which studies the future of warfare and the weapons and technologies the U.S.
military will need to maintain its technological edge.

President Donald Trump and Elon Musk appear to have repaired their once-strained relationship, according to a post shared by the billionaire Tesla founder on X.
In a post shared Sunday, Musk wrote, "Had a lovely dinner last night with @POTUS and @FLOTUS," before adding, "2026 is going to be amazing!"
The photo, taken from a Saturday evening event at Mar-a-Lago in Florida, sparked speculation that the pair’s bromance may be back on after months of tension.
After the 2024 campaign, Musk became one of the Republican Party’s biggest political donors, contributing hundreds of millions of dollars, according to Reuters.
TRUMP LAYS OUT WHERE HE STANDS WITH ELON MUSK AFTER BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL BLOWUP
Trump later tapped Musk to advise the government efficiency effort and set up DOGE, focused on reducing federal spending and streamlining operations – but Musk stepped back from the role in mid-2025 amid mounting criticism.
Tensions also resurfaced when Musk publicly criticized Trump-backed spending proposals and raised concerns about the size of federal outlays.
TRUMP TEASES MUSK AT FORUM AS ONCE-FROSTY DYNAMIC SEEMS TO TAKE A TURN
"I’m sorry, but I just can’t stand it anymore," Musk said in a June 3 post about Trump's "big beautiful bill."
"This massive, outrageous, pork-filled Congressional spending bill is a disgusting abomination.
Shame on those who voted for it: you know you did wrong.
You know it," Musk complained.
Trump shot back that he was "very disappointed" in Musk's criticism of his bill at the time before adding, "Elon and I had a great relationship.
I don’t know if we will anymore."
Musk shot back on X saying, "Without me, Trump would have lost the election, Dems would control the House and the Republicans would be 51-49 in the Senate."
At one point, Musk suggested he could form a new political party.
But by late 2025, both sides appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone.
In September, the two were seen shaking hands at Charlie Kirk's memorial service in a box at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona.
Musk was also seen at a White House dinner in November as Trump hosted Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
TRUMP AND MUSK'S UNEXPECTED TRUCE COULD BE AMERICA'S SECRET WEAPON IN THE GLOBAL TECHNOLOGY RACE
FOX Business’ Edward Lawrence asked Trump at a Cabinet meeting on Dec.
2 if Musk was "back in [his] circle of friends" after their falling out.
"Well, I really don't know.
I mean, I like Elon a lot," Trump replied.

polymarket-6440122.text:
Elon Musk attends Trump's dinner with Saudi crown prince
(Reuters) -Elon Musk joined a dinner with U.S President Donald Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman at the White House on Tuesday, the second joint public appearance since a bitter public feud earlier this year.
Musk's attendance could be a sign of reconciliation in a turbulent relationship between the Tesla CEO and the U.S.
president.
Musk supported and funded Trump's election last year and became a close adviser to his administration early this year, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and overseeing cuts to federal funding and jobs.
But the two soon had a falling out.
The billionaire businessman took to social media to attack Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill as fiscally reckless, and said he planned to create a new political party.
Trump hit back threatening to cut off the billions of dollars in subsidies that Musk's companies received from the federal government.
The feud, along with Musk's far-right political rhetoric, hurt Tesla's brand image, sales and stock price, analysts have said.
Musk and Trump have rarely come together publicly since.
Musk was last spotted shaking hands with Trump at a memorial for conservative activist Charlie Kirk in September.
Trump is hosting the Saudi de facto ruler as the latter seeks to rehabilitate his global image and deepen ties with Washington.
Others at the dinner included Portugal's soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
(Reporting by Steve Holland and Abhirup Roy, writing by Christian Martinez; editing by Scott Malone and Stephen Coates)

Musk joins Trump family for Thanksgiving dinner at Mar-a-Lago
Tesla CEO Elon Musk had a seat at the family table for Thanksgiving dinner at Mar-a-Lago, joining President-elect Donald Trump, Melania Trump and their 18-year-old son Barron, in the latest indicator of Trump's growing bond with the world's richest man.
Musk was seated right next to Trump in a video posted by Michael Solakiewicz, which shows the pair enjoying a campaign rally classic, "Y-M-C-A."
Trump slapped his hand on the table and gave Musk's shoulder a friendly pat, and Musk pumped both fists in the air.
Musk, who owns the social media platform X, wore a black blazer and a t-shirt with an "X" emblazoned on it.
Trump smiled, turning to Barron and Melania, as other dinner guests stood around taking photos and clapping along.
Musk reposted another TikTok of him at the Thanksgiving celebration chatting with Trump ally Sylvester Stallone, as the President-elect greeted people at a table nearby.
"I was telling @TheSlyStallone that I just watched Demolition Man again and how well it predicted the crazy woke future 30 years ago!" Musk posted on X.
In the incoming Trump administration, Musk has been selected to run the newly created "Department of Energy Efficiency," or DOGE, along with former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.
The choice in particular of Musk - who leads companies with existing, lucrative government contracts - raised immediate questions about potential conflicts of interest.
During the presidential transition, Musk has spent significant time at Trump's Florida club, something even Trump joked about at a gala earlier this month.
"He likes this place.
I can't get him out of here.
He just likes this place," Trump said at the America First Policy Institute Gala at Mar-a-Lago.
Musk sat at a table directly to the right of the podium.
Musk has been in the room when multiple world leaders have phoned Trump, and he has weighed in on staffing decisions, with the SpaceX and Tesla CEO even making clear his preference for certain roles.
Musk was with Trump at Mar-a-Lago when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called to congratulate the president-elect the day after the election, according to a source briefed on the call.
Trump put the call on speaker, and Zelensky thanked Musk for his help providing communications to Ukraine through the billionaire's Starlink internet service.
Musk is not the only social media owner spending face time with Trump.
Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg was at Mar-a-Lago on Wednesday, CNN previously reported.
But Musk has gained an almost familial standing.
On the day after the election, Musk was seen in a Trump family photo at Mar-a-Lago posted by Trump's granddaughter Kai.
Posting another picture with Musk, Kai said he had achieved "uncle status."
Trump has also spent time on Musk's turf, attending the SpaceX Starship rocket test launch in Texas last week.

Elon Musk to return to the White House to co-lead study on the future of war: report
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Tesla CEO Elon Musk will come back to the White House and advise President Donald Trump on the future of war.
Musk will be co-leading a study described by the Pentagon as studying the future of warfare.
During a speech at the Quantico military base located in Virginia, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the project would be called “Project Meridian.”
"We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists," he said during the speech.
Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey and former GOP House Speaker Newt Gingrich will be leading the study alongside Musk, according to Yahoo News.
Musk used to be head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and left in May of 2025.
In the same speech at Quantico, Hegseth also announced a 20% cut in how many generals and admirals are in the U.S.
military.
"The number crunchers sat we've fired 10% of the generals and admirals across the force and that number sounds about right," he said.
"And I know because I directed it.
We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10%.
So yes, a 20% reduction across the board.
Now the media calls that a purge.
I call it accountability and [it's] long overdue."

polymarket-6440122.text:
Elon Musk lands new Trump administration role shaping future of American warfare
Pete Hegseth tapped Musk alongside Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich for the 120-day initiative
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
Elon Musk is taking on a new role in the Trump administration, this time helping the Pentagon determine which weapons and technology American troops will need to fight the wars of the future.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that Musk will co-lead Project Meridian, a new Pentagon initiative tasked with looking years and even decades ahead to identify emerging domains of warfare and the capabilities the U.S.
military will need to dominate them.
Musk, the former leader of the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), will lead the effort alongside defense tech billionaire Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich under the direction of War Department Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael.
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
EXCLUSIVE: HEGSETH TO DOUBLE CUTS TO GENERALS, ADMIRALS IN MAJOR PENTAGON SHAKEUP
"The best forecasters of future conflict do not solely reside inside the Pentagon," Hegseth said during his State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico.
"There are obvious biases and risks to asking ourselves to both ask the questions and answer them."
Hegseth said the initiative would begin immediately, and he would meet with Musk, Luckey and Gingrich in a secure site just 200 yards from the stage after his speech.
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
Project Meridian will have 120 days to "ruthlessly map the trajectory of wars, domains and technologies," culminating in a public rollout of its findings and a classified annex.
Hegseth described a sweeping mandate that stretches "from under the Earth to beyond the moon."
Rather than developing new military strategies or policies, the group will seek to identify "the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master" and focus on "discovering, developing and fielding" weapons and systems that could be needed by future generations of American troops.
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
Musk and Luckey enter the effort with firsthand experience developing technology for the U.S.
military.
Musk's SpaceX is a major Pentagon contractor, while Luckey founded Anduril Industries, a defense technology company specializing in autonomous weapons and other advanced military systems.
Their industry experience positions both men to bring an unusually close view of emerging technology and the modern battlefield to the Pentagon's long-range planning.
It could also raise potential conflict-of-interest questions as executives whose companies compete for defense business help identify the capabilities and technologies the military should pursue.
BATTLEFIELD ROBOTS OPEN NEW FRONT IN INNOVATION WAR WITH MAJOR US ADVERSARY
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
Meridian was one piece of a broader push announced by Hegseth Wednesday to remake the military around autonomous warfare and rapidly emerging technology.
Hegseth announced the creation of Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, a new four-star combatant command with what he described as "service-like authorities" to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force.
The War Department will also begin phasing in new occupational frameworks across the military departments to create dedicated career paths for what Hegseth called a new generation of "autonomous warfighters."
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
"We should have been thinking about Autonomous Warfare Command ten years ago," Hegseth said, explaining that Meridian is intended to look far enough ahead to anticipate the next technological transformation before the military falls behind.
The announcements came during the second iteration of what the War Department has dubbed Hegseth’s annual State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico.
The setting was the same as last year, but the audience was markedly different.
Hegseth summoned generals, admirals and other senior military leaders from around the world to Quantico for his first address, where he laid out sweeping changes to military standards, personnel and what he called the "warrior ethos."
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
This time, Hegseth addressed a younger generation of military leaders, including top-performing E-6 enlisted service members and O-3 officers from across the force.
He called them the military’s "current and future leaders on the front lines" and said the address would become an annual opportunity to assess the state of the force and lay out his vision for its future.
Hegseth used Wednesday’s speech to unveil six new initiatives, ranging from the military’s embrace of autonomous warfare to an effort to make U.S.
bases and defense supply chains less vulnerable to foreign disruption.

{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
The secretary also used the address to deliver some of his most pointed rhetoric yet about his effort to reshape the culture of the military and about the news media.
"We are no longer the woke department or the weak department," Hegseth said.
"No fatties, no trainees, no weirdos, no beardos, no wimps, no radicals.
Just warriors."
Hegseth later accused some journalists of engaging in "partisan activism" that jeopardizes military operations and service members, calling such reporting "fundamentally anti-American."
{{#rendered}} {{/rendered}}
"It’s sick.
It’s a national betrayal.
It’s treason, actually," Hegseth said.

polymarket-6440122.text:
In a nearly hourlong speech Wednesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced six initiatives aimed at dramatically transforming the United States military.
Among them is a new autonomous warfare command to prepare for battles fought with artificial intelligence, robotics and drones and a new effort to imagine the future of warfare led by billionaire tech entrepreneurs Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey.
“We have the most powerful and the most prepared military on the planet.
Nobody can touch us,” Hegseth said during a speech to troops at the Marine Corps Base in Quantico, Virginia.
“My job, your job, our job is to keep it that way.”
Hegseth announced Wednesday that he is creating a new Autonomous Warfare Command, which he described as an effort to build and scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the armed forces as part of what he said is the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history.
“Drone warfare supercharged by (super intelligence)-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he said.
Hegseth said the new Auto WarCom, as he calls it, will build on the drone dominance program he initiated last year to accelerate the purchasing and deployment of drones to the battlefield.
He said the U.S.
military needs quantities of drones to enhance limited supplies of elite and expensive weapons and cited Ukraine defenses against Russia as demonstrating the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt.
“We will fuse procurement with operations at scale and then allow war fighters and engineers and entrepreneurs to learn, adapt and rapidly iterate on their domain and their mission.”
Hegseth has tapped billionaire tech entrepreneurs Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich to lead a new effort called Project Meridian that will study the future of warfare.
“The future of warfare is not about developing new strategies or policies.
We already do that,” Hegseth said.
“The purpose is to creatively look at the future and identify the domains we must conquer and capabilities we must master.”
He said the focus of Project Meridian will be discovering, developing and fielding weapons and systems that will be needed in the future “without any creative limitations or restrictions on any future battlefield from under the earth and beyond the moon.”
He has asked for a Project Meridian report to be completed and submitted in 120 days.
Hegseth said his first meeting with the group would happen immediately following his speech.
Calling it a “national insurance policy for the American homeland,” Fortress America is a plan for every military installation in the United States to generate its own power independent of the civilian energy grid.
It also calls for the U.S.
to mine and refine the critical materials it needs in the United States and to build a strategic reserve of munitions, fuel, medicine and blood that will allow the U.S.
to continue fighting, as well as to secure the airwaves, satellites and spectrum necessary for the military to communicate.
Saying the United States hasn’t built a new military base in 40 years, Hegseth called on the governors of all U.S.
states to bid on a new base that can host between 15,000 and 25,000 American troops.
The base will consist of “hundreds of thousands of acres with organic power generation, modern air defenses and cutting-edge tech,” he said.
The selection process will be transparent, he said, adding that governors will be invited to the Pentagon to pitch their plans.
Hegseth said the country’s three military academies at West Point, New York; Annapolis, Maryland; and Colorado Springs, Colorado, are critically important because they commission the most military officers.
But he said the armed forces need more officers from other academic institutions.
Hegseth announced Wednesday that the Pentagon has partnered with Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University and Hillsdale College as part of a new America’s Corps of Cadets.
“This flagship effort is central to our goal of increasing patriotic leaders of character,” Hegseth said, adding that the Pentagon will announce additional universities soon.
“The status quo of our officer pipeline is pretty good, but the future will be even better,” he said.
Hegseth said 95% of U.S.
troops identify as religious, but many of them are forced to disconnect from their faith communities when they join the military.
“Our department has a sacred duty: first-class religious support wherever we send our warriors.”
For too long, he said, military chaplains had been sidelined with paperwork.
“That ends now,” he said.

U.S.
envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday he believes Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, while Kyiv's European allies expressed concerns about President Donald Trump's meeting in China with the Kremlin leader.
Kushner's remarks came after Trump wrapped rare three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi.
According to fellow U.S.
envoy Steve Witkoff, Trump discussed a peaceful end to the Russia-Ukraine war during the trilateral meeting — which was billed as a historic but seemed to lack breakthroughs.
The trio, convening in China, was also meant to discuss the war with Iran and how to reduce the dangers posed by nuclear arsenals.
But after roughly 70 minutes behind closed doors, they agreed to a far narrower agenda: To reform the United Nations, refine more fossil fuels and curb the reach of the International Criminal Court.

Hawley on 2028: ‘I have a lot of thinking to do’
Before the midterms, Republican Sen.
Josh Hawley seemed to rule out a presidential bid, with the Missouri senator telling the Washington Examiner that “I have no intention of doing so, period.”
Now, after the catastrophic midterms for the GOP, Hawley is dropping hints that he’s changing his mind.
“After this most recent election, I think everybody that cares about the future of the party, the future of the country, has a lot of thinking to do,” Hawley told The Associated Press on Thursday when asked about his presidential ambitions.
“So I’ll just say I have a lot of thinking to do.”
Hawley said the main takeaway for him from the midterms was that voters want the party to focus on affordability issues and that Republicans needed to cater more to a blue collar electorate.
“We’re a blue collar state,” Hawley said, referring to Missouri.
“And I think the Republican Party will either be a blue collar party or we will be a permanent minority party.”
US withholds judgement on ICJ genocide verdict in Myanmar case over treatment of Rohingya Muslims
The State Department said Thursday that it was “studying the decision to fully assess its implications” before offering an opinion on the International Court of Justice verdict.
The Trump administration has taken a dim view of international law, in particular vowing to dismantle the International Criminal Court, which it regards as a renegade globalist institution.
The ICJ and ICC are separate entities and the administration has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The State Department said “the proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ.”
The department reiterated U.S.
support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups.” It noted the U.S.
is the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
FEMA head commits to ‘breaking the cycle of federal dependency’ in disaster management
FEMA administrator Cameron Hamilton told House lawmakers Thursday that the agency was "restoring federalism to emergency management" and "breaking the cycle of federal dependency," the latest indication that the Trump administration still aims to rebalance the federal role in disasters.
Hamilton told members of a House Homeland Security subcommittee that he was committed to delivering assistance quickly, but that FEMA would refocus to support states, tribes and territories “only when disasters truly exceed their capacity,” instead shoring up local capability and resilience.
Lawmakers on both sides maintained the need for FEMA readiness and funding support.
Democrats offered a glimpse of how they might push back on the Trump administration’s management of FEMA in the next Congress.
" Politicizing FEMA " would be part of future oversight investigations, Democratic Representative Delia Ramirez of Illinois told Hamilton.
"I look forward to seeing you very soon again," she said.
Iran war costs surpass $48B as lawmakers demand unreleased estimates on base damage
The Iran war’s costs have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov.
13, but that doesn’t include damage to U.S.
bases attacked in the Middle East.
Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest figure Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee.
It’s considering Miller’s nomination to be Navy comptroller, among those of other officials for roles in the military.
Democratic Sen.
Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to U.S.
installations, which Miller said he didn't have.
An Associated Press analysis found Iran attacked aircraft hangars, systems that detect incoming strikes, troop housing and more, causing billions of dollars in damage.
Republican Sen.
Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee’s chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible.
Ecuador is Hegseth’s latest stop in South America trip
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has stopped in Ecuador following a surprise visit a day earlier to Venezuela, where he signed a new military cooperation agreement.
The Pentagon said early Thursday that Hegseth would meet with President Daniel Noboa about working together on defense and countering drug trafficking.
After departing Caracas, Hegseth flew to Bogota, Colombia, where he presided over the delivery of a military transport plane.
The plane’s delivery comes as Colombia’s new president embraces Trump’s policies on countering drug trafficking.
Kushner says he believes Russia is ‘comfortable’ with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end war
U.S.
envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark.
Another American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said U.S.
President Donald discussed Ukraine and a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral talks with the Russian and Chinese leaders earlier Thursday.
Kushner and Witkoff met with European allies in Berlin to discuss their support for Ukraine.
Trump dials into a meeting of European allies to discuss Ukraine after he spoke with Putin, Xi
U.S.
President Donald Trump placed a call Thursday to talk to a meeting of European allies to discuss Ukraine after the American leader spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin in China.
U.S.
envoy Jared Kushner said Trump spoke to the allies, who were meeting in Berlin as part of the so-called “Coalition of the Willing.”
He did not disclose what was said during the discussions between the European leaders and Trump.
Trump announces news conference for Friday afternoon
Trump will hold a news conference Friday, soon after his return from an Asia trip that included meetings with China and Russia, the president said Thursday in a social media post.
The news conference is set for noon, he said.
“Heading back to Washington, D.C., from China.
It was a Great and Highly Consequential Trip,” Trump said in a Truth Social post.
He added: “Also, will be discussing the Trade Deals with Thailand, the Philippines, and others.”
Sen.
Thune says he’s ‘with Ukraine’ after Trump’s meeting with Putin and Xi
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday that he’ll wait to see “what was discussed, and maybe what was agreed to” after President Donald Trump met in China with President Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
But the South Dakota Republican said that “as far as I’m concerned, I’m with Ukraine” amid its war against Putin’s Russia.
Thune said he thinks most senators would agree with him.
“I think that’s going to be where most of my colleagues find themselves,” he said.
Some Democrats unimpressed with Elon Musk’s change in tenor
Responding to Musk’s turnabout on X, the social media platform Musk owns, Democratic Sen.
Ruben Gallego of Arizona was concise: “You are still getting a subpoena.”

President Trump Presents National Medals of Science and National Medals of Technology and Innovation
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Today at the Science: A New Golden Age Summit, President Donald J.
Trump presented National Medals of Science and National Medals of Technology and Innovation, our nation’s highest honors for exemplary achievement and leadership in science and technology, to six of America’s greatest living innovators.
Since 1963, the President of the United States has bestowed the National Medal of Science on those deserving of special recognition for their outstanding contributions to science in service of the United States.
Since it was first awarded in 1985, the National Medal of Technology and Innovation has recognized American innovators whose vision, intellect, creativity, and determination have strengthened America’s economy and improved our quality of life.
President Trump is committed to restoring U.S.
global scientific and technological leadership for a New Golden Age, from harnessing super intelligence for scientific discovery to ushering in a nuclear renaissance; from ensuring American space superiority to strengthening America’s quantum advantage.
These medalists have pioneered breakthroughs in science and engineering for the new age of super intelligence, from fundamental advances in general-purpose parallel computing and semiconductor design to engineering and business leadership in building the foundations of hyperscale infrastructure in the U.S., around the world, and even into space.
Their work has advanced American global technology leadership for the 21st Century and laid the foundation for a new Golden Age of Science.
The recipients are listed below.
Recipients of the National Medal of Science
- Elon Musk – “For engineering achievements of extraordinary ambition and scale that have pushed the frontiers of space exploration, intelligent systems, communications, and beyond, renewing American technological leadership and opening a new chapter in American manufacturing.”
- Sergey Brin – “For the development of foundational algorithms for information retrieval and data processing that revolutionized how the world accesses information across science, commerce, and in the course of everyday life.”
- Jensen Huang – “For advancing the graphics processing unit into a general-purpose computing architecture through innovations in processor design and software, transforming massively parallel computation and powering breakthroughs in scientific computing and super intelligence.”
- Lisa Su – “For a lifetime of leadership in semiconductor engineering and high-performance computing through innovations in processor architecture and chiplet-based integration that powered the world’s first exascale supercomputer and opened new frontiers in computational performance.”
Recipients of the National Medal of Technology and Innovation
- Michael Dell – “For advancing a vision of widespread adoption of personal and enterprise computing; for his technical and business management skills building a worldwide technology company; and for his support for the next generation of American scientists, engineers, and technologists.”
- Satya Nadella – “For his transformative leadership of a critical American technology company, which led to its rejuvenation for a new era of cloud computing, and for his construction of the hyperscale infrastructure that enabled the training and global deployment of American super intelligence.”
“Each of these medalists has transformed their field or industry, laying the foundations for technologies we already can barely imagine living without,” said Michael Kratsios, Assistant to the President and Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.
“While we in government work to deliver the efforts a New Golden Age of Science will require, we know that scientific progress and technological innovation depend on the insight and character of individuals.
Innovators like these six awardees are the architects of the future.”
About the Science: A New Golden Age Summit:
Science: A New Golden Age, released in July 2026 by White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios, is the first comprehensive rethinking of the U.S.
science and technology enterprise since Vannevar Bush’s 1945 Science: The Endless Frontier.
The report observes significant changes to how scientific discovery happens today, particularly the increased role of industry in driving R&D and the close integration of applied and foundational research.
It provides concrete recommendations for how government, industry, academia, and philanthropy can seize the opportunities presented by these changes to accelerate scientific discovery and empower the Nation’s best and brightest scientists.
Core recommendations include strengthening support for early-career scientists, reviving the national pursuit of ambitious scientific missions, launching new funding and organizational models for transformative research, building the metascience infrastructure to continuously improve the research enterprise, and scaling SI-driven scientific discovery through the Genesis Mission.
The Science: A New Golden Age Summit convenes leading scientists and innovators to examine these changes and translate the report’s ideas into the next chapter of American scientific progress.
Throughout the day, the Trump Administration will provide major announcements, in coordination with private sector partners and research institutions, to realize the vision of Science: A New Golden Age and the Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science.

- Published On
- June 12, 2025
- Written by
- Stephanie Sugars from Freedom of the Press Foundation
Behind a decade of attacks on the media lies the president’s strategy of control
From the launch of his political career, Donald Trump has used social platforms — first Twitter, then Truth Social — to attack, belittle and discredit journalists, news outlets and the industry as a whole, branding the media “the enemy of the people.”
Even ChatGPT, when asked to write Truth Social posts in his voice, recognized attacks on the press as an indelible element of Trump’s platform.
Requests for posts about the artificial intelligence chatbot’s choice of topics produced the humorous (“There’s nothing like a great, luxurious bathtub to soak away the fake news and tired losers”) as well as the startlingly plausible:
“The media is the enemy of the people.
They lie, twist stories, and try to destroy anyone who disagrees with them.
I’ve been fighting them from day one, and the truth is, they’re desperate because they know I’m winning.
They spread fake polls, fake scandals, and fake news nonstop.
It’s a total disgrace.
We deserve honest reporting, not propaganda.
The American people see through the lies, and one day, the media will pay the price for their treasonous behavior.
They’re the biggest problem in this country.”
To better understand the scope and impact of Trump’s anti-press rhetoric, we have systematically cataloged his posts attacking the news media.
This dataset spans from June 16, 2015, the day he launched his winning campaign, through his removal from Twitter in January 2021 in the wake of the Jan.
6 riot at the U.S.
Capitol.
It picks back up on Nov.
15, 2022, when Trump officially launched his latest campaign, and will continue through his tenure in the White House.
With 10 years since Trump descended the golden escalator in his eponymous tower in New York City, the collection of now nearly 3,500 social posts provides not just a historical archive but also an urgent warning.
These posts form a revealing portrait of a political figure whose polarizing messaging has undermined press freedom and endangered journalists.
The blustering bully
While a combative relationship with the journalists covering them isn’t unique among U.S.
presidents, Trump’s use of social media has enabled him to broadcast his hostility toward the press with unprecedented frequency and reach.
Above all, he has wielded his social platforms as a cudgel against outlets and journalists he claims have reported on him, his administration or his allies unfairly.
But Trump hasn’t just criticized coverage: He has branded swaths of reporting “fake news,” called respected journalists “disgraceful” and accused entire networks of lying to the American people.
Like any bully, he often relies on derisive nicknames, be it the standards from his first term — “The Failing New York Times,” “MSDNC” and “Fredo” (in reference to reporter Chris Cuomo) — or the newly minted — “Washington Compost,” “The Globalist Street Journal” and “Fake Tapper” (CNN host Jake Tapper).
The schoolyard jabs are often snappy and have been adopted by his supporters both in and outside the government.
In some cases, the insults paved the way for concrete action.
In April 2024, Trump posted that NPR was a “TOTAL SCAM” and “LIBERAL DISINFORMATION MACHINE,” and called for the elimination of federal funding for the broadcaster.
Nearly a year later, Republican Rep.
Marjorie Taylor Greene led a hearing titled “Anti-American Airwaves: Holding the heads of NPR and PBS accountable,” in which she accused NPR of having a “communist agenda” and PBS of being “one of the founders of the trans child abuse industry.”
“NPR and PBS have increasingly become radical, left-wing echo chambers for a narrow audience of mostly wealthy, white, urban liberals and progressives who generally look down on and judge rural America,” Greene said in her opening remarks.
Public broadcasters now face threats to their funding on multiple fronts.
Individual journalists have also felt the impact of targeting by Trump.
In November 2019, Trump trashed Washington Post journalists Carol Leonnig, Josh Dawsey and Matt Zapotosky as “lowlife reporters” and the Post as a “garbage newspaper.” Leonnig told the Committee to Protect Journalists that the post triggered “a significant uptick” in hate mail.
“Some of the hate mail is a bit vitriolic and describes me as part of the evil Deep State and stupid as a rock,” she said.
“I was tweeted at by people who called me garbage and repeated the president’s low-life description.”
For other journalists, being singled out by Trump has led to real-world harassment and threats.
Whether calling for boycotts of particular outlets, demanding that a journalist be fired or lobbing threats of civil or criminal action, Trump has routinely used his social platforms to intimidate and chill reporting, with his supporters often in lockstep behind him.
The conditional friend
Ostensibly mainstream or liberal news outlets are far from the only ones on the receiving end of Trump’s ire: In August 2023 alone, Fox News was the target of 27 of the then-candidate’s negative posts about the press.
And when reporting reflects favorably on him — even when it comes from outlets he often rails against — it’s received warmly.
“The ABC News/Washington Post Poll originally came out at a 9-point lead for your favorite President, but that was immediately corrected by them, to 10 points,” Trump wrote in September 2023.
“The only Network that didn’t correct it was Fox News, they left it at 9 points.
Gee, I wonder why?”
Rupert Murdoch’s network and the journalists it employs are actually the second-most targeted by Trump just behind CNN, with 451 posts to CNN’s 460.
The “failing” Times is a distant third, at 369.
Other conservative-leaning news outlets have also come under fire over the years, ranging from the National Review to Drudge Report, the New York Post to Blaze Media.
The pattern is clear: While campaigning in a primary, Trump does not hesitate to turn the beam of his outrage onto conservative journalists and newsrooms that, in his view, have strayed from unwavering loyalty.
Indeed, nearly 75% of the posts targeting Fox News and all of those naming the conservative-leaning outlets above were made in the lead-up to the 2016 and 2024 elections.
Once in office, Trump’s attacks on conservative outlets slow if not stop entirely.
That is, unless other journalists from less favored outlets are involved.
In March 2025, it was Fox’s White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich, whom Trump belittled for her support of the White House Correspondents’ Association.
Two months later, Trump urged Howard Kurtz, host of Fox’s “Media Buzz,” to retire because he has “Every Woke Anchor in the Business” as guests on the show.
Trump has in turn bolstered new conservative media — particularly Newsmax and One America News — both online and through selection for the press pool that accompanies him.
This tactic of elevating allies and punishing perceived betrayal has reshaped the conservative media landscape, rewarding partisanship and punishing dissent.
The calculated critic
Trump’s bluster against the press is deliberate, and he has directly said as much.
During an off-camera conversation with CBS News correspondent Lesley Stahl after winning the 2016 election, he began to attack the press.
“I said, ‘You know, that is getting tired.
Why are you doing this?’” Stahl recalled at an event in 2018.
“‘You’ve won the nomination.
Why do you keep hammering at this?’ And he said, ‘You know why I do it?
I do it to discredit you all and demean you all, so that when you write negative stories about me, no one will believe you.’”
She later told CPJ that she had underestimated how effective it would be: “When you say something over and over, it’s had a huge impact.
Repetition is part of its impact.”
Trump has attacked the press in social media posts an average of once a day since declaring his candidac
polymarket-6596314.title: On Social Media, Trump Targets the Press on Average Once a Day for 10 Years and Counting

polymarket-6596314.text:
Trump's Truth Social lays bare narrow obsessions of an extremely online president
Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.
On March 1, the day after U.S.
forces bombed Iran and began a war that's now more than nine weeks long, President Trump posted 30 times on Truth Social.
Just after midnight, he posted about the bombing campaign, including a threat to retaliate if Iran itself retaliated ("THEY BETTER NOT DO THAT").
Loading...
But he soon had a lot more on his mind; mid-morning, he posted a video portraying Senator Mitch McConnell as the floppy, deceased Bernie from Weekend at Bernie's.
He posted a Tiktok video praising his State of the Union – a speech he had given five days prior – then reposted that video, along with a screenshot of a post on the social media site X.
Just after noon, he posted an update on the war ("we have destroyed and sunk 9 Iranian Naval Ships, some of them relatively large and important").
Mid-afternoon, he posted a string of Trump-friendly news coverage, including a New York Post article from September 2024 about how Lady Gaga's father endorsed Trump in the presidential race.
Shortly thereafter, in the span of five minutes, he posted 10 times, all of them lists of screenshots of praise from X users for his State of the Union address.
He later posted a video update about the war in Iran, followed by a video marked as being from an Instagram user called @truthaboutfluoride, purporting to show San Francisco as a run-down city filled with poverty.
During his first presidential campaign, Trump's constant stream of seemingly unvetted tweets was a sideshow that quickly became inescapable – the boasts, insults, and lies at times hijacked news cycles.
Once he was elected, they presented a new frontier in American politics: a real-time view into a president's mind.
Ten years, one Twitter ejection, one Twitter return, and a move to Truth Social later, Trump's posts still make news – like when he announces a war or tries to pick a fight with the pope – but for many have become the background noise of American politics.
The president of the United States is now communicating with the public sometimes dozens of times a day on a social media platform that he himself created, and most Americans (and perhaps even journalists) never see most of those posts.
Of course, most of those posts are not individually newsworthy.
But looking at them together provides a picture of exactly what, in the aggregate, the president of the United States is thinking about and saying to the world at all hours.
Loading...
To try to grasp that, NPR analyzed the first four months of Trump's Truth Social posts this year.
What emerged is a portrait of an extremely online president with scattered focus – who, even while he dealt with fallout from his policies such as war in Iran and immigration enforcement in Minneapolis, was also busy insulting his critics, posting pictures of his proposed ballroom, and continuing to insist on the lie that he won the 2020 election.
The president also has unorthodox posting habits that illustrate that, even as arguably the most powerful person on earth, he remains focused on how he is seen.
What the president is posting about
To quantitatively analyze the president's posts, NPR compiled the president's first four months of posts, using a data scraper maintained by CNN.
We then classified each post based on its topic (tariffs, the war in Iran, Greenland) and the type of post it was (sharing a news story, reposting someone else, making a threat).
Trump posted 2,249 times in the first four months of 2026, an average of just under 19 posts per day.
The most common topic Trump posted about – at about 14% of his posts – was 2026 elections.
These posts – more than 300 of them – consist largely of either candidate endorsements or posts touting a Trump-backed candidate's win.
However, Trump at times did not give a simple endorsement, instead adding attacks on an endorsee's opponents.
For example, in endorsing Republican candidates for the Indiana state Senate, the posts became paragraph-long screeds as Trump attacked sitting senators as "RINOs" (Republicans in name only) if they voted against a Trump-backed redistricting plan.
The next most common topics after elections were Iran (247 posts) and the economy (177).
He also posted dozens of times about alleged fraud in Minnesota's safety net programs, the SAVE Act, and his belief that the justice system was weaponized against him.
To the degree that his posts measure what he's thinking about, the president's social media feed suggests he is as preoccupied – or even more so – with his personal projects and vendettas than he is with pressing policy matters.
President Trump posted about the 2020 election 71 times in the first four months of 2026, more than he posted even about tariffs (57 times – all of which we coded as a subset of posts about the economy).
Those 2020 election posts all promoted the lie that via massive voter fraud or other malfeasance, Joe Biden stole that election.
Trump posted 68 times about his various Washington, D.C., building projects, including his White House ballroom and a proposed massive arch across the Potomac near Arlington National Cemetery.
That's slightly more than he posted about Venezuela, more than he posted about the SAVE Act he's promoting, and more than he posted about protesters and federal agents in Minneapolis, including federal agents killing two U.S.
citizens.
He posted more than six times as often (105) about his various legal grievances than he did about healthcare policy (17).
Also notable are the topics that get little attention.
While tariffs and the war in Iran do affect, for example, the farm economy, Trump posted just four times specifically about American farming during the first four months of the year – less than half as many times as he posted (nine times) about his anger at comedian Bill Maher.
As for the top types of posts, the largest category – at just under one-quarter of his posts – are social media reshares.
These take several formats – some are screenshots of posts from X, and others are videos reposted from other social media sites, such as TikTok.
This emphasizes the technological differences between now and Trump's first term.
Near the end of his first term, the videos Trump posted were largely from Fox News or other right-leaning news outlets, or they were videos produced by the White House.
Now, there's an endless array of TikTok and Instagram videos and memes the president can repost, many of them from amateurs or generated by AI.
Some have been outright offensive, as when he posted a racist video that depicted former President Obama and Michelle Obama as apes.
The White House initially defended the video, with White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt telling reporters, "Please stop the fake outrage." Trump later said he hadn't seen the full video, telling reporters, "I looked at the beginning of it.
It was fine." He did not apologize, and the post was later deleted.
Other posts have promoted conspiracy theories, as with a video that baselessly proposed that Democratic Minnesota Gov.
Tim Walz was involved in the 2025 killing of Minnesota Democratic State Rep.
Melissa Hortman.
Occasionally, those videos have nothing to do with current events, or even Trump, but are the kind of inane posts littering many people's Facebook feeds.
Around 11 p.m.
one night in February, Trump posted a TikTok video of a person's pet corgi reacting to a can of Reddi-wip.
A minute later, he reposted that video along with a screenshot of a supporter's X post ("Good Night Patriot Friends!").
A minute after that, he posted a 15-second video of Bruce Lee fighting, which he similarly reposted alongside another X screenshot seconds later.
Reposting material from X
This posting-then-reposting pattern is one of the more notable oddities of the president's Truth Social posts.
It appears to be a makeshift way of reposting things from X.
polymarket-6596314.title: Trump's Truth Social lays bare narrow obsessions of an extremely online president (NPR)

polymarket-6596314.text:
Here's How Many Times Trump Has Posted About Each Late Night Host In 2025
When President Donald Trump isn’t suggesting that Democratic lawmakers be hanged for sedition, he is often posting on Truth Social about his deep and burning hatred for the late night television show hosts of America.
He typically posts these little flurries of fury during the exact hours the shows are airing live, leaving the possibility open that he’s live-tweeting his viewing experience like fans of Game of Thrones in 2014.
He’s railed against Jimmy Kimmel, Stephen Colbert, Jimmy Fallon, and Seth Meyers.
The president does not like that they get on television every night and make fun of him.
Wednesday night, Trump blasted Kimmel for his “biased” coverage of the president.
Don't Miss
“Why does ABC Fake News keep Jimmy Kimmel, a man with NO TALENT and VERY POOR TELEVISION RATINGS, on the air?
Why do the TV Syndicates put up with it?
Also, totally biased coverage,” Trump wrote.
“Get the bum off the air!!!”
But that post is just the tip of a very large, very bitter iceberg.
Using the Roll Call social media archive for the president, we have exact stats for each time Trump has targeted a late night show host in 2025.
Let’s dig in.
Starting with the host that has been targeted the least, Trump posted about Jimmy Fallon two times in 2025.
Perhaps Fallon’s desire to take an apolitical approach to late night shielded him, somewhat, from the president’s ire.
Trump still called Fallon “weak, and very insecure,” on July 25.
Stephen Colbert had just three Truth social posts directed at him this year.
This is perhaps because the president feels victorious over The Late Show host.
Colbert and the entire program will exit the network when Colbert’s contract expires in June 2026.
Still, Trump didn’t reign in the gloating.
“Everybody is saying that I was solely responsible for the firing of Stephen Colbert from CBS, Late Night,” Trump wrote, in part.
“That is not true!
The reason he was fired was a pure lack of TALENT, and the fact that this deficiency was costing CBS $50 Million Dollars a year in losses — And it was only going to get WORSE!”
Trump posted about the host of Late Night with Seth Meyers five times in 2025.
The first Truth Social post of the year was on January 14 at 1:24 am EST.
“I got stuck watching Marble Mouth Meyers the other night, the first time in months, and every time I watch this moron I feel an obligation to say how dumb and untalented he is, merely a slot filler for the Scum that runs Comcast,” Trump wrote, in part.
The next four times, in August, September, and twice in November, Trump referred to Meyers as a “total loser,” said he had the “personality of an insecure child,” said he was “the least talented person,” and urged, “NBC should fire him, IMMEDIATELY!
The president posted about Jimmy Kimmel seven times in 2025, starting on July 18.
On that day, Trump wrote: “I absolutely love that Colbert’ got fired.
His talent was even less than his ratings.
I hear Jimmy Kimmel is next.
Has even less talent than Colbert!
Greg Gutfeld is better than all of them combined, including the Moron on NBC who ruined the once great Tonight Show.”
Trump’s attacks on Kimmel include the president calling the host “untalented” and “a FOOL.” Most notably however, Trump’s hatred of Kimmel is connected to the host getting yanked off air after Federal Communications Commissioner Brendan Carr threatened ABC and Disney about his show.
For a week, Kimmel was offline, only to make a triumphant return with a historic ratings boost.
You would think the president would be well aware that all press is good press.
But in the fog of wrath, Trump’s Truth Social posts helps late night show hosts be exactly what he says they arent: relevant.

polymarket-6596314.text:
From mocking his opponents’ appearances to inventing nicknames that sound like playground taunts, the president rarely misses an opportunity to take a cheap shot.
But his latest attempt to rewrite his reputation has one of his biggest political enemies reaching for the receipts.
Trump’s propensity for dishing out insults has become so predictable that his critics barely have to wait for the next one.
What makes his latest claim even more remarkable is that he apparently expected everyone to forget the countless times he has publicly humiliated his political rivals.
California Gov.
Gavin Newsom has made a sport of exposing Trump’s contradictions.
The two have traded insults for over a year, with the Democrat’s press office frequently turning the president’s own words into embarrassing social media moments.
Now Newsom’s team has caught Trump in another spectacular case of double talk.
This time, the president appeared determined to convince Americans that his approach to politics is far more diplomatic than his critics suggest.
Unfortunately for Trump, his own mouth refused to cooperate.
During an Oct.
14 interview with Gray Media correspondent Jon Decker, Trump offered an interesting explanation for how he handles people he needs to negotiate with.
“Look, I have to make deals with people.
So I don’t go around calling them names.
I’m a deal-maker, I’ve always been a very good deal-maker, ” Trump declared.
“I became very rich because of deals.
So I don’t go around mocking people.”
That newfound restraint lasted approximately one hour.
While campaigning in Arizona, Trump turned his attention to Democratic Gov.
Katie Hobbs.
“Katie Hobbs—she is a dumb person.
I don’t give a damn,” he announced.
Newsom’s press office promptly posted screenshots of both clips side by side on Threads, exposing the remarkable turnaround.
“Took 1 hour for the President to do the opposite of what he said … new record?” the account mocked.
The internet needed little encouragement.
“He doesn’t even know what he’s saying from one minute to the next,” one Threads user wrote.
Another observed, “An hour?
He does it in the same breath: ‘I never attacked him on his look, and believe me, there’s plenty of subject matter right there.’”
X users were equally amused.
One person said, “… yall he truly has lost his damn mind we can play HOURS of footage of him mocking people.” Someone else noted, “Calling people names is all he does and it’s usually caught on camera.”
One critic offered a simple suggestion: “Run the tape.”
And the tape stretches back months.
Illinois Gov.
JB Pritzker also became the target of a joke after Trump labeled him a “big fat slob” during a Thanksgiving ceremony in 2025.
In July of this year, Trump called Sen.
Adam Schiff “watermelon head” and “pencil neck,” while referencing his “fat, ugly head.”
In August, Trump had described New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman as an “unattractive person both inside and out” on Truth Social.
October brought another round of attacks.
Fox News personality Jessica Tarlov was branded a “loser,” while New York Attorney General Letitia James faced particularly vicious remarks.
Trump called James “that disgusting Leticia dog” on Oct.
9.
Days later, he labeled her a “DIRTY AND DISGUSTING COP.” His insults have even overshadowed solemn occasions.
During a September ceremony honoring 9/11 victims and first responders, Trump recounted an unverified story about firefighters carrying him to safety near the World Trade Center.
“I’m not the smallest guy in the world,” he acknowledged, an interesting admission from someone who regularly mocks other people’s weight.
Trump has also repeatedly called Democrats “Dumocrats,” explaining his spelling invention during a May interview with Lara Trump.
Newsom’s office responded with its own vocabulary lesson: “Idiot ends with a T, but most people don’t know that.
(The ‘T’ stands for Trump).”
For someone who claims he doesn’t mock people, Trump has certainly accumulated an impressive collection of insults.
And Newsom apparently intends to keep every receipt.
Subscribe To The ABS Newsletter — Get our stories in your inbox.
Independent journalism still matters.
We hope this story was worth your time.
For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run.
We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us.
Our readers did that.
Corporate support for Black media has always been thin.
Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S.
advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020.
That's the backdrop.
It's not why we're asking.
The wider picture isn't any steadier.
Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide.
When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.
We know a request for support isn't why you came here.
But without readers choosing to fund this work directly, the depth of reporting we can do at home and abroad shrinks along with everyone else's.
If you're not in a position to give, that doesn't change how much we value you as a reader.
If you are able to, a recurring contribution does more for us than a single one-time gift, because it lets us plan the next investigation instead of just the next invoice.
It takes about 30 seconds, no long form, no account.
Thank you for continuing to support independent journalism and freedom of the press.

The NVIDIA CORP / US DOLLAR (Equity.US.NVDA/USD) price feed delivers a live NVDA price, updated in real time on Pyth Network.
Prices are aggregated from first-party publishers - exchanges, market makers and trading firms pricing from their own order flow - with a confidence interval on every update.
Available on 100+ blockchains.
US equities do not trade continuously.
Each weekday cycle is split into four sessions with different venues, participants and liquidity: overnight (8:00 PM-4:00 AM ET, Sunday-Thursday, on alternative trading systems such as Blue Ocean ATS), pre-market (4:00-9:30 AM ET), regular hours (9:30 AM-4:00 PM ET, with opening and closing auctions on the primary listing exchange and LULD circuit breakers active) and post-market (4:00-8:00 PM ET, typically with wider spreads, and the window in which many companies release earnings).
From Friday 8:00 PM to Sunday 8:00 PM ET no session runs, a 48-hour gap.
Within the regular session, trading is fragmented across many registered exchanges, dark pools and alternative trading systems, with the SIP consolidating exchange quotes into the NBBO.
Each stock has a primary listing venue, usually NYSE or NASDAQ, which runs its opening and closing auctions.
Pyth US equity prices are contributed directly by first-party institutions that make markets, run venues or route order flow in the stock.
Every update carries a price and a confidence interval, and consumers pull the latest price on demand instead of waiting for a scheduled push.
Publisher prices are benchmarked against the mid-point at the stock's primary listing venue.
On Pyth Pro, supported tickers are priced across all four sessions, and every update carries a marketSession field so risk logic can be session-aware.
Unlike crypto, which trades 24/7, US equity trading activity is fragmented across multiple venues and four distinct trading sessions within each 24-hour cycle.
Each session may have different participants, liquidity profiles and venues, which directly impacts how prices are formed and how much they can move.
| Tier | Participants | Role in price formation |
|---|---|---|
| Primary listing exchanges (NYSE, NASDAQ) | Designated or registered market makers, institutional and retail flow during regular hours | Run each stock's opening and closing auctions; the reference venue for Pyth's publisher benchmark |
| Other registered exchanges (including Cboe, IEX and MEMX) | Broker-dealers, market makers | Contribute quotes to the NBBO; share of volume varies by venue and by stock |
| Dark pools and alternative trading systems (ATS) | Institutional block flow; overnight venues | Off-exchange matching; the overnight session (8:00 PM-4:00 AM ET, Sunday-Thursday) trades on alternative trading systems |
| SIP (Securities Information Processor) | Quotes from all registered exchanges | Consolidates exchange quotes into the NBBO, the best bid and offer across registered exchanges |
Venues do not contribute equally to price discovery.
A price taken from one venue reflects that venue's quotes and liquidity, not the market as a whole.
| Session/Window | Time (ET) | Character |
|---|---|---|
A price gap occurs when a stock opens at a significantly different price from its previous session's close.
Because each of the four sessions has a different liquidity profile and participant base, price information does not flow smoothly across boundaries.
The resulting gaps are a structural feature of equity markets, not anomalies.
| Factor | Impact |
|---|---|
| Earnings | Often released after the 4:00 PM ET close, so the initial move forms in the post-market session on thinner liquidity |
| Company, sector and macro news | Contract awards, guidance changes, regulatory decisions and macro data can move a stock sharply in the overnight or pre-market sessions |
| Analyst upgrades/downgrades | Rating changes and large disclosed positions can trigger multi-day volatility.
Pre-market reactions can set the tone before RTH |
| Weekend / holiday gaps | The 48-hour weekend void (Friday 8:00 PM-Sunday 8:00 PM ET) is the longest scheduled closure of a normal week.
The overnight session from the Sunday open provides the first price signal |
| LULD halts | Limit Up-Limit Down circuit breakers pause trading during RTH when price moves too fast.
On resumption, price can gap up or down |
| Corporate actions | Stock splits, reverse splits and delistings create planned price discontinuities.
A 4:1 split drops the price 75% overnight: not a market move, but a structural repricing that must be handled explicitly |
Worked example.
A company reports quarterly results after the 4:00 PM ET close.
The first prices reacting to the print form in the post-market session, on thinner liquidity and wider spreads, and the next regular-session open is a gap against the prior 4:00 PM close rather than a continuation of it.
If the move is large enough to trip an LULD band after the open, trading pauses: no trades, no feed updates, and a discontinuous price on resumption.
Neither event is an anomaly; both are the normal mechanics of a four-session market.
Liquidity in US equities is not a single number.
It is typically deepest in the regular session, when market makers quote across every exchange and the SIP consolidates exchange quotes, and it thins outside it.
The windows where liquidity disappears or degrades are:
| Event | What happens |
|---|---|
| LULD halt | Trading pauses during regular hours when price breaches its band.
No trades and no feed updates while halted; price free to gap on resumption |
| After-hours earnings | The initial move forms in the post-market session, on thinner liquidity and wider spreads, before the next regular open |
| Stock split | A planned discontinuity.
Publishers apply the split ratio before the ex-date session opens, under the workflow in the Asset-Specific Handling section |
| Weekend void, every week | 48 hours (Friday 8:00 PM-Sunday 8:00 PM ET) with no session.
Positions held through the weekend carry gap risk across the longest closure of the week |
Pyth US equity feeds aggregate first-party contributions from institutions that make prices in this market: firms with direct market access, their own pricing engines and the ability to distribute their own data, including exchanges and trading venues, banks, non-bank market makers and trading firms.
Pyth does not enumerate individual publishers per feed.
The publisher set for US equities draws on four types of contributor:
Publishers are selected per session on two criteria: price freshness through the trading day, and accuracy against the primary-market benchmark described in the What Makes Pyth Data Different section.
Publisher accuracy is benchmarked against the mid-point price at each stock's primary listing venue, and publishers are held to a deviation limit against that benchmark.
This anchors the aggregate to the venue that runs each stock's opening and closing auctions.
| Traditional US equities data | Pyth Network |
|---|---|
| Redistributed venue feeds, per-terminal licensed | First-party contributions from the institutions that own the data |
| A single price with no uncertainty measure | Price plus confidence interval with every update |
The Pyth price for a US equity feed is an indicative reference price derived from an aggregate of publisher submissions.
It is venue-agnostic: it does not represent the price available on any particular exchange or trading system, and it is not an offer to buy or sell the security.
Always verify price freshness before use with getPriceNoOlderThan() and a threshold appropriate to this feed's schedule.
A threshold that is correct during the trading session will reject every price while the underlying market is closed; threshold logic must be schedule-aware, not a single global constant.
For US equities, thresholds are session-specific as well as schedule-specific:
getPriceNoOlderThan() with strict thresholds appropriate for the session.
Regular-session prices up

Symbology & Reference Data
Field-by-field reference for Pyth Pro symbol metadata: identifiers, classification, data quality, trading schedules, and futures expiration
Pyth Pro publishes reference data describing every feed it offers: identifiers, classification, data-quality parameters, trading schedules, and (for derivatives) expiration metadata.
This data is distinct from the real-time price payload: it describes what a feed is, not its current value.
Reference data is served by the Symbology & Reference Data API:
The endpoint returns one JSON object per feed.
This page documents every field on that object.
For the request schema and query parameters for filtering (for example by asset_type or instrument_type), see the interactive API reference.
Example response
Every feed is returned as a single JSON object with the same top-level shape.
The tabs below show feeds that populate different optional fields, depending on asset class and instrument type.
BKNG, a US equity with regular, pre_market, post_market, and over_night sessions, a nasdaq_symbol, and a corporate_actions stock split:
Every field is documented below.
Field reference
Field invariants
Useful guarantees when mapping these fields in your own systems:
- name is not guaranteed to be unique; the same short name can appear on more than one feed.
- symbol is unique, but in rare cases it can change without notice.
Usepyth_lazer_id as the stable key for external mappings.
- asset_type andinstrument_type are open enums whose set of values can grow over time, so handle unknown values gracefully.
Identity & naming
| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| pyth_lazer_id | u32 | Stable numeric identifier for the feed in Pyth Pro.
Use it when subscribing to prices.
|
| name | string | Short symbol name, e.g.
BTCUSD .
Dated futures suffix the family root with a month code and year digit, e.g.
theEM (E-mini S&P 500) family becomesEMU6 ; see Futures Terminology.
|
| symbol | string | Fully-qualified Pyth symbol, e.g.
Crypto.BTC/USD orEquity.US.EMU6/USD .
Encodes asset class, optional region, root, and quote currency.
|
| description | string | Human-readable description, e.g.
BITCOIN / US DOLLAR .
|
| hermes_id | string?
| Hex feed ID used by Pyth Core / Hermes for the same underlying.
null when the feed has no Pyth Core counterpart.
