How US Equities Actually Trade: Sessions, Gaps, and What Most Data Providers Miss
US equities trade across four sessions and 16+ venues.
Most price feeds cover one.
Here's how the market actually works and how Pyth prices all of it.
The stock market is not open from 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM.
That is one session out of four.
US equity trading activity spans a full 24-hour cycle, fragmented across different venues, participant bases, and liquidity regimes.
Any system consuming equity price data that only covers regular trading hours is blind to more than 16 hours of price discovery per day.
This is the first entry in Know Your Feed, a series breaking down how price data actually works across every major asset class.
Starting with the most complex: US equities.
Four Sessions, Four Different Markets
Unlike crypto, which trades 24/7 on a relatively unified set of venues, US equity trading is split into four distinct sessions within each 24-hour cycle.
Each session operates with different participants, different liquidity profiles, and often different price behavior.
Overnight (Sun-Thu, 8:00 PM to 4:00 AM ET) is currently dominated by Blue Ocean ATS, an SEC-registered Alternative Trading System.
This session opens the trading week on Sunday evening and handles over $1B in average nightly volume.
Pre-market (Mon-Fri, 4:00 AM to 9:30 AM ET) is driven by institutional flows and early reactions to overnight news.
Liquidity builds significantly after 8:00 AM when economic data releases begin.
Only limit orders are accepted.
Regular trading hours (Mon-Fri, 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM ET) is the primary session on NYSE and NASDAQ.
This is where the highest liquidity, tightest spreads, and full designated market maker participation occur.
LULD (Limit Up-Limit Down) circuit breakers are active during this window.
Post-market (Mon-Fri, 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM ET) sees heavier retail participation via broker platforms.
Earnings releases are commonly issued in this window, making it a high-volatility period with wider spreads than regular hours.
The implications for anyone consuming equity price data are significant.
A price feed that only covers regular hours will miss overnight reactions to geopolitical events, pre-market institutional positioning, and post-market earnings gaps.
For DeFi protocols using equity feeds for mark-to-market, funding rates, or liquidations, this gap in coverage is a structural risk.
The Single-Venue Problem
US equity trading is fragmented across 16 registered exchanges, numerous dark pools, and alternative trading systems.
The SIP (Securities Information Processor) consolidates quotes from all these venues into the NBBO, the best bid and offer available across the entire market.
Not all venues contribute equally to price discovery.
Some market data providers, especially those targeting crypto and DeFi use cases, source equity prices from a single low-volume venue attracted by simpler licensing terms.
The problem is significant: these venues handle a fraction of total US equity spot volume.
Spreads are meaningfully wider than on primary exchanges like NASDAQ and NYSE, where the majority of price discovery occurs.
A price from a single low-volume venue is that venue's price.
It is not "the stock price."
For any system using equity prices for collateral valuation, funding rate calculation, or liquidation triggers, the source venue matters.
A price that deviates from the primary exchange can trigger false liquidations or create arbitrage opportunities against the protocol's users.
The cheaper the licensing, the further the price may sit from where real volume trades.
Why Prices Gap Between Sessions
A price gap occurs when a stock opens at a significantly different price than the previous session's close.
Because each session has different liquidity profiles and participant bases, price information does not flow smoothly across boundaries.
These gaps are a structural feature of equity markets, not anomalies.
The most common catalysts include earnings releases (often announced in post-market), geopolitical or macro events (which can move prices sharply in overnight or pre-market sessions), analyst upgrades and downgrades (which set the tone before regular hours open), and the weekend itself.
The 64+ hour window between Friday at 8:00 PM and Sunday at 8:00 PM is the largest information accumulation period in the weekly cycle.
The overnight session on Sunday provides the first price signal after that void.
LULD circuit breaker halts also create intra-session gaps.
When a stock moves too fast during regular hours, trading is paused.
Upon resumption, price can jump in either direction.
For DeFi protocols, these gaps represent a distinct category of risk.
Lending protocols valuing equity collateral may face instant under-collateralization after an earnings gap.
Perpetual futures platforms need to handle session boundaries where the feed transitions from one data source to another.
Stop-loss logic that works in continuous crypto markets does not protect against the discontinuous pricing inherent in equities.
How Pyth Approaches Equity Data Differently
The Pyth Network's equity feeds are built on a fundamentally different architecture than most data providers in the crypto ecosystem.
Three design choices define the approach.
First-party institutional publishers.
Pyth's US equity feeds receive data from a curated subset of institutional data providers, including market makers, exchanges, and trading firms with direct market access across all sessions.
These are the institutions that participate in price discovery, not intermediaries repackaging someone else's data.
Primary-venue benchmarking.
Publisher accuracy is measured against the mid-point price at the primary market for each stock.
The 99th percentile deviation from this benchmark must remain within 20 basis points.
This ensures the aggregate price reflects where real, high-volume price discovery occurs, not where licensing is simplest.
Session-specific publisher curation.
Because different publishers participate in different sessions, Pyth maintains separate feed configurations for each trading window.
Each feed requires a minimum of five active publishers, selected based on price freshness (95%+ of prices delivered fresh within each trading day) and accuracy against the primary-venue benchmark.
24/5 Coverage Through Blue Ocean ATS
Through an exclusive data partnership, Pyth is the only blockchain-based oracle provider publishing overnight US equity trading data from Blue Ocean ATS.
This addresses the most significant gap in modern equity data infrastructure: the overnight session.
Blue Ocean ATS is an SEC-registered Alternative Trading System with FINRA oversight.
It covers US National Market System (NMS) stocks from Sunday through Thursday, 8:00 PM to 4:00 AM ET.
The pricing is executable and ATS-sourced, meaning it reflects actual trades on a regulated venue, not indicative quotes or AMM-derived estimates.
Other data providers either go dark during the overnight window or attempt to fill the gap with indicative pricing and modeled estimates.
Pyth publishes prices from actual trades on a regulated ATS.
That distinction matters for any system where pricing accuracy has financial consequences.
Combined with pre-market, regular, and post-market coverage, this gives Pyth the only true 24/5 US equity data feed available to DeFi and institutional consumers.
Pyth Pro: The Enterprise Layer
Pyth Pro delivers this multi-session equity data through standard APIs (WebSocket, REST, FIX) designed for institutional integration.
Key capabilities for equity consumers include on-demand pricing (subscribers pull prices when needed), customizable payloads with fields including price, bestBid, bestAsk, confidence, and marketSession, and cryptographic verification for onchain settlement across EVM, Solana, and other formats.

Extended-Hours US Equity Data Moves to Pyth Pro
Extended-hours US equity feeds (.PRE, .POST, .ON) move from Pyth Core to Pyth Pro on June 15th.
Here's what changes and how to migrate.
On June 15th 2026, Pyth Core will deprecate all extended-hours and session-based US equity feeds — pre-market (.PRE), post-market (.POST), and overnight (.ON).
The full list of affected tickers is in the developer forum post.
Applications relying on these feeds should transition to Pyth Pro before June 15th to maintain access.
This change applies to roughly 50 US equity tickers across all three session categories, including AAPL, TSLA, NVDA, COIN, MSTR, META, SPY, QQQ, and others.
Regular-session feeds for these tickers remain on Pyth Core through the broader Core upgrade on July 31st.
What to do
Applications using any of the affected .PRE, .POST, or .ON feeds need to:
- Sign up for Pyth Terminal at app.pyth.com
- Subscribe to a Pyth Pro plan that includes US equities — either the U.S.
Equities plan ($5,000 / month) or All Asset Classes ($10,000 / month)
- Generate an API key and update integrations to point to the new endpoint
The full session-feed catalog and updated symbol mappings are available on Pyth Terminal.
For chain or feed support questions, email data@dourolabs.xyz.
Why this is moving
Extended-hours and overnight equity data is some of the most premium data in the legacy market data economy.
Pre-market, post-market, and overnight pricing for US equities is tightly licensed, expensive to source, and historically reserved for institutional desks paying through dedicated vendor contracts.
Pyth is one of the only providers offering true 24/5 US equity pricing onchain at all.
That coverage exists because of the network's institutional publisher base — firms with direct access to extended-hours liquidity in venues like Blue Ocean ATS, where overnight US equity trading happens.
Aggregating that data and pricing it as a paid product brings Pyth in line with how the rest of the market data world treats this category.
This is consistent with the broader Pyth Core upgrade launching on July 31st: the most valuable feeds and the highest-quality data flow through Pyth Pro, with revenue accruing to the Pyth DAO.
What stays on Pyth Core
Regular trading session equity feeds remain available on Pyth Core through July 31st, when the broader Core upgrade takes effect.
After July 31st, all Pyth Core data access requires an active Starter or Pro plan through Pyth Terminal.
The publishers are the same.
The data quality is the same.
What changes is the commercial relationship — and which Pyth product carries which category of data.
Getting started
Sign up for a Pyth Pro plan at app.pyth.com.
Read the migration documentation.
On June 15th, Pyth Core will deprecate extended-hours and session-based US equity feeds — pre-market, post-market, and overnight pricing for roughly 50 tickers including AAPL, TSLA, NVDA, and SPY.
This data now moves to Pyth Pro, where it belongs alongside the rest of the market's premium pricing categories.

The shares were up almost 4% before the open but reversed sharply as investors faced life after Huang, as reported by Yahoo Finance.
Analysts cited in that report said new board chair Harvey Jones handled the messaging on the timeline for naming Huang's replacement poorly and lacked urgency.
Per CNBC, Jones said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate Huang, who had said before the results that he was open to returning.
CNBC added that the stock is down more than 13% over the past week.

Supporting Factors
Third-quarter revenue of $115.84 billion topped the $109.10 billion analysts expected, and the $130 billion fourth-quarter guide was above the $125.1 billion LSEG consensus, per CNBC.
Nvidia raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to 75% from 70% three months earlier, Yahoo Finance reported.
Interim CEO Colette Kress said of the company's customers, "They are all continuing to be with us," according to CNBC.
Nvidia held $98 billion in cash and marketable securities against about $39 billion in debt and lease liabilities at the end of the third quarter, Investing.com reported.
Risks
Moody's Ratings revised its outlook on Nvidia's credit to stable from positive on Wednesday, citing governance uncertainty after Huang's departure and the lack of a formal succession plan, according to Investing.com.
Fourth-quarter gross margin guidance of 71.0% to 72.0% sits below the third quarter's 74.8% GAAP gross margin, and the outlook assumes no data center compute revenue from China, per the company's release.
Huang is slated for closed-door interviews with three House committees on December 1, and a House committee has asked Kress for a briefing by December 2, CNBC reported.

Somehow, Nvidia keeps raising the bar.
The chip giant's stellar earnings for the third quarter have sparked a round of price-target raises from analysts who think the stock can climb even higher.
Nvidia, the most expensive company in the world by market cap, pulled $57.01 billion in revenue, up 62% year-over-year.

"Nvidia's earnings were another major validation moment for the AI Revolution and tech stocks.

Nvidia shares sell off as CEO Jensen Huang resigns
Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO as longtime chief executive Jensen Huang stepped down amid scrutiny of his personal conduct
Nvidia shares plunged further Thursday after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down, sending shockwaves through the artificial intelligence industry and pressuring stocks tied to the sector.
Huang's departure comes after reports that Nvidia's board was considering removing the longtime executive amid scrutiny of his personal conduct and alleged ties to a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent replacement, the company said Thursday, according to Reuters.
The chipmaker also named former Synopsys CEO and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever board chairman.
Huang will leave Nvidia's board as well.
Nvidia shares fell more than 7% in Thursday morning trading after dropping more than 10% in premarket trading following the announcement.

The selloff extended across several AI-related companies and weighed on the broader U.S.
stock market, highlighting concerns about the impact of Huang's departure on one of the world's most influential chipmakers.
The Nasdaq, S&P 500 and Dow opened lower on Thursday.
The selling extended to several companies tied to the AI industry.
Intel, Marvell Technology and Micron Technology fell between 2.7% and 3.5% in premarket trading, while AI infrastructure company CoreWeave dropped approximately 7%.
Meanwhile, Nvidia rivals Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom moved in the opposite direction, gaining 2.3% and 1.4%, respectively.
The leadership shake-up followed a Wall Street Journal report that Nvidia's board met Wednesday to consider removing Huang.
The reported deliberations came amid scrutiny of two extramarital affairs involving the longtime executive, including one with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
The chipmaker announced Sunday that it had launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, is overseeing the review.
In its statement, Nvidia said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised and expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.
DEMOCRATIC SENATORS DEMAND NVIDIA RECORDS FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OVER ALLEGED CHINESE SPY TIES
Huang's exit raises questions about leadership continuity at Nvidia, a company valued at approximately $4 trillion whose processors are central to the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The departure also comes as investors scrutinize the enormous spending commitments fueling the AI boom, with concerns mounting over whether technology companies will generate sufficient returns on their investments.
Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as its chief executive throughout the company's rise to become a dominant supplier of AI processors.
He is also the company's fourth-largest investor, holding a stake of approximately 3.61%, according to Reuters.
The leadership shake-up also comes at a closely watched moment for Nvidia's business, with investors preparing to assess demand for its AI chips and data center products in the company's upcoming quarterly results.

What is Ethereum?
Ethereum is the second-largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, currently valued at around $233 billion.
It’s well behind Bitcoin’s roughly $1.33 trillion market cap—but far ahead of the third largest option, Tether, at $183 billion.
Here’s a stark difference between Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies: It’s not just digital money.
It’s actually a decentralized computing platform, meaning users can build and run apps on it without the oversight of any company or bank.
In short, developers build apps on Ethereum’s blockchain network (instead of, say, Amazon or Google servers), to do things like borrow, lend, invest, trade, etc.
The token ETH is the currency you’ll spend to do those sorts of things.
Ethereum price history
Ethereum’s initial coin offering (ICO) launched in 2014 for just 31 cents per share.
Since then, its value has increased by more than 60,000%.
Over the past five years (2020-2025), Ethereum has risen by a still respectable 46%.
But that’s not the whole story.
Ethereum has been subject to serious volatility, reaching nearly $5,000 at its peak in August 2025.
That’s nearly 1.6 million percent in growth from its original ICO.
Kind of makes that previous 60,000% increase a little less impressive.
ETH has since seen gains of more than 80%, drops of more than 60%, and essentially every wild swing in between.
Early 2026 saw a sharp decline in Ethereum value for a few reasons, from recession worries to Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin selling many millions of dollars worth of ETH.
The takeaway is that Ethereum can deliver massive gains and massive losses—about on par with what you’d expect from other major cryptocurrencies.
Ethereum vs.
Bitcoin
After Bitcoin, Ethereum is a distant second in the rankings for largest cryptocurrency.
But again, Ethereum wasn’t initially created to be primarily a currency; a decentralized computing platform was the main impetus for its conception.
There are a variety of real-world uses for Ethereum—and its developer community is enormous.
Investors like that because it has the potential to grow beyond a simple “alternative currency.”
Here’s an easy way to think about the difference between these two currencies:
- Bitcoin is often thought of like “digital gold.” It’s strictly a currency.
- Ethereum might be thought of like “digital oil.” It powers decentralized apps and contracts.
What is Ethereum staking?
Staking is another feature that sets Ethereum apart from Bitcoin.
Until 2022, Ethereum’s network was secured by thousands of computers racing to solve random puzzles (called “proof of work”).
When your computer solves a puzzle, you’ll receive some ETH as a reward.
Sounds odd (and it was), but it was effective in keeping an honest account ledger.
Because this process burned a lot of electricity and didn’t make a ton of sense, anyway, Ethereum decided to ditch it in favor of an activity called “staking.” Staking is when you lock up your ETH as a security deposit to help validate transactions.
Doing this will earn you a reward similar to the return for proof of work.
You’re effectively earning interest for your stake.
What affects Ethereum’s price?
Many factors affect the price of Ethereum, including:
- Investor speculation: Like most crypto, Ethereum’s short-term price is heavily driven by trader sentiment and hype.
Speculative trading tends to dictate price movements more than anything else in the near term.
- Network usage and decentralized finance adoption: When more people use Ethereum’s network, demand for ETH goes up.
The decentralized finance (DeFi) boom of 2020–2021 was a great example of this.
- Economic health: Crypto isn’t as sensitive to interest rates as stocks, but the health of the economy still matters.
When people have money to invest, they’re more willing to explore alternative assets like Ethereum.
- Regulations: Because crypto is still somewhat new, regulations are still evolving and major regulatory decisions can either scare or assuage investors.
- Competition from other blockchains: Ethereum isn’t the only “smart contract” platform anymore.
Competitors like Solana and Avalanche offer, in some cases, faster and cheaper transactions.
Depending on how Ethereum pivots will dictate its value in the long-term.
How to buy and invest in Ethereum
There are many ways to invest in Ethereum with varying degrees of risk.
Below are some of the most popular options.
Buy Ethereum on a crypto exchange
Directly purchasing ETH is the most hands-on investment method.
Open an account with a cryptocurrency exchange and link your bank account to buy and hold the ETH in a digital wallet.
Invest in Ethereum ETFs
If you’d rather not manage crypto directly, including dealing with wallets and private keys, an Ethereum ETF might be a better fit.
These funds effectively hold the crypto on your behalf while their shares trade on stock exchanges like a regular stock.
Buy Ethereum-related stocks
Investing in publicly traded companies that are closely tied to Ethereum is a way to bet on ETH without owning it.
This could include blockchain tech companies, firms that hold a significant amount of ETH on their balance sheets, etc.
This lets you benefit from its performance by proxy.
Open a crypto IRA that holds Ethereum
A crypto IRA lets you hold Ethereum in a tax-advantaged retirement account.
It works like a traditional or Roth IRA—with the same contribution limits and tax benefits.

Ethereum is one of the most ubiquitous cryptocurrencies, but it’s far from the only option.
Consider the following options when deciding where to place your money.
- Bitcoin: Bitcoin is the original cryptocurrency and remains the most popular crypto coin on the market.
Again, it’s a decentralized digital currency that is designed primarily to be a store of value and a peer-to-peer payment system.
- Tether: Tether is a stablecoin, meaning its value is tied to another asset.
In this case, its value is linked to the U.S.
dollar.
This makes Tether generally less volatile than Ethereum—but it also lacks Ethereum’s growth potential.
- XRP: XRP is a cryptocurrency specifically designed to move funds from one country to another quickly and with low fees.
Is it a good time to invest in Ethereum?
Ethereum is still relatively young compared with tried-and-true blue chip stocks like Exxon Mobil, Johnson & Johnson, or IBM.
Of course, there’s no way to truly know ETH will perform in the years and decades to come.
But it’s been one of the best-performing assets of the last decade, and its utility can go far beyond just being a coin you trade.
It’s the backbone of a growing ecosystem of financial applications and developer tools, after all.
Just keep in mind Ethereum’s history of brutal downturns and be prepared to weather the storms.
It’s not for those who spook easily.
Also keep an eye on competing blockchain networks.
Avoid going all-in on ETH, and instead smartly treat it as a minority asset in your diversified portfolio.

TL;DR: US spot Ether ETFs saw approximately $139.7 million in net outflows on November 2, Farside Investors’ daily data show.
The amounts are published for specific trading dates and can be adjusted by data providers.
On November 2, BlackRock’s ETHA was responsible for roughly $138.3 million of the reported net withdrawal.
That clustering suggests the fund-level series deserves careful reading.
Investors can track one issuer and the whole category without treating the two as interchangeable, particularly when other funds show smaller and sometimes opposite daily movements.
US spot Ether ETFs saw approximately $139.7 million in net outflows on November 2, Farside Investors’ daily data show.
The previous listed sessions were also negative, with approximately $155.7 million leaving on October 30 and $105.5 million on October 29.
The sequence offers a more informative starting point than any single day, although the scale of redemptions varies from session to session.
The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.
ETH ETF flows are subscriptions and withdrawals through an investment wrapper, not a direct count of ETH sold by everyone in the ecosystem.
Exchange traders, staking participants, derivatives desks and users of Ethereum applications have different motives and do not all appear in the same table.
ETF holdings reflect a familiar securities-market channel that may lag or diverge from blockchain activity.
A series of negative sessions can change how investors talk about Ethereum exposure, especially when a large issuer accounts for most of a particular day’s redemptions.
But a falling ETF share count and weaker network fundamentals are not synonymous.
Analysts should compare flows with changes in broader risk appetite, fund allocations and the health of Ethereum-based services rather than assume one metric explains the others.
Ethereum has multiple sources of demand and risk: trading, staking, stablecoin settlement, application fees and long-term treasury allocation.
A change in one part of that system should be tested against the others instead of promoted into a universal explanation.
The market often overreacts when one publicly available metric is mistaken for the whole network economy.
For additional perspective, it is worth reading our existing reporting on an earlier Ethereum ETF outflow comparison and the October Bitcoin and Ether ETF weekly review.
Those background reports help separate established facts from a new, still-developing announcement.
The amounts are published for specific trading dates and can be adjusted by data providers.
They do not tell us who redeemed, whether positions were hedged or whether the cash moved to Bitcoin, other funds or unrelated assets.
Nor does this table establish that protocol staking withdrawals caused the ETF activity; those are different processes with distinct timing and constraints.
For investors, the right comparison is between liquidity, expected holding period and obligations.
Staked ETH, ETF shares and treasury holdings may all track the same underlying asset, but their exit routes and operating constraints differ.
A useful report therefore asks not simply how much ETH is involved, but how readily the exposure can be changed when conditions deteriorate.
The next useful evidence is the issuer breakdown over several additional sessions, alongside spot-market depth and whether redemption pressure broadens.
A return to sustained net creations would change the recent trend, but an isolated inflow would not erase the larger pattern.
Investors should keep ETF demand separate from claims about Ethereum’s throughput, staking or rollup adoption.

Symbology & Reference Data
Field-by-field reference for Pyth Pro symbol metadata: identifiers, classification, data quality, trading schedules, and futures expiration
Pyth Pro publishes reference data describing every feed it offers: identifiers, classification, data-quality parameters, trading schedules, and (for derivatives) expiration metadata.
This data is distinct from the real-time price payload: it describes what a feed is, not its current value.
Reference data is served by the Symbology & Reference Data API:
The endpoint returns one JSON object per feed.
This page documents every field on that object.
For the request schema and query parameters for filtering (for example by asset_type or instrument_type), see the interactive API reference.
Example response
Every feed is returned as a single JSON object with the same top-level shape.
The tabs below show feeds that populate different optional fields, depending on asset class and instrument type.
BKNG, a US equity with regular, pre_market, post_market, and over_night sessions, a nasdaq_symbol, and a corporate_actions stock split:
Every field is documented below.
Field reference
Field invariants
Useful guarantees when mapping these fields in your own systems:
- name is not guaranteed to be unique; the same short name can appear on more than one feed.
- symbol is unique, but in rare cases it can change without notice.
Usepyth_lazer_id as the stable key for external mappings.
- asset_type andinstrument_type are open enums whose set of values can grow over time, so handle unknown values gracefully.
Identity & naming
| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| pyth_lazer_id | u32 | Stable numeric identifier for the feed in Pyth Pro.
Use it when subscribing to prices.
|
| name | string | Short symbol name, e.g.
BTCUSD .
Dated futures suffix the family root with a month code and year digit, e.g.
theEM (E-mini S&P 500) family becomesEMU6 ; see Futures Terminology.
|
| symbol | string | Fully-qualified Pyth symbol, e.g.
Crypto.BTC/USD orEquity.US.EMU6/USD .
Encodes asset class, optional region, root, and quote currency.
|
| description | string | Human-readable description, e.g.
BITCOIN / US DOLLAR .
|
| hermes_id | string?
| Hex feed ID used by Pyth Core / Hermes for the same underlying.
null when the feed has no Pyth Core counterpart.
|
| nasdaq_symbol | string?
| Nasdaq ticker, for equities sourced via Nasdaq.
null when not applicable.
|
| cmc_id | integer?
| CoinMarketCap ID, for crypto assets.
null when not applicable.
|
Classification
| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| asset_type | string | Broad asset class (open enum, may grow).
The table after this one lists the values.
|
| instrument_type | string | Instrument form: spot ,future ,perp ,rate ,index , ornav .
May be an empty string when unspecified.
|
| quote_currency | string | Currency the price is quoted in, e.g.
USD ,EUR ,KRW ,JPY .
|
| groups | string[] | Discovery/grouping tags, e.g.
pyth-indices .
Empty for most feeds.
|
| exchange_id | u32?
| Numeric ID of the primary exchange the feed trades on.
null when the feed has no exchange.
|
The asset_type values:
| asset_type | Covers |
|---|---|
| crypto | Real-time prices for cryptocurrencies and digital assets |
| crypto-redemption-rate | Real-time swap rates derived from smart contracts for the redemption of liquid staking and liquid restaking tokens (LSTs and LRTs), liquidity provider tokens (LP Tokens) and interest-bearing assets, including tokenised notes |
| crypto-index | Real-time prices that measure the performance of baskets of cryptocurrencies and digital assets |
| equity | Real-time prices for equities, ETFs and equity futures, including US and Hong Kong listings |
| fx | Real-time prices for fiat currency pairs |
| metal | Real-time prices for precious and base metals |
| commodity | Real-time prices for commodity futures, such as energy and agricultural contracts, and indices built on them |
| interest-rate | Benchmark interest rates such as SOFR, and US Treasury prices and yields |
| rates | Benchmark interest rates such as SOFR and EFFR, under the Rates.
symbol prefix |
| funding-rate | Funding rates of perpetual futures on exchanges such as Binance and Deribit |
| nav | Net asset values (NAVs) of tokenized funds |
Pricing & data quality
| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| exponent | i16 | Decimal exponent: actual_price = mantissa × 10^exponent .
Same meaning as in the price payload.
|
| min_publishers | u16 | Minimum number of publishers required for the feed to produce a price.
|
| min_channel | string | Highest-frequency channel the feed supports: real_time ,fixed_rate@50ms , orfixed_rate@200ms .
You can subscribe at this channel or any slower one.
|
| state | string | Lifecycle state: stable (live),coming_soon (announced, not yet publishing), orinactive (retired/expired).
|
| interval | string?
| Funding interval for funding-rate feeds (instrument type rate ), e.g.8h .null otherwise.
|
Scheduling
| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| schedule | string | The regular session's trading schedule, in the form TZ;<weekly>;<holidays> .
Each day is open (O ), closed (C ), or a set of hour ranges (e.g.0000-1700&1800-2400 ).
Identical tomarket_session_schedule.regular .
|
| market_session_schedule | object | A schedule string per session, keyed by session name ( regular ,pre_market ,post_market ,over_night ).
|
| market_sessions | object | The full per-session configuration: each session carries its own schedule ,min_pub , andstate .
|
Three schedule fields, three altitudes
These describe the same trading calendar at increasing detail:
- schedule : the regular session's schedule (identical tomarket_session_schedule.regular ), not a union across sessions.
- market_session_schedule : a schedule string for each session the feed has (regular ,pre_market ,post_market ,over_night ).
- market_sessions : the richest form, carrying per-sessionschedule plusmin_pub andstate .
The price payload's marketSession field tells you which of these sessions is currently active for a given update.
Pick an example or paste a schedule string to decode it into market hours:
America/New_York
| Monday | Open 24h |
|---|---|
| Tuesday | Open 24h |
| Wednesday | Open 24h |
| Thursday | Open 24h |
| Friday | Open 24h |
| Saturday | Open 24h |
| Sunday | Open 24h |
Futures
expiration_time describes an individual dated feed.
The other three fields describe the chain that feed belongs to — the family of feeds measuring the same underlying at different expirations — and carry the same values on every feed in the chain.
| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| expiration_time | string?
| Expiration timestamp (RFC 3339) for a dated futures feed, e.g.
2026-12-15T13:30:00-05:00 .
|
| symbol_chain_id | string?
| Root symbol for the chain of all the futures that measure the same underlying with different expiration times, e.g.
CA for the cocoa chain thatCAZ6 belongs to.
Note this is the bare root, not a fully-qualifiedsymbol .null for feeds that are not part of a futures chain.
|
| expiration_pattern | string[]?
| The total set of expirations per a single year applicable to the chain, as lowercase three-letter month abbreviations, e.g.
["mar", "may", "jul", "sep", "dec"] .
|
| availability_pattern | string[]?
| The subset of expirations per single year already priced or expected to be priced by Pyth, as month codes, e.g.
["H", "K", "N", "U", "Z"] .
|
The two patterns use different encodings
expiration_pattern lists month abbreviations (mar), availability_pattern lists month codes (H).
Normalize before comparing them.
The two often differ in length as well as encoding: copper (CC) expires in all twelve months but Pyth prices only ["H", "K", "N", "U", "Z"].
Chains with no fixed annual cycle — such as the LME 3-month feeds (Metal.AL3M/USD) — report ["none"] for both.
Corporate actions
| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| corporate_actions | object[]?
| Corporate actions o

The NVIDIA CORP / US DOLLAR (Equity.US.NVDA/USD) price feed delivers a live NVDA price, updated in real time on Pyth Network.
Prices are aggregated from first-party publishers - exchanges, market makers and trading firms pricing from their own order flow - with a confidence interval on every update.
Available on 100+ blockchains.
US equities do not trade continuously.
Each weekday cycle is split into four sessions with different venues, participants and liquidity: overnight (8:00 PM-4:00 AM ET, Sunday-Thursday, on alternative trading systems such as Blue Ocean ATS), pre-market (4:00-9:30 AM ET), regular hours (9:30 AM-4:00 PM ET, with opening and closing auctions on the primary listing exchange and LULD circuit breakers active) and post-market (4:00-8:00 PM ET, typically with wider spreads, and the window in which many companies release earnings).
From Friday 8:00 PM to Sunday 8:00 PM ET no session runs, a 48-hour gap.
Within the regular session, trading is fragmented across many registered exchanges, dark pools and alternative trading systems, with the SIP consolidating exchange quotes into the NBBO.
Each stock has a primary listing venue, usually NYSE or NASDAQ, which runs its opening and closing auctions.
Pyth US equity prices are contributed directly by first-party institutions that make markets, run venues or route order flow in the stock.
Every update carries a price and a confidence interval, and consumers pull the latest price on demand instead of waiting for a scheduled push.
Publisher prices are benchmarked against the mid-point at the stock's primary listing venue.
On Pyth Pro, supported tickers are priced across all four sessions, and every update carries a marketSession field so risk logic can be session-aware.
Unlike crypto, which trades 24/7, US equity trading activity is fragmented across multiple venues and four distinct trading sessions within each 24-hour cycle.
Each session may have different participants, liquidity profiles and venues, which directly impacts how prices are formed and how much they can move.
| Tier | Participants | Role in price formation |
|---|---|---|
| Primary listing exchanges (NYSE, NASDAQ) | Designated or registered market makers, institutional and retail flow during regular hours | Run each stock's opening and closing auctions; the reference venue for Pyth's publisher benchmark |
| Other registered exchanges (including Cboe, IEX and MEMX) | Broker-dealers, market makers | Contribute quotes to the NBBO; share of volume varies by venue and by stock |
| Dark pools and alternative trading systems (ATS) | Institutional block flow; overnight venues | Off-exchange matching; the overnight session (8:00 PM-4:00 AM ET, Sunday-Thursday) trades on alternative trading systems |
| SIP (Securities Information Processor) | Quotes from all registered exchanges | Consolidates exchange quotes into the NBBO, the best bid and offer across registered exchanges |
Venues do not contribute equally to price discovery.
A price taken from one venue reflects that venue's quotes and liquidity, not the market as a whole.
| Session/Window | Time (ET) | Character |
|---|---|---|
A price gap occurs when a stock opens at a significantly different price from its previous session's close.
Because each of the four sessions has a different liquidity profile and participant base, price information does not flow smoothly across boundaries.
The resulting gaps are a structural feature of equity markets, not anomalies.
| Factor | Impact |
|---|---|
| Earnings | Often released after the 4:00 PM ET close, so the initial move forms in the post-market session on thinner liquidity |
| Company, sector and macro news | Contract awards, guidance changes, regulatory decisions and macro data can move a stock sharply in the overnight or pre-market sessions |
| Analyst upgrades/downgrades | Rating changes and large disclosed positions can trigger multi-day volatility.
Pre-market reactions can set the tone before RTH |
| Weekend / holiday gaps | The 48-hour weekend void (Friday 8:00 PM-Sunday 8:00 PM ET) is the longest scheduled closure of a normal week.
The overnight session from the Sunday open provides the first price signal |
| LULD halts | Limit Up-Limit Down circuit breakers pause trading during RTH when price moves too fast.
On resumption, price can gap up or down |
| Corporate actions | Stock splits, reverse splits and delistings create planned price discontinuities.
A 4:1 split drops the price 75% overnight: not a market move, but a structural repricing that must be handled explicitly |
Worked example.
A company reports quarterly results after the 4:00 PM ET close.
The first prices reacting to the print form in the post-market session, on thinner liquidity and wider spreads, and the next regular-session open is a gap against the prior 4:00 PM close rather than a continuation of it.
If the move is large enough to trip an LULD band after the open, trading pauses: no trades, no feed updates, and a discontinuous price on resumption.
Neither event is an anomaly; both are the normal mechanics of a four-session market.
Liquidity in US equities is not a single number.
It is typically deepest in the regular session, when market makers quote across every exchange and the SIP consolidates exchange quotes, and it thins outside it.
The windows where liquidity disappears or degrades are:
| Event | What happens |
|---|---|
| LULD halt | Trading pauses during regular hours when price breaches its band.
No trades and no feed updates while halted; price free to gap on resumption |
| After-hours earnings | The initial move forms in the post-market session, on thinner liquidity and wider spreads, before the next regular open |
| Stock split | A planned discontinuity.
Publishers apply the split ratio before the ex-date session opens, under the workflow in the Asset-Specific Handling section |
| Weekend void, every week | 48 hours (Friday 8:00 PM-Sunday 8:00 PM ET) with no session.
Positions held through the weekend carry gap risk across the longest closure of the week |
Pyth US equity feeds aggregate first-party contributions from institutions that make prices in this market: firms with direct market access, their own pricing engines and the ability to distribute their own data, including exchanges and trading venues, banks, non-bank market makers and trading firms.
Pyth does not enumerate individual publishers per feed.
The publisher set for US equities draws on four types of contributor:
Publishers are selected per session on two criteria: price freshness through the trading day, and accuracy against the primary-market benchmark described in the What Makes Pyth Data Different section.
Publisher accuracy is benchmarked against the mid-point price at each stock's primary listing venue, and publishers are held to a deviation limit against that benchmark.
This anchors the aggregate to the venue that runs each stock's opening and closing auctions.
| Traditional US equities data | Pyth Network |
|---|---|
| Redistributed venue feeds, per-terminal licensed | First-party contributions from the institutions that own the data |
| A single price with no uncertainty measure | Price plus confidence interval with every update |
The Pyth price for a US equity feed is an indicative reference price derived from an aggregate of publisher submissions.
It is venue-agnostic: it does not represent the price available on any particular exchange or trading system, and it is not an offer to buy or sell the security.
Always verify price freshness before use with getPriceNoOlderThan() and a threshold appropriate to this feed's schedule.
A threshold that is correct during the trading session will reject every price while the underlying market is closed; threshold logic must be schedule-aware, not a single global constant.
For US equities, thresholds are session-specific as well as schedule-specific:
getPriceNoOlderThan() with strict thresholds appropriate for the session.

polymarket-7210452.text:
Research
·
How US Equities Actually Trade: Sessions, Gaps, and What Most Data Providers Miss
US equities trade across four sessions and 16+ venues.
Most price feeds cover one.
Here's how the market actually works and how Pyth prices all of it.
The stock market is not open from 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM.
That is one session out of four.
US equity trading activity spans a full 24-hour cycle, fragmented across different venues, participant bases, and liquidity regimes.
Any system consuming equity price data that only covers regular trading hours is blind to more than 16 hours of price discovery per day.
This is the first entry in Know Your Feed, a series breaking down how price data actually works across every major asset class.
Starting with the most complex: US equities.
Four Sessions, Four Different Markets
Unlike crypto, which trades 24/7 on a relatively unified set of venues, US equity trading is split into four distinct sessions within each 24-hour cycle.
Each session operates with different participants, different liquidity profiles, and often different price behavior.
Overnight (Sun-Thu, 8:00 PM to 4:00 AM ET) is currently dominated by Blue Ocean ATS, an SEC-registered Alternative Trading System.
This session opens the trading week on Sunday evening and handles over $1B in average nightly volume.
Pre-market (Mon-Fri, 4:00 AM to 9:30 AM ET) is driven by institutional flows and early reactions to overnight news.
Liquidity builds significantly after 8:00 AM when economic data releases begin.
Only limit orders are accepted.
Regular trading hours (Mon-Fri, 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM ET) is the primary session on NYSE and NASDAQ.
This is where the highest liquidity, tightest spreads, and full designated market maker participation occur.
LULD (Limit Up-Limit Down) circuit breakers are active during this window.
Post-market (Mon-Fri, 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM ET) sees heavier retail participation via broker platforms.
Earnings releases are commonly issued in this window, making it a high-volatility period with wider spreads than regular hours.
The implications for anyone consuming equity price data are significant.
A price feed that only covers regular hours will miss overnight reactions to geopolitical events, pre-market institutional positioning, and post-market earnings gaps.
For DeFi protocols using equity feeds for mark-to-market, funding rates, or liquidations, this gap in coverage is a structural risk.
The Single-Venue Problem
US equity trading is fragmented across 16 registered exchanges, numerous dark pools, and alternative trading systems.
The SIP (Securities Information Processor) consolidates quotes from all these venues into the NBBO, the best bid and offer available across the entire market.
Not all venues contribute equally to price discovery.
Some market data providers, especially those targeting crypto and DeFi use cases, source equity prices from a single low-volume venue attracted by simpler licensing terms.
The problem is significant: these venues handle a fraction of total US equity spot volume.
Spreads are meaningfully wider than on primary exchanges like NASDAQ and NYSE, where the majority of price discovery occurs.
A price from a single low-volume venue is that venue's price.
It is not "the stock price."
For any system using equity prices for collateral valuation, funding rate calculation, or liquidation triggers, the source venue matters.
A price that deviates from the primary exchange can trigger false liquidations or create arbitrage opportunities against the protocol's users.
The cheaper the licensing, the further the price may sit from where real volume trades.
Why Prices Gap Between Sessions
A price gap occurs when a stock opens at a significantly different price than the previous session's close.
Because each session has different liquidity profiles and participant bases, price information does not flow smoothly across boundaries.
These gaps are a structural feature of equity markets, not anomalies.
The most common catalysts include earnings releases (often announced in post-market), geopolitical or macro events (which can move prices sharply in overnight or pre-market sessions), analyst upgrades and downgrades (which set the tone before regular hours open), and the weekend itself.
The 64+ hour window between Friday at 8:00 PM and Sunday at 8:00 PM is the largest information accumulation period in the weekly cycle.
The overnight session on Sunday provides the first price signal after that void.
LULD circuit breaker halts also create intra-session gaps.
When a stock moves too fast during regular hours, trading is paused.
Upon resumption, price can jump in either direction.
For DeFi protocols, these gaps represent a distinct category of risk.
Lending protocols valuing equity collateral may face instant under-collateralization after an earnings gap.
Perpetual futures platforms need to handle session boundaries where the feed transitions from one data source to another.
Stop-loss logic that works in continuous crypto markets does not protect against the discontinuous pricing inherent in equities.
How Pyth Approaches Equity Data Differently
The Pyth Network's equity feeds are built on a fundamentally different architecture than most data providers in the crypto ecosystem.
Three design choices define the approach.
First-party institutional publishers.
Pyth's US equity feeds receive data from a curated subset of institutional data providers, including market makers, exchanges, and trading firms with direct market access across all sessions.
These are the institutions that participate in price discovery, not intermediaries repackaging someone else's data.
Primary-venue benchmarking.
Publisher accuracy is measured against the mid-point price at the primary market for each stock.
The 99th percentile deviation from this benchmark must remain within 20 basis points.
This ensures the aggregate price reflects where real, high-volume price discovery occurs, not where licensing is simplest.
Session-specific publisher curation.
Because different publishers participate in different sessions, Pyth maintains separate feed configurations for each trading window.
Each feed requires a minimum of five active publishers, selected based on price freshness (95%+ of prices delivered fresh within each trading day) and accuracy against the primary-venue benchmark.
24/5 Coverage Through Blue Ocean ATS
Through an exclusive data partnership, Pyth is the only blockchain-based oracle provider publishing overnight US equity trading data from Blue Ocean ATS.
This addresses the most significant gap in modern equity data infrastructure: the overnight session.
Blue Ocean ATS is an SEC-registered Alternative Trading System with FINRA oversight.
It covers US National Market System (NMS) stocks from Sunday through Thursday, 8:00 PM to 4:00 AM ET.
The pricing is executable and ATS-sourced, meaning it reflects actual trades on a regulated venue, not indicative quotes or AMM-derived estimates.
Other data providers either go dark during the overnight window or attempt to fill the gap with indicative pricing and modeled estimates.
Pyth publishes prices from actual trades on a regulated ATS.
That distinction matters for any system where pricing accuracy has financial consequences.
Combined with pre-market, regular, and post-market coverage, this gives Pyth the only true 24/5 US equity data feed available to DeFi and institutional consumers.
Pyth Pro: The Enterprise Layer
Pyth Pro delivers this multi-session equity data through standard APIs (WebSocket, REST, FIX) designed for institutional integration.
Key capabilities for equity consumers include on-demand pricing (subscribers pull prices when needed), customizable payloads with fields including price, bestBid, bestAsk, confidence, and marketSession, and cryptographic verification for onchain settlement across EVM, Solana, and other formats.
The marketSession field is particularly important for equity consumers.

Supporting Factors
Revenue of $115.8 billion and data center revenue of $107.6 billion both grew more than 100% from a year earlier, according to the company's release.

Kress is interim CEO while the board searches for a new chief executive and an independent board committee investigation continues, the release noted.
The Guardian, citing The Wall Street Journal, reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia's business in China.
New US chip rules issued on Monday, November 16, bar advanced US chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely, according to TechCrunch, which reported a Jefferies estimate that they could cut $44 billion to $62 billion from Nvidia's data center revenue next year.
Kress said the demand backlog means no impact on top-line revenue, a company view.
The release guided fourth-quarter gross margin to 71.0% to 72.0%, below the third quarter's 74.8% GAAP gross margin.

Gotrade News - In the latest Nvidia stock news, shares of Nvidia (NVDA) closed at $150.96 on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, down $4.50 or 2.89%.
Nvidia stock gave up an early gain after its third-quarter report, as financial media tied the reversal to investor unease over who will lead the company after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12.

Volume reached 349.8 million shares, 83.31% above the average of 190.8 million.
The drop came on a split day for the broader market.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.42% to 24,429.88, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.23% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.32%, leaving Nvidia 3.31 percentage points behind the Nasdaq.
The 10-year Treasury yield eased 3.0 basis points to 5.07%.
Other AI names split.
AMD (AMD) gained 5.31% and Broadcom (AVGO) rose 3.64%, while CoreWeave (CRWV), one of the neocloud operators CNBC said Nvidia dragged lower, fell 4.13%.
Nvidia now sits 37.97% below its 52-week high of $243.37 and only 1.45% above its 52-week low of $148.80.
Financial media tied the drop to concerns over Nvidia's CEO succession, which outweighed quarterly results that beat analyst expectations.
Wednesday was the first session after the earnings report.
According to Nvidia's third-quarter fiscal 2027 release, revenue reached $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, and data center revenue rose 110% to $107.6 billion.
The company released the figures after the market close on Tuesday, November 17 and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%.
The shares were up almost 4% before the open but reversed sharply as investors faced life after Huang, as reported by Yahoo Finance.
Analysts cited in that report said new board chair Harvey Jones handled the messaging on the timeline for naming Huang's replacement poorly and lacked urgency.
Per CNBC, Jones said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate Huang, who had said before the results that he was open to returning.
CNBC added that the stock is down more than 13% over the past week.
NVDA Stock Analysis: Supporting Factors and Risks
Supporting Factors
Third-quarter revenue of $115.84 billion topped the $109.10 billion analysts expected, and the $130 billion fourth-quarter guide was above the $125.1 billion LSEG consensus, per CNBC.
Nvidia raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to 75% from 70% three months earlier, Yahoo Finance reported.
Interim CEO Colette Kress said of the company's customers, "They are all continuing to be with us," according to CNBC.
Nvidia held $98 billion in cash and marketable securities against about $39 billion in debt and lease liabilities at the end of the third quarter, Investing.com reported.
Risks
Moody's Ratings revised its outlook on Nvidia's credit to stable from positive on Wednesday, citing governance uncertainty after Huang's departure and the lack of a formal succession plan, according to Investing.com.
Fourth-quarter gross margin guidance of 71.0% to 72.0% sits below the third quarter's 74.8% GAAP gross margin, and the outlook assumes no data center compute revenue from China, per the company's release.
Huang is slated for closed-door interviews with three House committees on December 1, and a House committee has asked Kress for a briefing by December 2, CNBC reported.

- Revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago
- Data Center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year ago
- Vera Rubin NVL72, the most versatile and advanced computing platform ever built, has shipped
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.
17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today reported revenue for the third quarter ended October 25, 2026, of $115.8 billion, up 20% from the previous quarter and up 103% from a year ago.
For the quarter, GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were 74.8% and 74.9%, respectively.
GAAP and non-GAAP earnings per diluted share were $2.70 and $2.68, respectively.
“Our momentum is real.
NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA.
“Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”
In September 2026, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors approved an increase of $150 billion to the company’s share repurchase authorization, without expiration.
During the third quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the form of shares repurchased and cash dividends.
As of the end of the third quarter, the company had approximately $227.3 billion remaining under its share repurchase authorization.
NVIDIA will pay its next quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share on December 23, 2026, to all shareholders of record on December 2, 2026.

Outlook
NVIDIA’s outlook for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which includes an additional week, is as follows:
- Revenue is expected to be $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%.
NVIDIA is not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in its outlook.
- GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins are expected to be between 71.0% and 72.0%.
- GAAP and non-GAAP operating expenses are expected to be approximately $11.0 billion and $10.7 billion, respectively.
- For the full year fiscal 2027, NVIDIA expects GAAP and non-GAAP tax rates to be between 16.0% and 18.0%, excluding any discrete items and material changes to NVIDIA’s tax environment.
Highlights
Data Center
- Third-quarter revenue was $107.6 billion, up 21% from the previous quarter and up 110% from a year ago.
- Ramped production and began shipping NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 — the fastest product ramp in the company’s history — with racks running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Nebius, and coming online soon at SpaceXSI.
- Expanded the Vera Rubin cloud ecosystem, announcing general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, general availability of Google Cloud’s Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances and the continued buildout of SpaceXSI’s infrastructure.
- Announced Vera Rubin open architecture advances to help the industry scale faster, and revealed that Cisco, Google, Meta, Microsoft and Visionbay are joining many technology leaders advancing infrastructure for Vera Rubin.
- Revealed that leading AI natives, cloud providers and neoclouds, including CoreWeave, Meta, Nebius, Nscale, OpenAI and Verda, are building with NVIDIA Vera CPUs to support the growing computing needs of businesses and developers, joining AWS, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and SpaceXSI.
- Expanded Anthropic’s access to NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers, and continued to collaborate on design and engineering to optimize future NVIDIA architectures for Anthropic’s workloads.
- Announced the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform for high-performance computing — combining NVIDIA’s first fully custom data center CPU with the gold standard for HPC networking to drive extreme efficiency and throughput for scientific modeling, simulation and agentic science.
- Introduced NVIDIA Rubin HPC, a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.
- Expanded collaboration with Meta on AI agent Muse and its family of models, with Meta planning expanded deployment of Vera Rubin, Vera CPUs, NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ networking and NVIDIA BlueField®-4 to scale training, inference and agents.
- Introduced DSX POD, a reference design for complete Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners inside modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery to accelerate infrastructure deployment.
- Announced European ecosystem adoption of NVIDIA DSX™ to reduce AI factory power requirements and enable near-zero facility cooling water consumption.
- Announced that NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training and Endpoints benchmark, and Vera Rubin NVL72 demonstrated leading inference performance in its MLPerf Inference preview debut.
- Launched NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform and introduced the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture, combining open source OpenShell software, Vera Rubin for model inference, Vera CPUs for agent execution and BlueField-4 DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry to independently monitor agent behavior and enforce security policies in silicon.
- Announced an agreement to acquire Hugging Face to scale its platform and make intelligence more open, capable and accessible.
- Announced plans with global supply chain partners, including Amkor Technology, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries and Unimicron Technology Corporation, to scale critical manufacturing capabilities to meet demand for NVIDIA infrastructure.
- Deepened partnership with MediaTek across cloud infrastructure, local computing and automotive, extending NVIDIA’s rack-scale platform to custom XPUs through NVIDIA NVLink Fusion™.
- Announced plans with Cisco for USFP, a new optical-module form factor designed to increase bandwidth density and power efficiency for next-generation AI factory networks.
- Announced collaboration with Australia’s data center ecosystem on infrastructure supporting a planned buildout of up to 2 gigawatts by 2027 for NVIDIA DSX AI factories.
- Introduced NVIDIA Nemotron for Science to help researchers build specialized agents for scientific discovery, and collaborated with global healthcare and life sciences organizations to advance protein design, accelerate drug discovery and expand precision patient care.
- Partnered with Palantir to bring sovereign AI intelligence and NVIDIA Nemotron™ open models to critical supply chains.
- Partnered with Firebird to scale the company’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity.
- Expanded the open source NVIDIA CUDA-Q™ platform with CUDA-Q Logical for fault-tolerant quantum computing development, and ran a record simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum processor on JUPITER at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre.
Edge Computing
- Third-quarter Edge Computing revenue was $8.2 billion, up 14% from the previous quarter and up 42% from a year ago.

polymarket-7210452.text:
- Jensen Huang Resigns
- Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO
- Harvey C.
Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer.
Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named.
The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.
Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013.
During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution.
Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.
The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C.
Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.
Mr.
Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.
“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors.
“She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap.
The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA.
“We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead.
Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound.
NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world.
The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.
NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m.
PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m.
PT.

Nvidia Q3 CY2026 deep dive: Leadership transition and surging AI demand drive outlook
Jabin Bastian /
November 18, 2026
Leading designer of graphics chips Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) announced better-than-expected revenue in calendar Q3 2026 [fiscal Q3 2027], with sales up 103% year on year to $115.8 billion.
On top of that, next quarter’s revenue guidance ($130 billion at the midpoint) was surprisingly good and 4.2% above what analysts were expecting.
Its non-GAAP profit of $2.68 per share was 8.4% above analysts’ consensus estimates.
Is now the time to buy Nvidia?
Find out in our full research report (it’s free for active Edge members).
Nvidia Q3 CY2026 highlights:
- Revenue $115.8 billion vs S&P analyst consensus of $109.5 billion (103% year-on-year growth, 5.8% beat)
- Adjusted EPS $2.68 vs S&P analyst consensus of $2.47 (8.4% beat)
- Adjusted operating income $77.88 billion vs analyst estimates of $71.63 billion (67.2% margin, 8.7% beat)
- Revenue guidance $130 billion at the midpoint for Q4 CY2026, above analyst estimates of $124.8 billion
- Operating margin 66.9%, up from 63.2% in the same quarter last year
- Inventory days outstanding 124, up from 119 in the previous quarter
- Market capitalization $3.75 trillion
StockStory’s take
Nvidia’s latest quarter was marked by a positive market reaction, as the company delivered results that exceeded Wall Street’s expectations.
Management cited accelerating demand for its AI compute platforms as the primary driver of performance, with strong uptake of the new Vera Rubin platform and continued momentum across hyperscale and enterprise customers.
Interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the rapid adoption of agentic AI workloads and broad-based customer engagement, noting, “Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start… making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia’s history.”
Looking ahead, Nvidia’s guidance is anchored by ongoing demand for AI infrastructure, rapid expansion of its Vera Rubin and Vera CPU platforms, and deepening relationships with key hyperscale and enterprise customers.
Kress pointed to a robust multi-year supply roadmap and expanded commitments from supply chain partners, stating, “We are well-positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position,” while acknowledging that capacity expansion and evolving export controls could impact the pace of growth.
Management expects sustained demand for agentic and open model AI to underpin future results.
Key insights from management’s remarks
Management credited the quarter’s outperformance to rapid deployment of next-generation products, broad-based AI demand, and resilience during a CEO transition.
- Vera Rubin platform ramp: The Vera Rubin compute platform shipped its first production units, generating nearly $20 billion in revenue and marking the fastest product introduction in company history.
Management highlighted broad adoption across hyperscale, enterprise, and government customers seeking advanced AI infrastructure.
- Data center and AI cloud growth: Demand for AI compute remained robust, with data center revenue up sharply.
Nvidia’s ecosystem now includes hyperscalers, neoclouds, and frontier AI labs, with customer cloud backlog rising to $2.5 trillion.
Open-source and proprietary models are fueling rapid growth in AI workloads, benefiting Nvidia’s infrastructure.
- Acquisition of Hugging Face: Nvidia announced a definitive agreement to acquire Hugging Face, a major open model community platform.
Management described this move as key to scaling open AI development and broadening the addressable market for Nvidia’s technologies.
- Agentic AI and CPU momentum: The adoption of agentic (autonomous software agents) workloads has accelerated, now accounting for a large share of compute demand.
The Vera CPU has seen strong uptake among cloud and enterprise partners, with total CPU revenue expected to more than double next year.
- Leadership transition and talent retention: Following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang, the board appointed Colette Kress as Interim CEO and initiated a search for a permanent leader.
Management stressed that employee commitment and customer relationships remain strong, and that operational continuity is a priority during the transition.
Drivers of future performance
Nvidia’s outlook is driven by persistent AI infrastructure demand, ramping product cycles, and disciplined supply chain investments.
- Supply-demand balance and capacity expansion: Management expects ongoing supply constraints to gradually ease as new agreements with global manufacturing partners expand capacity for wafers, substrates, and advanced packaging.
The company is focused on supporting demand from hyperscale, neocloud, and enterprise customers while maintaining discipline in capital commitments.
- Margin outlook and pricing dynamics: Nvidia anticipates gross margins will bottom in the next quarter before improving, supported by product mix and pricing discipline.
Management acknowledged competitive pressures from custom silicon and application-specific chips but believes its full-stack AI offering supports premium pricing and operational efficiency.
- Export controls and regulatory landscape: New U.S.
export controls could affect certain product sales, but management expects the overall impact to be limited due to strong demand elsewhere.
The company has established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to navigate regulatory risks and maintain compliance in key markets.
Catalysts in upcoming quarters
Looking ahead, the StockStory team will watch (1) the continued adoption and scaling of Vera Rubin and Vera CPU platforms, (2) execution on the Hugging Face integration and its impact on the open model ecosystem, and (3) the pace of capacity expansion and supply chain resilience as new manufacturing partnerships ramp.
The company’s ability to navigate regulatory changes and deliver on its buyback program will also serve as key indicators.

How Gold Prices Work: A Guide to XAU Market Structure
Gold trades across three venues with three different prices.
Here's how LBMA, COMEX, and OTC markets actually work — and what it means for gold data.
Gold is one of the most traded assets in the world, but its pricing is often misunderstood.
Unlike equities, which trade on centralized exchanges with a single quoted price, gold trades across multiple venues with different settlement terms, contract specifications, and participant bases.
This guide explains how gold price discovery actually works—from the London benchmarks to New York futures to bilateral OTC trading—and what it means for institutions and developers working with gold market data.
The Three Layers of Gold Price Discovery
Gold prices emerge from three interconnected market layers, each serving a distinct function.
LBMA: The Benchmark for Physical Gold
The London Bullion Market Association runs twice-daily electronic auctions at 10:30 AM and 3:00 PM London time.
Fifteen participating banks submit buy and sell orders, and the auction finds a clearing price where supply meets demand.
This price—known as the LBMA Gold Price—serves as the global reference for physical gold settlement.
It anchors custody reporting, audit processes, and contractual settlement for physical bullion worldwide.
The LBMA also sets the standard for "Good Delivery" bars: 350-430 troy ounces at minimum .995 purity.
These specifications define what qualifies as institutional-grade physical gold.
COMEX: The Futures Engine
COMEX, part of CME Group, is the world's most liquid gold futures market.
It processes approximately 27 million ounces in daily volume through standardized 100-ounce contracts at .995 fineness.
Futures markets absorb macroeconomic information faster than physical markets.
Interest rate decisions, inflation data, and geopolitical developments hit COMEX first, with prices adjusting in milliseconds.
Most COMEX contracts settle in cash rather than physical delivery.
This makes the market highly liquid but also means COMEX prices reflect financial positioning as much as physical supply and demand.
OTC: Where Physical Demand Shows Up
The over-the-counter market handles approximately $150 billion in daily bilateral trading volume.
Unlike the standardized contracts on COMEX, OTC trades are negotiated directly between counterparties with custom settlement terms.
OTC prices reflect real physical demand: regional premiums, delivery logistics, and counterparty credit considerations.
When central banks accumulate gold or jewelry demand spikes in Asia, the signal often appears in OTC spreads before it shows up in benchmark prices.
How These Markets Stay Connected
Arbitrage keeps prices aligned across venues.
When COMEX futures diverge too far from LBMA spot, traders step in to capture the spread.
The typical COMEX-LBMA spread runs around $3.84 per ounce—narrow enough to indicate efficient markets, but persistent enough to reflect real differences in settlement and delivery terms.
This spread also reflects the cost of carrying gold: storage, insurance, and financing.
Under normal conditions, futures trade above spot (contango) because holders must be compensated for these costs.
When spot trades above futures (backwardation), it signals tight physical supply or urgent demand.
Until 2009, gold had only been in backwardation for eight total days in its modern trading history.
What Moves Gold Prices?
Gold responds to a specific set of macroeconomic drivers:
Interest rates affect the carry cost of holding gold.
Higher rates typically push futures into steeper contango, while rate cuts are often bullish for spot prices.
USD strength has an inverse relationship with gold.
A strong dollar makes gold more expensive in other currencies, dampening demand.
Real yields (nominal rates minus inflation) historically correlate with gold performance.
Negative real yields make non-yielding assets like gold more attractive.
Central bank demand provides a structural floor.
Central banks have purchased over 1,000 tonnes annually in recent years, representing steady institutional accumulation.
Geopolitical risk triggers flight-to-safety flows.
Gold's role as a store of value outside the banking system makes it a hedge against systemic uncertainty.
Why Market Structure Matters for Gold Data
Gold's multi-venue structure creates complexity for anyone building with gold prices.
A single data source—one exchange API or one benchmark—captures only a partial view of the market.
This matters for several use cases:
Collateral valuation requires prices that reflect actual liquidation conditions, not just a benchmark quote.
Risk models need to account for spread dynamics between physical and paper markets.
Settlement and clearing may reference different benchmarks depending on jurisdiction and contract terms.
Trading applications require latency and update frequency that matches the speed of futures markets.
How Pyth Prices Gold
Pyth's XAU/USD feed aggregates prices from institutional publishers with direct access to LBMA, COMEX, and OTC markets.
Publishers include trading desks, market makers, and financial institutions that actively trade gold across venues.
Each publisher submits both a price with Pyth's aggregation methodology combines these inputs to produce a single price that updates every 50 milliseconds.
This architecture reflects gold's actual market structure: multiple venues, multiple price points, aggregated into a single feed with transparent methodology.
