GOLD / US DOLLAR
The GOLD / US DOLLAR (Metal.XAU/USD) price feed delivers a live XAU price, updated in real time on Pyth Network.
Prices are aggregated from first-party publishers - exchanges, market makers and trading firms pricing from their own order flow - with a confidence interval on every update.
Available on 100+ blockchains.
Gold does not have one price.
It has a set of prices generated across three market layers that arbitrage keeps aligned.
The London OTC market is the largest layer by notional, with bilateral trades that capture physical demand, regional premiums and institutional accumulation.
COMEX futures (CME Group) is the speed layer: standardised 100-ounce contracts, mostly cash-settled, and typically the quickest venue to react to rate decisions and geopolitical shocks.
The LBMA benchmark is the physical reference: twice-daily electronic auctions at 10:30 and 15:00 London time with participating banks.
Central bank purchases, refinery invoices and mining contracts settle against it.
The three layers stay coupled through arbitrage; the gap between COMEX and London is usually a few dollars an ounce.
The Pyth feed follows the Metal schedule: open from Sunday 18:00 ET to Friday 17:00 ET with a daily 17:00-18:00 ET break, closed over the weekend (Hermes schedule, verified 2026-09-16).
A separate 24/7 Pyth gold index covers the weekend gap.
Pyth's gold price is aggregated from first-party publishers - institutions with direct access to the London and New York gold markets that generate quotes from their own trading activity rather than relicensing an exchange API.
Every update carries a confidence interval that widens when publisher quotes diverge and narrows when they agree, so a protocol can gate liquidations or settlements on uncertainty, not just on price.
The feed is delivered on a pull model, with updates supported as fast as every 1 millisecond and sub-100 ms end-to-end latency (2025), against a physical benchmark that prints twice a day.
For gold specifically, the contrast with a crypto-exchange XAU pair matters: that pair is a derivative of institutional pricing with extra spread and latency baked in, whereas Pyth's publishers are the institutions setting the original price.
The structural fact that makes gold different from an equity or a crypto asset is that it has no primary exchange.
Price forms across three interlocking venues - a bilateral OTC market, a futures exchange and a twice-daily auction - each with a different function, and arbitrage between them is what produces "the gold price".
An oracle that samples only one layer inherits that layer's blind spots.
| Tier | Participants | Role in price formation |
|---|---|---|
| London OTC market | Bullion banks, brokers, refiners, sovereign and institutional buyers trading bilaterally | The largest layer by notional.
Often the first to reflect physical demand, regional premiums and large institutional accumulation.
|
| COMEX futures (CME Group, New York) | Futures traders, hedgers, macro funds, market makers | Standardised 100 oz, .995 fineness contracts, mostly cash-settled.
Typically the quickest venue to absorb macro information; price discovery and hedging rather than physical delivery.
|
| LBMA benchmark auction (London) | Participating banks submitting through the ICE Benchmark Administration (IBA) platform | Twice-daily reference price for physical settlement.
Central bank, refinery and mining contracts reference it.
|
In a normal market (contango) futures trade above spot by the cost of carry: storage, insurance and financing.
The gap between COMEX and London is usually a few dollars an ounce, narrow enough to confirm tight coupling and wide enough to reflect real differences in contract terms and delivery logistics.
| Session / Window | Time (ET unless stated) | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Factor | Impact |
|---|---|
| Real yields | Gold has no yield, so its opportunity cost is the real return on safe assets.
Falling real yields are typically supportive; this is one of the variables most closely associated with gold price movements.
|
| USD strength | Gold is priced in dollars.
A stronger dollar raises the cost for non-dollar buyers and weighs on demand; the DXY-gold correlation is persistently negative but not perfect.
|
| Central bank demand | Net purchases above 1,000 t a year in 2022-2024 and 863 t in 2025 (World Gold Council, full year 2025) have made central banks a significant source of demand, a shift from the net selling of the 1990s and 2000s.
|
| Inflation expectations | Can move independently of real yields if nominal rates rise in step.
Forward breakevens from TIPS are the cleanest read.
|
| Geopolitical risk | Wars, sanctions and sovereign debt stress drive safe-haven buying.
The move is typically acute, then mean-reverting as markets adapt.
|
| Physical supply constraints | Mine output was a record 3,672 t in 2025, barely above 2024 (World Gold Council), with a 10-15 year discovery-to-production lag.
Supply cannot respond to price quickly, so demand shocks transmit directly.
|
These drivers interact; single-variable models are unreliable.
A rate cut with rising inflation expectations, for example, pushes real yields down and the dollar lower at the same time, compounding the effect on gold.
Worked example: 21 October 2025.
After a run to a record close to $4,380 per ounce, spot gold fell more than 6% in a single session, roughly $300 an ounce, its largest one-day fall in twelve years, as US-China trade tensions eased, the dollar strengthened and positioning unwound (Kitco, Forbes, 21 October 2025).
Nothing about physical supply or demand changed that day; the move was positioning and the dollar.
For a feed consumer the lesson is the shape: publisher quotes diverged as the move accelerated, so the confidence interval widened before the price settled, which is the signal a lending protocol uses to pause liquidations rather than execute them into a falling knife.
Gold liquidity is deep on weekdays but not uniform.
The thinnest windows for the Pyth feed are the daily 17:00-18:00 ET maintenance break (no updates) and the weekend from Friday 17:00 ET to Sunday 18:00 ET, when the underlying OTC and futures markets are closed and the feed's last price ages by more than two days.
The Sunday 18:00 ET reopen is the first print after two days of accumulated news and is where confidence intervals should be expected to be widest.
The two LBMA auction windows (10:30 and 15:00 London) are the moments when the physical benchmark re-anchors; the COMEX-LBMA spread can move around them.
Because the physical benchmark prints only twice a day while futures and OTC quote continuously, an oracle that follows the auction alone will lag by hours.
Pyth's publishers quote from the continuous markets, so the feed moves with COMEX and OTC and does not wait for the fix.
The confidence interval exists for these windows.
When publisher quotes diverge - on a rate decision, a geopolitical shock or a thin reopen - the interval widens and a consuming protocol can pause liquidations or settlements rather than acting on a contested price.
| Event, date | What happened |
|---|---|
| COMEX-London dislocation, 23-24 March 2020 | COMEX April futures traded $50-70 above loco-London spot, briefly around $100 on 24 March, against a normal premium near $1.50, after Swiss refineries closed and passenger flights (which carry bullion) were grounded.
The exchange-for-physical arbitrage that holds the layers together stopped working for days (Singapore Bullion Market Association, "The Day the EFP Broke", 2020).
|
| One-day fall, 21 October 2025 | Spot gold fell more than 6%, about $300/oz, the largest single-day drop since 2013, after reaching about $4,380/oz; silver fell roughly 9% the same day (Kitco, Forbes, 21 October 2025).
|

Data Methodology
Where does this price data come from?

Understanding the Troy Ounce Gold Price
The gold price per ounce is the standard international quote, represented as XAU/USD under the ISO 4217 currency code system.
COMEX is the world's largest gold futures market, and the troy ounce is the universal trading unit for investment-grade gold.
When financial media report "the gold price," they are referring to the price per troy ounce in US dollars.
The troy ounce has been the standard unit for weighing precious metals since the Middle Ages, named after the French market town of Troyes, a major medieval trading hub.
One troy ounce equals 31.1035 grams, approximately 10% heavier than the avoirdupois ounce (28.3495 grams) used in everyday measurements.
This distinction matters: a "1 oz" gold coin contains 31.1 grams of gold, not 28.3 grams.
The troy system persists in precious metals because centuries of established commercial practice survived the widespread adoption of the metric system.
On COMEX, the benchmark gold futures contract (ticker: GC) represents 100 troy ounces of gold with a minimum purity of 995 fineness.
These contracts trade electronically on CME Globex nearly 24 hours a day, five days a week, providing continuous price discovery.
The spot price, what you see quoted on our charts, represents the price for immediate settlement derived from the nearest active futures contract, adjusted for time value.
Futures contracts for later delivery months trade at a slight premium to spot, reflecting financing and storage costs.
The LBMA Gold Price, set twice daily in London by a panel of accredited market makers through an electronic auction, serves as the authoritative benchmark for settling gold contracts, valuing gold-backed financial products, and pricing physical deliveries worldwide.
Together, the COMEX futures market and the LBMA benchmark form the global pricing framework that central banks, miners, refiners, jewelers, and individual investors all rely on.

Because COMEX in New York anchors global price discovery, the US gold price per ounce shown here is the same benchmark rate dealers reference worldwide, and the spot gold price today per ounce is identical across sellers; what differs from dealer to dealer is the premium added on top.

Gold fell to US$3,830.74 a troy ounce on November 16, 2026, its lowest level since October 2, 2025, as higher US government bond yields, a strong dollar and expectations of further interest rate rises weighed on prices.
Gold’s decline from January’s record of US$5,594.82 a troy ounce has reached 31.5%, according to Reuters analysis.
The metal is heading for its worst annual performance since 2015.
The US dollar has been trading near its strongest level since April 2025, making gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies and weakening demand in recent months.
Rising yields on US Treasury bonds have also reduced the appeal of gold, which pays no interest.
Markets expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 25 basis points, or 0.25 percentage points, at its next meeting in December, with a smaller chance of a 50-basis-point increase, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.
“Markets expect higher interest rates ahead, boosting the dollar and compounding gold’s headwinds, leaving it exposed to deeper declines,” said Nikos Tzabouras, senior financial editorial writer at FXCM.
The US-Israeli war against Iran, which began in late February 2026, has raised oil prices and fuelled inflation concerns, strengthening expectations of tighter monetary policy around the world.
Gold is often bought as protection against inflation, but rising interest rates typically make the metal less attractive because it offers no yield.
Nvidia’s falling market value has added to the pressure on gold.
The company had lost US$1.9 trillion in value from early October to November 13, when its market capitalisation stood at US$3.9 trillion.
“In the short term gold is a liquidity asset … the thing you sell to raise cash,” said Nicky Shiels, head of research and metals strategy at MKS PAMP.
Physically backed gold exchange-traded funds attracted inflows of 211 tonnes in the third quarter of 2026 despite higher bond yields and a stronger dollar.
Demand for gold bars and coins, however, fell sharply over the same period.
Central banks bought an estimated 675 tonnes of gold between January and September, according to the World Gold Council (WGC).
The WGC total combines reported purchases with estimates of buying that has not been disclosed.
Poland, the most active official buyer, may have paused purchases in November after its central bank reached its gold reserve target of 700 tonnes.
The Polish central bank’s governor nevertheless left open the possibility of further purchases.
China remained a notable source of gold demand, with its central bank buying bullion for two years and supporting confidence among local investors.
Analysts noted that gold had so far remained above US$3,800 a troy ounce, a level they regard as psychologically important.

Gold (XAU/USD) struggles to gain traction on Tuesday, easing off its intraday high of $3,886.
The metal continues to face headwinds from a firm US Dollar (USD) and elevated US Treasury yields as hawkish Fed rhetoric reinforces expectations of higher-for-longer interest rates.
At the time of writing, XAU/USD trades around $3,853, hovering just above the 13-month low of $3,832 touched on Monday.
Traders have fully priced in a December rate hike and see a nearly 70% chance of another increase in January, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.
The pricing follows remarks from several Fed officials over the past week suggesting the central bank still has work to do to bring inflation back to its 2% target.
On Monday, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said she favours smaller rate hikes but left the door open to larger moves if the Fed falls behind in its fight against inflation.
Meanwhile, prospects for a US-Iran deal remain uncertain.
A rise in attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz keeps energy-driven inflation risks alive, even as recovering Middle East exports and expectations of a supply surplus weigh on Oil prices.
Gold is often seen as an inflation hedge, but it tends to come under pressure when borrowing costs rise, as interest-bearing assets become more attractive.
A stronger US Dollar also makes the metal more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
The US Dollar Index (DXY), which tracks the Greenback’s value against a basket of six major currencies, trades around 103.50, near a 19-month high.
Strategists at OCBC remain "cautiously optimistic over the medium term" on gold, pointing to support from "central-bank diversification, investment demand, geopolitical uncertainty and longer-term fiscal concerns." However, they caution that "elevated real yields and USD resilience may continue to constrain the sustainability of near-term rebounds," even as prices attempt to stabilise after recent technical weakness.
Looking ahead, attention turns to US Retail Sales and fresh Fed commentary later in the American trading hours, with the minutes of the Fed’s October meeting due on Wednesday.
Traders will also watch Nvidia’s earnings after Tuesday’s US market close, as the results could sway risk appetite and move the US Dollar, in turn influencing Gold.
On the daily chart, XAU/USD keeps a bearish near-term tone as spot holds beneath a stacked band of moving average resistance.
Momentum indicators reinforce this capped backdrop, with the Relative Strength Index (14) hovering in the high 30s and the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) line aligned negatively, hinting that bounces are likely to be sold while these barriers remain intact.
On the topside, initial resistance is seen at the nearby horizontal level around $3,900, ahead of the 21-day Simple Moving Average (SMA) at $4,002.
A daily close above these would be needed to ease immediate downside pressure and open the way toward the 50-day SMA at $4,133 and then the 100-day SMA at $4,194.
On the downside, immediate support is located at the horizontal line near $3,850, where a break lower on a daily closing basis would likely invite a continuation of the prevailing downtrend, exposing fresh lows while momentum remains subdued.
(The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool.
Know more.)
Gold has played a key role in human’s history as it has been widely used as a store of value and medium of exchange.
Currently, apart from its shine and usage for jewelry, the precious metal is widely seen as a safe-haven asset, meaning that it is considered a good investment during turbulent times.
Gold is also widely seen as a hedge against inflation and against depreciating currencies as it doesn’t rely on any specific issuer or government.
Central banks are the biggest Gold holders.
In their aim to support their currencies in turbulent times, central banks tend to diversify their reserves and buy Gold to improve the perceived strength of the economy and the currency.
High Gold reserves can be a source of trust for a country’s solvency.
Central banks added 1,136 tonnes of Gold worth around $70 billion to their reserves in 2022, according to data from the World Gold Council.
This is the highest yearly purchase since records began.
Central banks from emerging economies such as China, India and Turkey are quickly increasing their Gold reserves.
Gold has an inverse correlation with the US Dollar and US Treasuries, which are both major reserve and safe-haven assets.
When the Dollar depreciates, Gold tends to rise, enabling investors and central banks to diversify their assets in turbulent times.
Gold is also inversely correlated with risk assets.
A rally in the stock market tends to weaken Gold price, while sell-offs in riskier markets tend to favor the precious metal.
The price can move due to a wide range of factors.
Geopolitical instability or fears of a deep recession can quickly make Gold price escalate due to its safe-haven status.
As a yield-less asset, Gold tends to rise with lower interest rates, while higher cost of money usually weighs down on the yellow metal.
Still, most moves depend on how the US Dollar (USD) behaves as the asset is priced in dollars (XAU/USD).
A strong Dollar tends to keep the price of Gold controlled, whereas a weaker Dollar is likely to push Gold prices up.

On Friday, 20 November 2026, spot gold fell as low as $3,513.54 an ounce, its lowest level since 4 September 2025, Reuters reported.
By 16:04 GMT, Kitco showed spot gold near $3,536, down about 2.4% on the day.
Meanwhile, the ANC Trading Community desk is following the slide live, and below we explain what is driving it.
Gold Price This Week: How Big Is the Drop?
First, the numbers behind the gold price this week.
Gold was on track for a weekly loss of about 8% to 9%, its sharpest since the week ending 20 March, according to Reuters.
US gold futures for December last traded near $3,545 as of 16:06 GMT, down about $141, or nearly 4%, from Thursday’s close of $3,685.50, based on Yahoo Finance data.
That leaves the contract more than $340 below last Friday’s close.
We also laid out the five red daily sessions in our Market Watch edition, Gold’s Worst Week Since March: How Five Red Days Unfolded.

Other metals fell too.

In addition, Swiss customs data showed gold exports fell 34% in October to 109.7 tonnes.
We covered the first leg of this move in Gold Price Today: Near a 14-Month Low After Hawkish Fed Minutes.
Fed Hike Bets Jump to 99%
The main driver of the gold price this week is the Federal Reserve.
Markets now see a 99.3% chance of a quarter-point rate hike in December, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, as reported by Reuters on Friday.
That is up from about 90% a day earlier and about 97% on Friday morning.
On Thursday, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said the Fed will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high.

Higher rates usually hurt gold, because the metal pays no interest.
At the same time, the US dollar held near a 19-month high on Friday.
A strong dollar makes gold more expensive for buyers in Europe, Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America.
The US 10-year Treasury yield, which closed near 5.05% on Thursday, eased to about 4.94% on Friday, based on Yahoo Finance data as of 15:58 GMT.

Forced Selling Adds to the Pressure
There is also a second force behind the gold price this week.
“There seems to be a bit of forced liquidation going on across the market in general,” said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, in comments to Reuters.
Investing.com reported that some investors sold gold to meet margin calls and cover losses elsewhere.
A sharp drop in technology shares has added to the strain.
Asian shares were also heading for their worst week since 2020, Reuters said.

- Global Market, Gold Market
- Posted on November 20, 2026
Gold Prices Plunge to Lowest Level in 14 Months as Nearly 9% Weekly Selloff Shakes Markets
Gold breaks below $3,600
Gold prices fell to their lowest level in approximately 14 months on Friday, November 20, as a sharp selloff pushed spot bullion below $3,600 per troy ounce.
Reuters reported spot gold at $3,551.68 at 02:57 GMT, down 1.9% in the session and approximately 8.9% for the week.
If sustained through the weekly close, the decline would mark the worst weekly performance in eight months.
These figures are an early-Friday snapshot, not final closing prices.
—
A sudden acceleration in selling
Earlier in the week, gold had already broken below $3,800.
A further move towards $3,552 represents a decline of roughly 6.5% from that threshold.
Such a rapid change can unsettle investors accustomed to viewing gold as a relatively defensive asset.
December US gold futures also fell, with Reuters reporting a 3.6% decline to about $3,551.90.
The scale of the weekly decline, rather than the latest Federal Reserve comments alone, is the central development.
—
Why is gold falling?
Several forces are working against bullion at once.
Expectations of additional US interest-rate increases have supported the dollar and reduced the relative appeal of assets that do not pay interest.
Higher Treasury yields can also raise the opportunity cost of holding physical gold.
At the same time, market participants have raised the possibility that some investors are selling liquid holdings to raise cash or reduce leveraged positions.
That liquidation explanation is plausible but cannot be quantified from the price movement alone.
—
The Federal Reserve and the dollar
Minutes from the Federal Reserve’s October 27–28 meeting, released November 18, showed broad expectations that further policy tightening could be appropriate if the economy developed as anticipated.
The Fed had held its benchmark target range at 3.75%–4.00%.
Market-implied probabilities cited in Reuters reporting on November 20 pointed strongly towards a quarter-point increase in December, but these probabilities change as trading and economic data evolve.
A stronger US dollar can make dollar-priced gold costlier for purchasers using other currencies, potentially weakening demand.
—
Why gold can fall during financial uncertainty
Gold is often described as a safe haven, but that does not mean its price rises in every period of stress.
Investors facing losses elsewhere may sell gold because it is liquid and readily traded.
In other circumstances, higher real yields or dollar strength can overwhelm safe-haven demand.
The current decline does not, by itself, prove that gold has permanently lost its diversification role.
Establishing whether forced liquidation is a major driver would require evidence from futures positioning, ETF flows, and broader funding markets.
—
Other precious metals also retreat
The pressure has extended beyond gold.
Reuters reported silver around $41.90 per ounce, platinum near $1,317 and palladium around $888.66 during early Friday trading, with each metal lower on the session.
These markets share some financial drivers with gold but also respond to industrial demand, especially in electronics, automotive manufacturing, and other production activities.
Their simultaneous decline suggests a wider reassessment of precious-metal exposure.
—
Physical gold flows offer another perspective
Swiss customs data released November 19 showed October gold exports of approximately 109.7 metric tonnes, down 34% from September.
Switzerland is a major gold refining and trading hub, so changes in shipments are relevant to physical bullion flows.
However, a decline in exports from one country is not equivalent to a matching decline in global demand: inventories, shipment timing, and changes in trading routes can all influence the figures.
—
What does this mean for buyers in India and the UAE?
A decline in the international spot price does not necessarily translate into an identical reduction in retail prices.
In India, changes in the rupee-dollar exchange rate, duties, taxes and local premiums influence the price paid for bars, coins and jewellery.
In the UAE, the dirham’s peg to the dollar makes international movements more directly visible in local currency quotations, although dealer spreads, premiums and making charges still matter.
Buyers should compare actual retail and resale quotations rather than relying on the global percentage decline alone.
—
Could prices fall further?
The next direction remains uncertain.
A further strengthening of the dollar or a rise in yields could extend the pressure, while softer inflation data or a less restrictive Federal Reserve outlook might improve conditions for gold.
ETF inflows or outflows, central-bank buying, and the behaviour of leveraged futures positions will also help clarify whether the latest selling reflects temporary market stress or a more durable change in investment demand.
A sharp drop can attract buyers, but it does not establish that a bottom has been reached.
—
Outlook
Gold’s move below $3,600 and the prospect of a nearly 9% weekly decline mark a significant new phase of the correction.
The immediate story is not simply that the Federal Reserve may raise rates, but that several pressures have converged to produce an unusually fast selloff.
Until the dollar, yields and investment flows stabilise, bullion may remain volatile.
Readers should treat early-Friday prices and weekly performance figures as provisional.

How the Gold Spot Price Works
The spot price is the market price for one troy ounce of gold for immediate delivery, quoted in U.S.
dollars.
It is derived from the most actively traded gold futures contract together with over-the-counter dealing, and it moves nearly around the clock as trading follows the sun from New York to London, Zurich, Shanghai and Hong Kong.
A troy ounce is 31.1034768 grams — about 10% heavier than the avoirdupois ounce used for groceries.
Physical bullion products trade at a premium above spot that covers fabrication and distribution; the premium is proportionally larger on small items than on large bars.
The chart above tracks this spot price.
The currency selector converts the same underlying quote into other currencies using live exchange rates.
Spot Price vs.
Futures Price
The spot price is for gold delivered now; a futures price is for gold delivered on a set date in the future, traded on exchanges such as COMEX.
The two normally differ by the cost of carrying gold to that date — storage, insurance and interest — which is why futures usually trade slightly above spot, a condition called contango.
When futures trade below spot — backwardation — it signals unusually strong demand for immediate physical delivery, and it’s rare enough in gold that it makes news when it happens.
The price on this page is the spot price; quotes you see for "gold futures" refer to the most active COMEX contract.
What Moves the Gold Price
Real interest rates and the Federal Reserve.
Gold pays no yield, so its strongest headwind is a high real (inflation-adjusted) interest rate — and its strongest tailwind is a falling one.
Fed rate decisions, inflation reports and Treasury yields are the events most likely to move the gold price on any given day.
Inflation and currency debasement.
Gold's reputation as an inflation hedge is best understood over long horizons: across decades, gold has broadly preserved purchasing power as paper currencies lost it, which is why demand rises when investors expect sustained inflation or growing government debt.
Over shorter periods the relationship is looser — in an inflation spike, what matters most is how the Fed responds, which is why real interest rates (above) are the better day-to-day guide.
The U.S.
dollar.
Gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar tends to lift the gold price and a stronger dollar tends to weigh on it — even when nothing about gold itself has changed.
To see how much of a move is gold versus the dollar, the Kitco Global Index (KGX) tracks gold’s value measured against a basket of major currencies with the U.S.
dollar’s influence stripped out.
Central bank buying.
Central banks are among the largest holders of gold, and sustained official-sector purchases have been a major driver of demand in recent years.
Reserve announcements from major central banks regularly move the market.
Safe-haven and investment demand.
In periods of market stress, geopolitical risk or currency uncertainty, investors move into gold, lifting the price.
Flows into and out of gold-backed ETFs provide a visible, daily measure of this investment demand.
Gold Value by Purity — Karats and Fineness
Most gold isn't pure 24-karat bullion.
U.S.
jewelry is most commonly 14K gold, with 10K the legal minimum that can be sold as gold in the United States, while investment bars and coins such as the American Gold Eagle and Gold Buffalo are high-purity bullion (the Buffalo is .9999 fine).
Karat measures gold content out of 24 parts.
Each purity also has a fineness mark — the small number stamped on jewelry — which tells you exactly what an item contains:

So a ring marked 585 is 14-karat gold, and its gold content is worth 58.3% of the pure gold price by weight.
The Gold Value by Purity calculator on this page applies these percentages to the live spot price to estimate melt value — the value of the pure gold an item contains.
Melt value is not necessarily the price paid when buying or received when selling: dealers buying scrap typically pay below melt, and finished jewelry retails above it.
To value a specific item by its exact weight and purity, use the expanded gold calculator.
Gold Price History and All-Time High
Gold's current all-time high in U.S.
dollars is $5,589.38 per ounce, set on January 28, 2026.
Earlier landmarks put today's price in context: gold peaked near $850 in January 1980 during the inflation crisis, and at roughly $1,920 in September 2011 after the financial crisis.
Adjusted for inflation, the 1980 peak stood as the real record for decades — until January 2026, when gold surpassed it in real terms as well.
About Gold
Gold has been used as money and a store of value for more than five thousand years, and it neither rusts nor tarnishes — coins recovered after centuries underwater emerge with their surfaces intact.
Jewelry accounts for roughly half of annual gold demand worldwide, with the remainder split among investment bars and coins, central bank reserves, and industrial uses such as electronics, where its corrosion resistance and conductivity matter more than its cost.

Global spot gold reached US$4,146.63 an ounce on November 5, 2026, its highest level since October 20, as a weaker US dollar and lower Treasury yields supported the metal.
Falling oil prices also eased inflation concerns ahead of a closely watched US employment report.
Spot gold subsequently traded 1% higher at US$4,100.27 an ounce at 2.05pm US Eastern Time, or 7.05pm GMT, on November 5.
US gold futures for December delivery settled 1% higher at US$4,113.50 an ounce.
Gold’s advance followed a jump of nearly 3.4% on November 4, its biggest daily gain since August 19.
At its November 5 intraday peak, gold had recovered more than US$250 an ounce from the one-year low of US$3,869.85 recorded on October 30.
The US dollar index hovered near its lowest level since September 30 on November 5, making gold cheaper for buyers using other currencies.
The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield was also near its lowest level in almost two months.
Brent crude remained below US$100 a barrel after falling nearly 9% on November 4.
The oil sell-off reflected hopes that strong Democratic gains in the US elections could reduce the risk of further escalation in the Iran war.
David Meger, director of metals trading at High Ridge Futures, said: “It's not that at this point rate hike expectation has completely disappeared.” Meger added that weaker energy prices could ease inflation fears and reduce the need for further interest-rate increases.
Traders assigned a 66% probability to a December interest-rate increase by the US Federal Reserve on November 5, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.
Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, which pays no interest.
Investors were awaiting the US non-farm payrolls report, scheduled for November 6, to assess the Federal Reserve’s likely policy direction.
Independent metals trader Tai Wong said recent payrolls figures had been volatile and that “gold could be vulnerable to a stronger-than-expected print”.
Wong added that a strong employment reading would probably reinforce the December rate rise already widely anticipated by the market.
Poland’s central bank has achieved its previously announced target of holding 700 tonnes of gold in its reserves.
The central bank has left open the possibility of further purchases.
Silver holds steady as platinum and palladium rise
Other precious metals recorded the following spot prices on November 5:
- Silver was unchanged at US$52.23 an ounce.
- Platinum rose 1.6% to US$1,520.75 an ounce.
- Palladium gained 3.8% to US$1,042.24 an ounce.

Salesforce and Microsoft Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Salesforce Customer Context and Sales Workflows to Microsoft Copilot
New integrations bring Salesforce customer context and sales workflows into Microsoft Copilot, enable real-time CRM collaboration in Microsoft Teams, and connect Salesforce Data 360 with Microsoft Fabric through bidirectional zero-copy data access.
Accenture is serving as a design and implementation partner along with being customer zero, deploying the integrations in its own global sales organisation.
SINGAPORE – November 19, 2026 – At Microsoft Ignite, Salesforce and Microsoft announced Copilotforce, a partnership bringing Salesforce to Microsoft’s expansive enterprise productivity ecosystem, alongside new integrations across Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft Fabric.
The collaboration extends Salesforce customer context, AI capabilities, and sales workflows into one of the largest enterprise software environments, bringing Salesforce closer to where employees already work.
With Salesforce in Microsoft Copilot, sellers will be able to access Salesforce customer context, analyse opportunities, prepare for meetings, prioritise opportunities, and take CRM actions informed by Teams conversations, Outlook emails, and shared documents.
Separately, bidirectional zero-copy capabilities connect Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric without duplicating datasets, allowing organisations to query Fabric data natively within Data 360 and securely share Data 360 intelligence into Fabric.
These capabilities build on Sales Cloud in Teams, which brings Salesforce CRM insights and workflows into Microsoft Teams, introduced at Dreamforce and currently in pilot.
Together, the integrations will allow sellers to prep for meetings in Copilot or Teams, or update supported opportunity details in Teams.
“Through Copilotforce, we’re bringing Salesforce to the largest surface in enterprise software today, embedding trusted Salesforce context and intelligent sales workflows directly where sellers work.
By bringing together the #1 CRM with the #1 productivity surface, we’re transforming AI from a standalone tool into a powerful driver of productivity, smarter decisions, and customer success.” – Miguel Milano, President, Chief Operating Officer, Salesforce
“AI is only as powerful as the data and context that grounds it.
Bringing Salesforce customer data and sales skills together with the work context delivered by Work IQ in Microsoft Copilot allows our joint customers to unlock actionable insights across their core business applications.
Copilotforce will give sales teams the intelligence they need to make faster, higher-confidence decisions while maintaining the governance and trust enterprises demand.” – Judson Althoff, CEO, Microsoft Commercial Business
AI context where employees already work
Powered by AIforce, the live interface layer that brings Salesforce capabilities into external AI environments, Salesforce in Microsoft Copilot will bring Sales Cloud workflows into the tools sellers already use.
Sellers will be able to prepare for meetings, review opportunities, and take supported sales actions using Salesforce customer context.
- Salesforce in Microsoft Copilot: Will enable sales and revenue teams to ask natural-language questions and receive grounded, actionable outputs; will also enable users to take Salesforce actions directly within Copilot.
Work IQ, the intelligence layer that powers Copilot, synthesises Salesforce insights with relevant relationships and content from Teams meetings, Outlook emails, and shared documents across SharePoint and OneDrive.
Key daily sales workflows will include:
- Customer Meeting Preparation: Combine account history and meeting transcripts into a single executive brief, saving hours of prep time and eliminating app-switching.
- Deal-Health Analysis: Surface hidden deal risks and customer sentiment, enabling sellers to focus on the right actions before deals stall.
- Pipeline Review & Action Plans: Turn complex pipeline data into ready-to-execute close plans directly inside Word and PowerPoint, slashing administrative overhead.
- Salesforce in Teams: Building on the pilot demonstrated at Dreamforce 2026, the Sales Cloud in Teams app will bring rich business context and real-time insights directly where over 400M active users already chat and collaborate.
Sellers will be able to act on those insights with Agentforce Coworker, with updates automatically syncing back to Salesforce, and it brings the same Salesforce permissions and governance coordinating the right Agentforce agents, and turns the chat into action.
Sellers will gain a real-time view of pipeline and quota progress, receive active deal notifications, and access AI-driven briefing materials.
Interactive adaptive cards will enable sellers to update supported opportunity details, with changes saved back to Salesforce, and share secure records in deal rooms to align cross-functional teams without tool-switching.
Enterprise-grade governance and source-level permissions
Enterprise AI requires strict data protection and governance controls.
Salesforce in Microsoft Copilot operates through authenticated user access, preserving the granular permissions, sharing rules, and audit trails established in both environments.
Customer data remains protected at every boundary: Salesforce controls data access and governs supported business actions, while Microsoft ensures communications and documents adhere to existing enterprise compliance policies.
Supported writeback actions to the CRM require explicit user confirmation and respect existing validation rules, helping ensure customer records remain governed and auditable.
Access enterprise context without migration or duplication
AI models and enterprise workflows are only as effective as the data and context they can reach.
Salesforce and Microsoft are delivering bidirectional Zero Copy integration between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric, allowing organisations to harmonise and activate data across platforms and turn customer, operational, and financial data into trusted context for AI, without maintaining duplicate datasets or running brittle ETL pipelines.
- Data Federation: Joint customers can now query and analyse supported Microsoft Fabric OneLake data directly within Salesforce Data 360, leaving the source data in Fabric.
This native Zero Copy connection brings Salesforce and Microsoft Fabric data together, turning it into enterprise-wide context across Salesforce experiences: Sales and service teams get a richer view of each customer, marketers build segments from the combined data, analysts explore it in Tableau, and Agentforce uses it to answer questions and complete tasks.
- Salesforce Data 360 Data Sharing: Organisations will be able to securely share curated Salesforce Data 360 customer context and intelligence into Microsoft OneLake.
Enterprise data science and business intelligence teams will be able to analyse customer trends alongside enterprise datasets, helping business leaders make decisions with a more complete picture of their customers and operations.
That combined context will support custom analytics, reporting, and enterprise AI workloads without maintaining duplicate datasets, helping teams make more informed decisions grounded in trusted customer context.
Trusted enterprise data for Microsoft AI and analytics ecosystem
Enterprise AI and analytics systems demand trusted data, rich business contexts, and governed access.
Through an expanded collaboration with Microsoft, Informatica helps customers make confident decisions, simplify AI development, and understand the data powering their AI and Analytics workloads.
The new Informatica Plugin for Copilot empowers business users to discover relevant data, address data quality issues, and verify the authoritativeness and reliability of the underlying data using natural-language queries.

What is Bitcoin?
Bitcoin holds the distinction of being the original cryptocurrency and remains the most widely followed digital coin in 2026.
Its market capitalization is around $1.33 trillion, putting it well ahead of Ethereum—the second-largest cryptocurrency—which has about $233 billion in market value.
Put simply, Bitcoin is a decentralized digital currency.
Rather than being issued or managed by a central bank or government, it runs on a peer-to-peer network.
That setup enables people to send money directly to one another without going through a traditional financial institution.
Many investors view Bitcoin as a possible shield against inflation or as another tool for diversifying their portfolios.
Its growth over the last decade has been remarkable, frequently beating the performance of major stock market indices, which has helped fuel investors’ interest.
However, like most cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin is known for sharp volatility and rapid changes in price.
Bitcoin price history
Since its creation in 2009, Bitcoin’s price action has been anything but boring.
One of the most famous early stories involves software developer Laszlo Hanyecz, who paid 10,000 Bitcoins for pizza; those coins would now be worth more than 668 million dollars.
Over roughly the past decade, Bitcoin has gained more than 15,000%.
That’s an extraordinary rise by any measure.
Yet this performance comes with substantial risk, as cryptocurrencies can be extremely unpredictable.
Bitcoin has endured steep corrections, with declines of tens of thousands of dollars over short periods, but it has also rebounded with powerful rallies.
By the end of 2025, it was trading about 30% below its record high from October of the same year.
What affects Bitcoin’s price?
A number of elements can move Bitcoin’s price, including:
- Investor speculation: As with many high-risk assets, Bitcoin is heavily influenced by what traders think and feel.
Short-term price changes often reflect speculative bets and market buzz more than long-term fundamentals.
- Adoption by major companies: When large, well-known companies embrace Bitcoin or crypto technology, it can support further growth.
For instance, Bitcoin experienced price increases after automakers like Tesla and Ferrari revealed plans to accept Bitcoin as a form of payment.
- Economy: Bitcoin doesn’t respond to inflation reports or Federal Reserve decisions in the same way as more traditional assets like stocks.
Still, it tends to do better when the U.S.
economy is strong, as people with more disposable income may be open to investing in higher-risk assets like crypto.
- Regulatory developments: Because the crypto space is still maturing, rules and regulations are still being developed.
New regulatory actions can unsettle the market and impact Bitcoin’s price, either positively or negatively.
How to buy and invest in Bitcoin
If you’re interested in adding Bitcoin to your portfolio, you have several choices.
Here are some popular ones.
Buy Bitcoin on a cryptocurrency exchange
One direct method is to buy Bitcoin yourself.
This involves opening an account with a cryptocurrency exchange, linking it to your bank, and using your deposited funds to purchase Bitcoin.
Invest in Bitcoin ETFs
If you’d rather not handle crypto directly, you can look at Bitcoin exchange-traded funds.
A Bitcoin ETF holds Bitcoin as its underlying asset, and the fund’s shares trade on regular stock exchanges.
This route lets you avoid managing your own crypto wallet and lowers the risk of losing access to your coins through lost passwords or wallet errors.
Buy crypto stocks
Another investment strategy is to buy shares of companies that are deeply involved in crypto.
These might include tech companies, publicly traded crypto exchanges, or payment processors that integrate Bitcoin.
When these businesses benefit from Bitcoin’s success, their stocks may respond, giving you indirect exposure.
Open a Bitcoin IRA
Retirement savers may consider a Bitcoin IRA.
This type of account works similarly to a traditional or Roth IRA in that it offers tax advantages and the same contribution limits, but it allows you to invest in Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as part of your retirement strategy.

other cryptocurrencies
Even though Bitcoin gets much of the attention, it’s just one of many cryptocurrencies to consider.

- Ethereum: Ethereum is the second-biggest cryptocurrency by market cap.
In contrast to Bitcoin, its primary function is not as a currency but as a decentralized platform that powers applications and smart contracts, making it especially popular among developers.
- Tether: Tether is classified as a “stablecoin” because it is pegged to another asset—in this case, the U.S.
dollar.
As a result, it tends to be less volatile than Bitcoin, though it also offers less potential for big gains.
- XRP: XRP is built for fast and inexpensive cross-border payments, allowing money to move between countries quickly and with relatively low fees.

But if you’re willing to hold through volatility and keep Bitcoin as one component of a diversified portfolio, allocating a portion of your money to it may make sense.

Weekend - Bitcoin fell to four-month low near $62,000 as crypto liquidations top $2 billion
Summary
- Bitcoin fell to about $62,000 over the weekend, its lowest since July, before recovering to $66,000, down 14% on the week.
The drop triggered roughly $2 billion in crypto liquidations, mostly long bets, as spot bitcoin ETF outflows extended.
The weekend flush has removed much of the leveraged long exposure that built up before the drop.
That lowers the risk of another forced-selling cascade in the near term, but it does not bring in new buyers by itself.
Sentiment is fragile.
Several possible drivers are in play at once: ETF redemptions, rate-hike expectations and lingering exchange-security worries after the Binance hack.
With that many headwinds, a recovery will need confirmation from flows rather than from price alone.
Ether’s steeper loss keeps the ETH/BTC cross under pressure heading into the new week.
---
Leveraged bulls paid for the weekend’s slide to a four-month low, and the bounce means little until ETF outflows stop.
Summary:
- Bitcoin hit about $62,000, its lowest since July, before recovering to $64,910 by late Sunday afternoon ET.
It was down 14.2% on the week.
- Over the same period ether fell 18.2% to $1,815 and Solana lost 19.7% to $71.68.
- Crypto liquidations totalled $2.02 billion from 8 a.m.
ET Saturday to 8 a.m.
ET Sunday.
Longs made up $1.68 billion and shorts $342.4 million.
The live 24-hour tally had eased to $742.9 million by about 4:30 p.m.
ET Sunday.
- Changpeng Zhao said Binance had not sold crypto after its Oct.
29 hack and that he had personally bought crypto in recent days.
- Zhao cited ETF outflows, Fed rate-hike expectations, investors possibly raising cash for Anthropic’s IPO, and security concerns as possible causes.
- Spot bitcoin ETFs had $1.91 billion in net outflows over seven straight sessions through Friday.
Spot ether ETFs shed $398.9 million last week, their seventh straight weekly outflow, one short of the record of eight.
Bitcoin dropped to its lowest level since July over the weekend, trading as low as $62,000 before recovering to $64,910 by late Sunday afternoon US time, according to The Block’s price data.
That still left the world’s largest cryptocurrency down 14.2% over the past seven days, and the selloff spread across the market to trigger roughly $2 billion in forced position closures.
The damage was heavier further along the risk curve.
Ether fell 18.2% over the week to $1,815, while Solana lost 19.7% to trade at $71.68, The Block reported.
Ether underperforming bitcoin in a broad selloff is a familiar pattern, but a weaker ETH/BTC relationship on its own does not mean ether is cheap or due to catch up.
CoinGlass hourly data showed crypto liquidations totalled $2.02 billion between 8 a.m.
ET Saturday and 8 a.m.
ET Sunday.
Long positions accounted for $1.68 billion of that, against $342.4 million in shorts.
A liquidation happens when an exchange closes a leveraged trade because the trader’s margin can no longer cover losses, and those forced sales can push prices lower and trigger the next round of liquidations.
The roughly five-to-one skew toward longs shows that traders were leaning bullish with borrowed money going into the drop.
By about 4:30 p.m.
ET Sunday, the live 24-hour tally on CoinGlass had eased to $742.9 million as prices steadied.
Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao used a post on X to deny rumours that the exchange had been selling crypto in the wake of its record hack on Oct.
29.
Zhao said he had personally bought crypto over the past few days using stablecoins he recently received.
He pointed to withdrawals from US spot bitcoin ETFs and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike as possible drivers of the slide, and suggested some investors may be raising cash for Anthropic’s planned IPO.
He also cited lingering security concerns after the Binance hack.
Those explanations are Zhao’s view rather than established causes.
The ETF data does support part of that argument.
US spot bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.91 billion in net outflows across seven straight trading sessions through Friday, The Block reported earlier.
Spot ether ETFs lost $398.9 million last week, their seventh consecutive week of withdrawals and one short of the record run of eight.
Outflows show reduced demand through these products, but they do not by themselves tell us who is selling or why.
What to watch next: the first test is whether bitcoin can hold above the weekend low near $62,000 now that much of the leveraged long exposure has been cleared out.
A halt to the ETF outflow streak, ideally confirmed over several completed sessions, would add evidence that product demand is stabilising.
If spot ether ETFs post an eighth straight week of withdrawals, they would match their record.
One calmer session after a liquidation flush is not proof of a bottom, so a practical approach is to watch both the flow trend and the price response before treating the recovery as durable.

The leading cryptocurrency was trading at around $63,800 on Thursday, down 1% on the day and 13% over the past week, according to Decrypt data.
It has hovered between roughly $63,000 and $65,000 since the weekend, briefly dipping below $63,000 and touching a 24-hour low of $62,068, per CoinGecko data.
"Bitcoin remains under selling pressure," Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, told Decrypt, noting that it has fallen roughly 26% from its late-September peak near $87,000.
"Elevated Treasury yields, dollar strength and expectations of further Fed tightening are weighing on risk appetite, while the broader technology selloff has added to the pressure."
ETF outflows mount
U.S.
spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $306.4 million in net outflows on Wednesday, after $239.9 million on Tuesday, according to SoSoValue data.
The funds have seen outflows on nine of the past 10 trading days, with Monday's small $8 million inflow the only exception, and have lost about $2.9 billion so far in November.
Their total net assets have fallen to $77.7 billion.
Bitcoin miners have added to the selling, with major miners including Riot and MARA selling some of their holdings to fund a shift into AI infrastructure.
Monday's brief inflow "does not signal a market inflection point," Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey, told Decrypt.
Net short positions in Bitcoin futures held by leveraged funds on CME have fallen to their lowest level since early 2023, and futures basis yields have narrowed, he said, indicating that hedge funds have largely unwound the basis trade that paired spot ETF purchases with short futures.
That means the current outflows are mainly driven by investors actively cutting their Bitcoin exposure, Sun said.
"If macro expectations do not improve, investors may shift from buying the dip to selling into rallies, creating additional overhead resistance on subsequent rebounds," he added.
"Recent Bitcoin ETF outflows and leveraged liquidations" have amplified the decline, Hathorn said.
"Despite stronger Nvidia earnings, the market has struggled to stage a significant rebound, suggesting confidence remains fragile.
A sustained recovery may require renewed ETF inflows and a more supportive interest-rate outlook."
Some traders have also pointed the finger at Anthropic's upcoming IPO for drawing money away from crypto, though analysts have disputed that the listing is draining crypto liquidity, attributing it instead to ETF outflows, forced selling and rising interest rates.
Traders see a 90.7% chance that the Fed will raise rates by a quarter point at its December 9 meeting, and a 9.3% chance of a half-point hike, according to CME FedWatch.
The odds of a half-point move have risen from 6.5% a day earlier.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller has called for an even bigger, half-point increase, unless policymakers signal another rise in January.
Levels to watch
Hathorn said $64,000 is the immediate level to watch, followed by support around $62,000 and the psychological $60,000 mark.
A sustained recovery above $66,000 to $68,000 could ease selling pressure, "but the broader trend remains bearish while lower highs persist," she said.
Onchain analytics firm Glassnode said in its weekly report on Tuesday that the crash had pushed investors’ realized losses to levels seen only near past market lows in 2018, 2020, 2022 and early 2023, a sign of capitulation.
Bitcoin is now holding a dense block of recent buyers between $62,000 and $66,000, which grew by about 66,000 BTC during the two days of heaviest selling, Glassnode said.
But a daily close below that block could set off a fast drop toward the June low of $58,500, and the Realized Price, the average price at which all Bitcoin last moved, at $53,700.
Traders on Decrypt Predict see a 43% chance that Bitcoin will fall to $60,000 at some point before the end of November, and a 12% chance that it will drop as low as $55,000.
They give just a 2% chance that it will climb back to $82,500 this month.
There are some signs of support.
About 1.1 million BTC, roughly 5.5% of supply, last changed hands at prices between $60,000 and $64,000, and that band has grown by more than 25,000 BTC in recent days, according to Neil Steinhardt, head of Nexo U.S., in a note shared with Decrypt Wednesday.
A dense base of holders with costs near current prices "can act as a support zone, though it is not a floor," he wrote.
Bitcoin has also held up better than gold.
The amount of gold one Bitcoin buys rose above its 200-day average this week, to about 17.1 ounces, around 40% above its March low, Steinhardt said.

What is Bitcoin?
Bitcoin holds the distinction of being the original cryptocurrency and remains the most widely followed digital coin in 2026.
Its market capitalization is around $1.33 trillion, putting it well ahead of Ethereum—the second-largest cryptocurrency—which has about $233 billion in market value.
Put simply, Bitcoin is a decentralized digital currency.
Rather than being issued or managed by a central bank or government, it runs on a peer-to-peer network.
That setup enables people to send money directly to one another without going through a traditional financial institution.
Many investors view Bitcoin as a possible shield against inflation or as another tool for diversifying their portfolios.
Its growth over the last decade has been remarkable, frequently beating the performance of major stock market indices, which has helped fuel investors’ interest.
However, like most cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin is known for sharp volatility and rapid changes in price.
Bitcoin price history
Since its creation in 2009, Bitcoin’s price action has been anything but boring.
One of the most famous early stories involves software developer Laszlo Hanyecz, who paid 10,000 Bitcoins for pizza; those coins would now be worth more than 668 million dollars.
Over roughly the past decade, Bitcoin has gained more than 15,000%.
That’s an extraordinary rise by any measure.
Yet this performance comes with substantial risk, as cryptocurrencies can be extremely unpredictable.
Bitcoin has endured steep corrections, with declines of tens of thousands of dollars over short periods, but it has also rebounded with powerful rallies.
By the end of 2025, it was trading about 30% below its record high from October of the same year.
What affects Bitcoin’s price?
A number of elements can move Bitcoin’s price, including:
- Investor speculation: As with many high-risk assets, Bitcoin is heavily influenced by what traders think and feel.
Short-term price changes often reflect speculative bets and market buzz more than long-term fundamentals.
- Adoption by major companies: When large, well-known companies embrace Bitcoin or crypto technology, it can support further growth.
For instance, Bitcoin experienced price increases after automakers like Tesla and Ferrari revealed plans to accept Bitcoin as a form of payment.
- Economy: Bitcoin doesn’t respond to inflation reports or Federal Reserve decisions in the same way as more traditional assets like stocks.
Still, it tends to do better when the U.S.
economy is strong, as people with more disposable income may be open to investing in higher-risk assets like crypto.
- Regulatory developments: Because the crypto space is still maturing, rules and regulations are still being developed.
New regulatory actions can unsettle the market and impact Bitcoin’s price, either positively or negatively.
How to buy and invest in Bitcoin
If you’re interested in adding Bitcoin to your portfolio, you have several choices.
Here are some popular ones.
Buy Bitcoin on a cryptocurrency exchange
One direct method is to buy Bitcoin yourself.
This involves opening an account with a cryptocurrency exchange, linking it to your bank, and using your deposited funds to purchase Bitcoin.
Invest in Bitcoin ETFs
If you’d rather not handle crypto directly, you can look at Bitcoin exchange-traded funds.
A Bitcoin ETF holds Bitcoin as its underlying asset, and the fund’s shares trade on regular stock exchanges.
This route lets you avoid managing your own crypto wallet and lowers the risk of losing access to your coins through lost passwords or wallet errors.
Buy crypto stocks
Another investment strategy is to buy shares of companies that are deeply involved in crypto.
These might include tech companies, publicly traded crypto exchanges, or payment processors that integrate Bitcoin.
When these businesses benefit from Bitcoin’s success, their stocks may respond, giving you indirect exposure.
Open a Bitcoin IRA
Retirement savers may consider a Bitcoin IRA.
This type of account works similarly to a traditional or Roth IRA in that it offers tax advantages and the same contribution limits, but it allows you to invest in Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as part of your retirement strategy.
Bitcoin vs.
other cryptocurrencies
Even though Bitcoin gets much of the attention, it’s just one of many cryptocurrencies to consider.
When choosing where to invest, it may also be worth evaluating the following.
- Ethereum: Ethereum is the second-biggest cryptocurrency by market cap.
In contrast to Bitcoin, its primary function is not as a currency but as a decentralized platform that powers applications and smart contracts, making it especially popular among developers.
- Tether: Tether is classified as a “stablecoin” because it is pegged to another asset—in this case, the U.S.
dollar.
As a result, it tends to be less volatile than Bitcoin, though it also offers less potential for big gains.
- XRP: XRP is built for fast and inexpensive cross-border payments, allowing money to move between countries quickly and with relatively low fees.
Crypto coverage from Fortune
See our newsroom’s recent coverage of what’s been happening in the world of crypto:
- Trump’s latest memecoin dinner poised to be a flop as just 130 wallets compete for 185 spots
- Pantera-backed Codex raises $30 million to link Asia to global markets with stablecoins
- Sam Bankman-Fried’s former employer poised for $35 billion windfall
Is it a good time to invest in Bitcoin?
By the standards of long-established blue-chip companies like Walmart, Procter & Gamble, and Coca-Cola, Bitcoin is still fairly young.
That makes it challenging to predict how it will behave far into the future.
Even so, its recent performance has been strong.
As merchants and corporations begin accepting Bitcoin for payments, its price may have room to climb—and as it matures, it could see somewhat less extreme volatility.
That said, you should avoid treating Bitcoin as a sure thing.
Only invest money you won’t need soon, and maintain a diversified portfolio so other assets can help balance any large moves in Bitcoin’s price.
For many people, Bitcoin is best viewed as a long-term, higher-risk holding rather than a short-term speculation.
It may not suit you if you cannot tolerate big price swings.
But if you’re willing to hold through volatility and keep Bitcoin as one component of a diversified portfolio, allocating a portion of your money to it may make sense.
Frequently asked questions
How much will Bitcoin be worth in 2030?
While the answer is obviously unknowable, crypto experts are generally optimistic about the short-term success of Bitcoin.
Some models price it at more than $700,000 by 2030, with conservative estimates closer to $300,000.
What is Bitcoin’s all-time high price?
As of this writing, Bitcoin reached its highest price ever on Oct.
6, 2025, pricing at a whopping $126,198.07.
Can you buy a fraction of a Bitcoin?
Yes, you can buy a fraction of a Bitcoin.
Most cryptocurrency exchanges offer fractional investing, meaning you can buy portions of crypto coins.
Thanks to fractional investing, you can invest in Bitcoin with as little as a few dollars.

What Is Bitcoin (BTC)?
Bitcoin (BTC) is a decentralized cryptocurrency and peer-to-peer payment network launched in 2009 by Satoshi Nakamoto.
Transactions are recorded on a public blockchain, with no central bank issuing the currency.
Bitcoin uses proof-of-work mining and has a protocol-defined supply limit of 21 million BTC.
The block subsidy is halved every 210,000 blocks, approximately every four years.
BTC can be used for digital payments, cross-border transfers and self-custody through cryptocurrency wallets.
How to Read BTC Open Interest, Funding Rates and Long/Short Ratios
Open interest is the total value of futures contracts that are still open.
If price rises while open interest grows, it is usually mostly new longs; if price rises while open interest falls, it is mostly shorts closing.
The funding rate is a fee exchanged periodically between longs and shorts to keep perpetual futures prices close to spot.
When it is positive, longs pay shorts.
The long/short ratio reflects the balance between longs and shorts.
Common types include the taker buy/sell ratio, accounts long/short ratio, top trader long/short ratio (accounts) and top trader long/short ratio (positions); because each is calculated differently, they can't be compared directly.
Read it alongside funding rates and open interest, since on its own it is easy to misread.

Jensen Huang’s Reinstatement Sparks U.S.
Stock Rally as BTC Gives Back Gains to Trade Near $61,000
🔍 Key Takeaways
-
📊 Market Overview
-
U.S.
stocks and precious metals rebounded sharply on Monday following last week’s global asset sell-off.
The Nasdaq rose 6.51%, the S&P 500 gained 4.73%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index advanced approximately 14%.
Gold rebounded around 3% and silver gained approximately 4.6%, recovering some of their earlier losses.
However, newly listed Anthropic fell 1.43%, highlighting continued divergence within the AI sector.
Crypto also benefited from improving risk appetite, with BTC briefly reaching $64,500 before quickly retreating toward $61,000.
ETH also fell back toward $1,700, leaving crypto’s recovery weaker than that of U.S.
equities.
U.S.
spot BTC ETFs recorded approximately $1.79 billion in net outflows last week, their fourth consecutive week of outflows.
Combined with shrinking stablecoin supply and weak U.S.
spot buying, crypto markets still lack sustained fresh capital.
In the near term, watch whether BTC can hold $60,000.
A renewed break below could lead to retests of $58,000 and $55,000.
On the upside, BTC needs to reclaim and hold $63,000–$65,000 to ease downward pressure.
This week’s focus remains on U.S.
PCE inflation, Fed rate-hike expectations and whether the equity rebound can continue.
-
BTC: $61,267.4 (-0.01%); ETH: $1,710.65 (-0.78%); NASDAQ: 24,089.56 (+6.51%); S&P 500: 7,237.90 (+4.74%); Fear & Greed Index: 11 (previously 11).
Data as of November 24, 2026, 00:00 UTC.
-
🧠 Market Insights
-
Jensen Huang’s reinstatement drives a sharp AI-sector rebound, but investigations and valuation pressures remain unresolved.
Nvidia’s board announced on November 23 that Huang would return as CEO and a director, just 11 days after his November 12 resignation amid controversy over personal relationships and potential national security concerns.
The board had previously rejected his return but reversed its decision after Trump publicly supported Huang and intervened in discussions.
It said its assessment found that his return posed no national security risk, while the independent investigation would continue.
Nvidia shares surged 31.48%, their largest single-day gain since 2003, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value and lifting chipmakers, computing infrastructure providers and other AI-related stocks.
The rally underscores investors’ confidence in Huang’s role across the AI industry and shows how sensitive tech stocks have become to positive catalysts following concentrated selling.
However, his return does not resolve Nvidia’s export-control, corporate governance or congressional investigation risks, nor does it directly address questions about returns on massive AI capital spending.
Anthropic’s failure to join the rally also suggests that investors are increasingly distinguishing between valuations for chips and computing infrastructure and those for AI model commercialization.
The near-term rebound has largely been driven by the unexpected announcement and a recovery in confidence.
Its durability will depend on regulatory developments, renewed capital flows into tech stocks and whether earnings can support current valuations.
-
BTC’s rebound is primarily driven by short covering, while continued ETF outflows and shrinking stablecoin supply point to a lack of fresh buying.
BTC recovered rapidly after falling toward $55,000 over the weekend, but derivatives data suggest the rebound was driven more by adjustments in leveraged positions than a meaningful recovery in spot demand.
Wintermute noted that approximately $68.8 million in shorts were liquidated within a single hour on November 21, compared with just $1.6 million in long liquidations, making concentrated short covering an important driver of the recovery.
Meanwhile, U.S.

Crypto week in review: bitcoin's 12% drop, a record IBIT outflow and a 30% slide in Strategy shares
Bitcoin briefly fell to about $55,300 before ending Saturday near $60,100, as ETF withdrawals, liquidations and the AI stock rout weighed on coins and crypto shares.
Key takeaways
- Bitcoin ended the week to Nov.
21 at about $60,100 on CoinGecko, down 12%, after touching about $55,300, its lowest since September 2024.
- US spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $1.25 billion in the week and $3.59 billion in November, with BlackRock's IBIT posting its largest daily outflow.
- Crypto stocks fell with the coins: Strategy lost 30.3%, IREN 34.9%, Bitmine 26.2%, and Coinbase and Robinhood about 20% each.
Bitcoin ended the week to Saturday, Nov.
21, at $60,121 at 7 p.m.
New York time on CoinGecko's prices, down about 12% from $68,314 a week earlier, after falling to about $55,300 early on Saturday, its lowest level since September 2024.
Ether finished at $1,683, about 13% lower, and CoinGecko valued the whole crypto market at about $2.08 trillion.
The week's decline came in stages.
Bitcoin traded above $70,000 early in the week, then fell below $65,000 on Tuesday, $62,000 on Thursday and $60,000 on Friday, Bitcoin.com News reported.
Overnight into Saturday, liquidations of leveraged futures positions topped $2 billion over 24 hours, according to CoinGlass figures cited by Bitcoin.com News and Eurasia Business News, before buyers lifted the price back above $60,000 by the afternoon.
The Crypto Fear and Greed Index from Alternative.me ended the week at 12, in "extreme fear."
Fund investors kept withdrawing.
US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds had about $1.25 billion of net outflows in the week, bringing November's total to about $3.59 billion, according to Farside Investors data reported by Finwire.
BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust lost $541.1 million on Thursday, Nov.
19, its largest daily outflow since its January 2024 launch.
Ether funds lost about $221.7 million in the week.
Stocks tied to crypto fell harder than the coins.
Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, dropped 30.3% to $77.80 in the week to Friday, according to Yahoo Finance prices, and bitcoin now sits about 20% below the company's $75,452 average purchase price.
Coinbase fell 20.1% to $101.97, Robinhood 20.2% to $62.17, stablecoin issuer Circle 23.6% to $47.51 and ether holder Bitmine Immersion Technologies 26.2% to $12.98.
Miners were hit from both sides.
IREN fell 34.9% and MARA Holdings 27.2%, as lower bitcoin prices squeezed mining revenue and the sell-off in AI shares weighed on the data-center businesses miners are building.
Bitcoin's mining difficulty dropped 9.1% at its Nov.
14 adjustment, according to mempool.space.
The broader market set the tone.
Hotter-than-expected October inflation data raised expectations of a Federal Reserve rate increase in December, and the Nasdaq Composite fell about 10% in the week, including 5.3% on Friday, Bitcoin.com News reported.
Market maker Wintermute warned that bitcoin could fall into the $50,000 range without renewed ETF inflows, according to the same report.
Several dates lie ahead.
MSCI is due to remove Strategy from its indexes after Nov.
30, and Strategy has typically reported its weekly bitcoin purchases in Monday SEC filings.
In Europe, crypto firms licensed under MiCA have until Jan.
8, 2027 to clear remaining exposures to stablecoins that do not comply with the rules, crypto.news reported, and the US GENIUS Act stablecoin law and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's rule implementing it take effect on Jan.
18, 2027.
Questions answered
How did crypto markets perform in the week to Nov.
21, 2026?
Bitcoin fell about 12% and ether about 13% on CoinGecko's prices between the evenings of Nov.
13 and Nov.
21, and the total crypto market was valued at about $2.08 trillion on Saturday evening.
What drove the crypto sell-off in November 2026?
Reports pointed to outflows from spot bitcoin ETFs, forced selling of leveraged positions, hotter-than-expected October inflation data that raised bets on a December Fed rate increase, and a sell-off in AI stocks that pushed the Nasdaq down about 10% for the week.
What crypto events are coming up?
Strategy is due to drop out of MSCI's indexes after Nov.
30, the EU deadline for clearing non-MiCA stablecoin exposures is Jan.
8, 2027, and the US GENIUS Act stablecoin law takes effect on Jan.
18, 2027.

Bitcoin ETFs flip negative for 2026 after $1.28 billion outflow week, worst since June
The 12 U.S.-listed spot bitcoin funds have now lost $914.1 million for the year, while ether, Solana and Hyperliquid ETFs all extended weekly outflow streaks in a brutal turn for crypto ETFs.
Quick Take
- U.S.
spot bitcoin ETFs saw $1.28 billion in net outflows last week, their worst weekly sum since late June.
- The outflows left bitcoin ETFs with about $914.1 million in net outflows for 2026, reversing their year-to-date gains.
- BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for 88% of Friday’s gross outflows, with $403 million leaving the industry-leading fund.
- Spot ether ETFs lost $365.3 million, their sixth consecutive negative week.
- Solana and Hyperliquid ETFs each logged a fifth straight week of outflows, the longest streaks for both types of funds since they each began trading.
U.S.
spot bitcoin ETFs logged $1.28 billion in net outflows last week, their worst week since late June, per The Block's analysis of SoSoValue data.
It was the funds' second straight negative week and made the top ten largest weekly outflows since they launched in January 2024 at #7.
The funds saw outflows every day except Wednesday last week, per the data.
They lost $398.6 million on Monday, $115.6 million on Tuesday, $430.2 million on Thursday and $411.9 million on Friday, with Wednesday's relatively modest $74.6 million inflow marking the only positive day.
The most recent worse week ended June 26, when the funds shed $1.79 billion in what The Block reported at the time was their second-worst week on record.
Bitcoin ETFs lost $202.6 million the week before last, including a $643.3 million Friday outflow that was the largest single-day exit in four months after the record Binance hack.
BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $403 million of Friday's loss, or about 88% of the day's gross outflows.
Bitwise's BITB and Ark & 21Shares' ARKB each lost about $20 million, and Grayscale's GBTC shed $11.1 million.
Fidelity's FBTC took in $42.8 million on Friday, after leading Thursday's outflows with $199.9 million, as The Block reported.
Bitcoin funds turn negative for 2026
The week's outflows erased bitcoin ETFs' gains for the year.
The funds entered the week with about $368 million in 2026 net inflows, after turning positive for the year in late September.
Monday's outflows pushed that figure below zero, and the funds closed Friday at about $914.1 million in net outflows year to date.
The total value of bitcoin held across the 12 funds dropped 2.3% to $95.9 billion, equal to about 6.3% of the cryptocurrency's market capitalization.
IBIT held $60.3 billion in net assets against $65.1 billion in cumulative inflows.
The outflows came amid a crypto and equities selloff after Tuesday's midterm elections.
Bitcoin fell 5.6% on Thursday alone, and analysts linked the slide to the Democratic sweep of Congress and doubts over AI spending, The Block reported Friday.
Analysts say Texas's blue wave in particular could result in slowed development in the state replete with bitcoin mining facilities and data centers.
Ether funds extend losing run to six weeks
Spot ether ETFs lost $365.3 million last week, per SoSoValue data, their sixth straight week of net outflows.
The run has drained about $2.02 billion from the funds since late September.
Ether ETFs have twice posted eight-week losing streaks, most recently when they matched that record in early July.
Like the bitcoin funds, ether ETFs had only one positive trading day last week, also on Wednesday, when they gained $53 million.
Monday's $139.8 million outflow was the week's largest, followed by $100 million on Thursday and $93.2 million on Friday.
BlackRock's ETHA accounted for $90.8 million of Friday's total, about 96% of the gross losses, mirroring the firm's bitcoin fund.
The products are now down about $405.6 million for 2026.
Net assets fell 2.9% over the week to $12.84 billion, against $11.92 billion in cumulative net inflows.
Solana, Hyperliquid funds post longest outflow runs
Spot Solana ETFs lost $26.3 million last week, per SoSoValue, nearly all of it on Friday.
It was their fifth straight negative week, the longest streak since the funds launched in October 2025, and brought five-week outflows to $165.4 million.
The streak began the week the funds ended a record 14-week inflow run.
Bitwise's BSOL led Friday's Solana outflows with $14.4 million, followed by Grayscale's GSOL at $5.4 million.
The funds held $1.31 billion in net assets as of Friday, down from $1.40 billion a week earlier, though they remain about $676.2 million positive for the year.
The three publicly traded Hyperliquid ETFs shed $15.6 million, also extending their outflow streak to five weeks, the longest since they began trading in May.
The funds have lost $58.4 million over that stretch, and their net assets fell about 17% on the week to $374.1 million.
Friday's $8 million outflow was led by Bitwise's BHYP.
Bitcoin traded near $75,880 on Saturday morning, while ether changed hands around $2,244, SOL near $89.84 and HYPE around $77.79, according to The Block's price pages.
